The UK evidence pointed one way all week. A labour market softening on every measure that matters to the Bank of England (Tuesday), inflation exactly on forecast at 2.9% with the rise coming from gas (Wednesday), manufacturing orders fifteen points better than expected (Thursday), and retail sales matching forecast on the headline while missing on everything underneath (Friday). An intervention that must be repeated within a day tells you about the strength of what it is pushing against.

The week in numbers. PWLB standard maturity, Monday's 315/26 to Friday's 324/26: 5-year 5.57% → 5.61% (+4bp), 10-year 6.07% → 6.11% (+4bp), 20-year 6.62% → 6.66% (+4bp), 50-year 6.50% → 6.53% (+3bp). Ten rounds, all inside eight basis points.

The 1-year SONIA swap went 4.127% Monday to 4.142% Friday, 1.5bp higher: even rate expectations finished up after a week of data arguing the opposite. Bank Rate 3.75%, the next move still priced as 25bp in November.

Monday's round would come in level with 324/26 — Friday's close finished within two tenths of a basis point of the market at the moment that round was struck. Policymakers still work to a 'safe-debt' model; investors have stopped.

It earns your time because his central warning is exactly the manoeuvre we watched: that intervention risks suppressing the market signal fiscal policymakers rely on to judge sustainability. Every rate we reported this week was set by the global market in government debt rather than by anything the UK published, and the largest single move came from a US debt-management decision. It is also a useful counterweight to the assumption that an intervention which calms a market has solved something.

We read seven candidates. Six did not qualify — four published outside the week under review, two unreadable without a login. We never pad.

The week ahead. Monday brings the first round and the German Ifo survey (forecast 87.2 against 86.6). Wednesday 13:30 brings US core PCE, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, forecast 0.2% against 0.1%. Nothing major on the UK calendar early. That the US figure is the release most likely to move UK borrowing costs is the week's lesson in one line.

Every significant UK number this week argued for cheaper borrowing, and borrowing got dearer anyway. A softening labour market, inflation exactly on forecast, the best manufacturing orders survey in months and a consumer visibly pulling back — and ten-year PWLB borrowing still ended the week 4bp higher at 6.11%. The deciding factor was somebody else’s debt.
THE WEEK

Monday opened with the previous week’s damage still on the board and the 10-year maturity rate at 6.07%. By Tuesday morning it was 6.15% — the week’s high, and it arrived overnight on nothing domestic at all. That set the pattern: the moves that mattered happened while London slept.

The UK evidence pointed one way all week. Tuesday’s labour market data softened on every measure that matters to the Bank of England. Wednesday’s inflation figure landed exactly on forecast at 2.9%, and the rise came from gas rather than anything persistent. Thursday brought manufacturing orders fifteen points better than expected. Friday brought retail sales that matched forecast on the headline and missed on every measure underneath it — annual growth more than halved, sales excluding fuel down nearly twice as much as expected.

None of it set the price. Ten-year borrowing ended the week 4bp above where it opened. On Thursday the clearest illustration of the whole week: manufacturing orders beat forecast by fifteen points and gilt yields eased in the quarter-hour afterwards. We reported the figure and the price separately, because joining them would have been invention.

What did set the price was the global market in government debt. The German 10-year spent the week at a 15-year high, the US 30-year at levels last seen in 2007, and by Friday’s close US 10-year borrowing costs were reported approaching a 20-month high.

The exception proves it. On Wednesday afternoon the US Treasury announced bond buybacks and the Treasury Secretary intervened publicly to steady the market. It produced the best move of our week — the whole curve 5.6 to 6.4bp lower within a quarter of an hour, and the relief stuck at long maturities, which is where a buyback programme buys. By Thursday’s close the market it started in had given all of it back, and the Treasury Secretary was talking about intervening again: ‘we have a big tool kit’. An intervention that has to be repeated within a day tells you about the strength of what it is pushing against.

Two things built underneath all of it. Energy escalated — Brent above $93, European gas reported doubled with worse expected, US sanctions on Iran widened, and energy is precisely what took UK inflation from 2.6% to 2.9% this month. And the public finances deteriorated, with Friday bringing an unexpected £1.8bn deficit ahead of the new Chancellor’s first Budget — a question about how much the government must borrow, and therefore about long-dated borrowing costs.

Rate expectations and the Bank Rate path:

  • 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year — 4.127% Monday, 4.142% Friday: 1.5bp higher. Even rate expectations finished the week up, after a week of data arguing the opposite.
  • Bank Rate 3.75%, unchanged, with the next move still priced as a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%. Nothing this week moved it.
  • Monday’s round — notice 324/26 was struck at Friday 12:06 and Friday’s close finished within two tenths of a basis point of the market at that moment. On that comparison Monday’s round would come in level with the rate in force. We are quoting the direct comparison rather than our usual modelled estimate, which did not behave this week and which we have set aside rather than publish.

A weekend stands in front of that, and this week’s two largest moves both arrived overnight. Treat it as a starting point, not a plan.

WORTH YOUR TIME

Hanno Lustig, ‘America’s Risky Debt: What Markets See That Policymakers Don’t’ — Aspen Institute Economic Strategy Group, published Thursday 20 August 2026. Free to download, no registration.

The argument: for decades global investors paid a premium for the safety and liquidity of US Treasury debt, and that premium has eroded. Lustig sets out three market signals — Treasuries no longer pricing at an advantage to comparable high-grade corporate debt, the old negative correlation between stocks and bonds having reversed so Treasuries no longer behave as a haven in stress, and foreign reserve managers trimming dollar holdings. Policymakers, he argues, still work to a ‘safe-debt’ model; bond investors have stopped.

Why it earns your time this week specifically. On Wednesday we watched the US Treasury intervene to steady its own bond market, and on Thursday we watched the entire effect disappear while the Treasury Secretary talked about doing it again. Lustig’s central warning is precisely about that manoeuvre: that central bank and Treasury intervention risks suppressing the very market signal fiscal policymakers rely on to judge whether the debt is sustainable. He proposes clearer criteria for what counts as market dysfunction, and a Fed–Treasury accord limiting when intervention is allowed.

For a treasurer this is not American trivia. Every rate we reported this week was set by the global market in government debt rather than by anything the UK published, and the single largest move of the week came from a US debt-management decision. This is the clearest recent account of why that market has become so sensitive — and it is a useful counterweight to the assumption, built into a lot of commentary, that an intervention that calms a market has solved something.

We read seven candidates this week. Six did not qualify — four were published outside the week under review, however good (a Bank of England decomposition of last year’s long-rate moves, a NIESR piece on the shortening of gilt issuance, an asset manager’s weekly, and an IPPR analysis), and two could not be read in full without a login. Only work published during the week under review and freely readable goes in, and we never pad.
THE WEEK AHEAD
  • Monday — the week’s first round, and notice 324/26 holds until it. 09:00 brings the German Ifo business survey, forecast 87.2 against 86.6.
  • Wednesday 13:30 — US core PCE price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation measure, forecast 0.2% on the month against 0.1%. Durable goods orders alongside it, forecast 0.7%.
  • Nothing major on the UK calendar in the first half of the week.

The US core PCE figure is the release most likely to move UK borrowing costs, which is itself the week’s lesson in one line. On a week when the UK published its inflation rate, its labour market and its retail sales, the rate that a British council pays was set in Washington and Berlin.

An empty domestic calendar has not meant a quiet week at any point this month. The two largest moves we reported both arrived overnight, from abroad, on days with nothing scheduled at home.

More

The market took the message and then let it go. A weak consumer is a disinflationary signal and the market priced it, twice — through the morning and again from 12:20. By the close most of it had gone: 2-year 4.347% (1.7bp below yesterday), 5-year 4.584% (0.9bp), 10-year 5.062% (0.2bp), 20-year 5.727% (0.1bp above), 30-year 5.807% (0.7bp above), 50-year 5.359% (0.2bp above).

The clearest measure is the 1-year SONIA swap: 3.1bp below yesterday at its low, 1.0bp below at the close. Two-thirds of the day's repricing returned within four hours. This was the week's strongest domestic argument for cheaper borrowing and its effect on the price lasted an afternoon — the same lesson Wednesday taught from the other direction, when a US intervention drove the best move of the week and was fully unwound inside a day.

Both rounds were struck on the market's higher side. 323/26 contained the retail sales figure and not the surveys, which landed twenty-four minutes after it struck. 324/26 was set at 12:06, fourteen minutes before the sharpest fall of the day, and carries none of it — the earliest of the week's five lunchtime rounds. Neither captured the afternoon; but with the close back near where 324/26 was fixed, the round in force is now within a basis point of the market and the gap has closed on its own.

Tonight's sheet: 5.31% / 5.61% / 6.11% / 6.66% / 6.74% / 6.53% at 2, 5, 10, 20, 25 and 50 years, 20bp lower on each with the certainty discount.

The week: ten rounds inside eight basis points, ending 4bp dearer than it opened. 6.07% Monday morning, 6.15% at Tuesday's high — made overnight, on nothing domestic — and 6.11% tonight. The domestic data argued for cheaper borrowing almost all week and did not get it: a labour market softening on every measure, inflation exactly on forecast, a CBI orders survey fifteen points better than expected, and today a consumer plainly pulling back. The direction was set abroad, by the German 10-year at a 15-year high and the US 30-year at levels last seen in 2007.

Three things carry into next week. The global sell-off is unresolved — Wednesday's US intervention bought one day and the Treasury Secretary is talking about intervening again. Energy is escalating — Brent above $93, European gas reported doubled, US sanctions on Iran widened this week, and energy is what took UK inflation from 2.6% to 2.9%. And the public finances have deteriorated ahead of the new Chancellor's first Budget, which is a question about gilt supply and therefore about long-dated borrowing costs.

Monday brings the German Ifo business survey, forecast 87.2 against 86.6; Wednesday the US core PCE price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, forecast 0.2% on the month against 0.1%. Nothing major on the UK calendar early in the week — which on this week's evidence does not mean quiet, since the two largest moves we reported both arrived overnight from abroad on days with nothing domestic scheduled.

324/26 stands until Monday morning. Bank Rate 3.75%, the path still showing 25bp in November.

THE MARKET TOOK THE MESSAGE AND THEN LET IT GO

Weak consumer spending is a disinflationary signal, and the market priced it: through the morning and again from 12:20 the whole curve fell, and the 2-year — the maturity that responds most directly to what the Bank of England is expected to do — reached 5.0bp below yesterday at 13:45.

By the close most of that had gone. Against yesterday: 2-year 4.347% (1.7bp below), 5-year 4.584% (0.9bp), 10-year 5.062% (0.2bp), 20-year 5.727% (0.1bp above), 30-year 5.807% (0.7bp above), 50-year 5.359% (0.2bp above).

The clearest measure is the 1-year SONIA swap — the best read on what markets expect the Bank to do over the coming year. It was 3.1bp below yesterday at its low and ends 1.0bp below. Two-thirds of the day’s repricing was returned within four hours.

Why that matters more than the day’s numbers. This was the week’s strongest domestic argument for cheaper borrowing, and its effect on the price lasted an afternoon. That is the same lesson Wednesday taught from the other direction, when a US intervention drove the best move of the week and was fully unwound inside a day.

BOTH ROUNDS, AND WHERE THEY LANDED

Standard maturity rates as they stand tonight, certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside:

  • 2-year 5.31% standard — 5.11% certainty
  • 5-year 5.61% standard — 5.41% certainty
  • 10-year 6.11% standard — 5.91% certainty
  • 20-year 6.66% standard — 6.46% certainty
  • 25-year 6.74% standard — 6.54% certainty
  • 50-year 6.53% standard — 6.33% certainty

323/26 contained the retail sales figure and not the surveys, which landed twenty-four minutes after it struck. 324/26 was set at 12:06, fourteen minutes before the sharpest fall of the day began, and carries none of it — the earliest of the week’s five lunchtime rounds, the others having been set between 12:16 and 12:32.

So both rounds were struck on the market’s higher side and neither captured the afternoon. Against the market at the moment 324/26 was set, gilt yields spent most of the afternoon 1.4 to 2.9bp lower — but with the close back near where the round was fixed, the round in force is now within a basis point of the market and the gap has closed on its own.

THE WEEK

The 10-year maturity rate, all ten rounds:

  • Monday — 315/26 6.07%, 316/26 6.08%
  • Tuesday — 317/26 6.15%, 318/26 6.13%
  • Wednesday — 319/26 6.10%, 320/26 6.11%
  • Thursday — 321/26 6.10%, 322/26 6.11%
  • Friday — 323/26 6.10%, 324/26 6.11%

Ten rounds inside eight basis points, and the week ends 4bp dearer than it opened. Tuesday morning was the high and it was made overnight, on nothing domestic. Nothing in the following seven rounds returned to Monday’s 6.07%.

The domestic data argued for cheaper borrowing almost all week and did not get it. A labour market that softened on every measure, inflation exactly on forecast, a CBI orders survey fifteen points better than expected, and today a consumer plainly pulling back. Borrowing still ended dearer, because the direction was set by government borrowing costs abroad — the German 10-year at a 15-year high, the US 30-year at levels last seen in 2007.

The one number that moved on domestic news and held some of it is the 1-year SONIA swap, 1.0bp lower on the day. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the path still shows a 25bp rise in November to 4.00% — unchanged by anything this week produced.

WHAT CARRIES INTO NEXT WEEK
  • The global sell-off is not resolved. Wednesday’s US buyback intervention bought one day; by Thursday’s close yields had given it all back and the Treasury Secretary was talking about intervening again. That question reopens on Monday.
  • Energy is escalating. Brent above $93, European gas reported doubled with worse expected, US sanctions on Iran widened this week. Energy is what took UK inflation from 2.6% to 2.9% this month, so this is the direct route into next month’s figure.
  • The public finances have deteriorated. An unexpected £1.8bn deficit this morning, ahead of the new Chancellor’s first Budget. That is a question about how much the government needs to borrow, which is a question about long-dated borrowing costs.

The calendar is quiet at the start and busier midweek. Monday brings the German Ifo business survey, forecast 87.2 against 86.6. Wednesday brings the US core PCE price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation measure, forecast 0.2% on the month against 0.1%, alongside durable goods orders.

Nothing major on the UK calendar in the first half of the week. On this week’s evidence that does not mean quiet: the two largest moves we reported both arrived overnight, from abroad, on days with nothing domestic scheduled.

324/26 stands until Monday morning — 6.11% on the 10-year, 5.91% with the certainty discount, 6.53% on the 50-year.

The 2-year's 4.8bp fall is its largest single day of the week, and it is the maturity that responds most directly to what the Bank of England is expected to do. The 1-year SONIA swap sits at 4.121%, 3.0bp below yesterday. Together they say the market has spent today repricing the path for Bank Rate, and has kept doing so through the afternoon.

For a borrower this changes nothing that can be acted on today. Notice 324/26 — 6.11% on the 10-year, 5.91% with the certainty discount, 6.53% at 50 years — was struck at 12:06 and stands until Monday morning. Measured against the market at the moment it was set, gilt yields are now 2.2 to 2.9bp lower across the curve. There is no further round this week to pick that up.

What it does is set up Monday. A weekend stands between here and the next round, and on this week's evidence the overnight gaps have been larger than anything the trading days produced — Tuesday's 7bp rise arrived that way. We will not carry that gap forward as an expectation.

Two of our twenty-four news sources are not responding this pass. Nothing material is missing and the position is unchanged; we note it because we would rather say so than not.

TODAY: TWO UK RELEASES, FOUR TURNS, NO NET CHANGE IN THE RATE

Today produced the clearest domestic argument of the week for cheaper borrowing and the clearest against, within two and a half hours of each other.

  • 07:00 retail sales — monthly on forecast at −0.5%, and everything underneath weaker: annual growth 1.6% against 2.2% expected, sales excluding fuel down 0.9% against 0.5%, last month revised down
  • 09:30 flash surveys — services 52.8 against 51.8 expected, composite 52.5 against 51.6, manufacturing exactly on forecast at 51.5

The market turned four times: down into the open, up on a euro area growth surprise at 08:30, down from 09:25 through the UK surveys, back up between 10:15 and 11:14, and down hard from 12:20. Both of today’s rounds came out at 6.11% on the 10-year regardless.

The one number that moved decisively is the 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year. It is 4.121%, 3.1bp below yesterday and the largest single-day move in it this week. Rate expectations took the retail sales message and kept it through a strong services survey. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the path still shows a 25bp rise in November to 4.00%.

More

The substance of that report is unaffected. Every other timestamp in it is a live print, and the finding it rested on — that yields began falling at about 09:25, before the 09:30 surveys, and continued through them — sits entirely outside the static window. The report is not being rewritten; this correction stands alongside it.

What we cannot give you today. Our estimate of the next round works by anchoring to the market as it stood when the current round was set. That anchor does not exist for 323/26: the only prices we hold for 09:06 are a repeat of 09:03:54. The engine suppresses the estimate rather than anchoring to a stale reading, which is the right behaviour, and it will stay suppressed for this round for the rest of the day. There will be no figure for the lunchtime round in any edition today. We would rather say that than publish a number with a false anchor.

What we can give you instead, which needs no anchor. The annuity sheet moved further at short maturities, down 2bp at 2 years. Yesterday morning's round tilted one way and this one tilts the other — 321/26 took 3bp off borrowing over twenty years while adding one at two; 323/26 does the reverse.

This round contains the retail sales figure and not the surveys. Retail sales reached us at 07:00, the round struck at 09:06, the purchasing managers' surveys landed at 09:30. Only the first is in this price.

The two releases point opposite ways. Retail sales matched forecast on the headline and missed underneath — annual growth 1.6% against 2.2%, sales excluding fuel down 0.9% against 0.5% expected, last month revised down. Then services activity came in at 52.8 against 51.8 expected, up from 52.1, with manufacturing exactly on forecast at 51.5 and the composite 52.5 against 51.6. Services is roughly four-fifths of the economy: households are buying less while the larger part of the economy speeds up. A weak consumer argues for cheaper borrowing; a strengthening services sector argues against.

Yields fell afterwards, and not because of the surveys. The 10-year against yesterday's close: 09:06 0.2bp below as the round struck · 09:14 level, the morning's high · 09:25 0.1bp below · 09:29 0.9bp below · 09:30 1.2bp below as the surveys landed · 09:43 1.8bp below. The fall began before publication and continued through it, and its direction is the opposite of what a strong services reading would ordinarily produce. We report the move and do not have a cause for it.

Last prints: 2-year 4.334% (2.9bp below yesterday), 5-year 4.571% (2.2bp), 10-year 5.046% (1.8bp), 20-year 5.711% (1.5bp), 30-year 5.788% (1.2bp), 50-year 5.342% (1.4bp). The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.134%, 1.7bp below yesterday and falling steadily since 07:00 — the retail sales message, which the surveys have not reversed.

For the afternoon. When 323/26 was set, the 30-year stood 0.5bp above yesterday's close; it is now 1.2bp below. The market has moved in the borrower's favour by roughly one and a half to two basis points at every maturity since the round struck. We are not putting a figure on the lunchtime round in this edition — our estimate re-bases onto each new round and has not yet settled onto this one, and publishing a number before it has would be inventing precision we do not have. The next edition will carry it.

What can be said without it: the afternoon round will be set on a lower market and will be the first to contain the surveys. Unlike the rest of this week, today gives a genuine choice between the two rounds, and on the morning's evidence waiting has a case.

Nine rounds this week inside eight basis points, and ten-year borrowing 4bp dearer than it opened Monday. Bank Rate 3.75%, the path still showing 25bp in November. The lunchtime round is the last of the week.

THE MORNING ROUND — NOTICE 323/26

Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against yesterday’s final round:

  • 2-year 5.31% standard — 5.11% certainty — down 1bp
  • 5-year 5.62% standard — 5.42% certainty — unchanged
  • 10-year 6.11% standard — 5.91% certainty — unchanged
  • 20-year 6.66% standard — 6.46% certainty — up 1bp
  • 25-year 6.74% standard — 6.54% certainty — up 1bp
  • 50-year 6.54% standard — 6.34% certainty — up 1bp

The annuity sheet moved further at the short end, down 2bp at 2 years and 1bp at 5.

Yesterday morning’s round tilted one way and this one tilts the other. 321/26 took 3bp off borrowing over twenty years and more while adding a basis point at two. 323/26 does the reverse. Two tilted rounds in two days, in opposite directions, on a curve that has spent the week being pulled from both ends.

TWO UK RELEASES, POINTING OPPOSITE WAYS

07:00 — retail sales. The monthly figure matched forecast at −0.5% and everything underneath missed: annual growth 1.6% against 2.2% expected and 3.8% before, sales excluding fuel down 0.9% against 0.5% expected, the annual rate excluding fuel more than halving to 2.3%. Last month was revised down as well.

09:30 — the flash purchasing managers’ surveys. Manufacturing landed exactly on forecast at 51.5. Services came in at 52.8 against 51.8 expected, up from 52.1 — a full point above forecast and an acceleration. The composite reading is 52.5 against 51.6. Above 50 means growth.

Services is roughly four-fifths of the UK economy, so that is the more consequential of the two surveys, and it argues the opposite of the retail figure: households are buying less while the larger part of the economy is speeding up.

For a borrower the tension is real rather than academic. A weak consumer argues for the Bank of England to move towards cheaper money, which pulls borrowing costs down. A strengthening services sector argues against, which pushes them up. Today has produced both before lunchtime, and the morning round was struck between them.

YIELDS FELL AFTERWARDS, AND NOT BECAUSE OF THE SURVEYS

The 10-year gilt against yesterday’s close, minute by minute through the fixing window:

  • 09:06 — 0.2bp below, as the round struck
  • 09:14 — level, the morning’s high
  • 09:25 — 0.1bp below
  • 09:29 — 0.9bp below
  • 09:30 — 1.2bp below, as the surveys landed
  • 09:43 — 1.8bp below

The fall began before the surveys were published and continued through them. That matters twice over: we cannot attribute it to the release, and the direction is the opposite of what a strong services reading would ordinarily produce. We report the move and we do not have a cause for it.

At the last prints to reach us: 2-year 4.334% (2.9bp below yesterday), 5-year 4.571% (2.2bp), 10-year 5.046% (1.8bp), 20-year 5.711% (1.5bp), 30-year 5.788% (1.2bp), 50-year 5.342% (1.4bp). Every maturity is lower, and shorter ones are lower by more — the same shape the whole day has had.

The 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year — is 4.134%, 1.7bp below yesterday and falling steadily since 07:00. That is the retail sales message, and the surveys have not reversed it.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE AFTERNOON

When 323/26 was set at 09:06, longer-dated gilt yields stood slightly above yesterday’s close — the 30-year 0.5bp above. They are now 1.2bp below. The market has moved in the borrower’s favour by roughly one and a half to two basis points since the round struck, at every maturity.

We are not putting a figure on the lunchtime round in this edition. Our estimate re-bases onto each new round and has not yet settled onto this one; publishing a number before it has would be inventing precision we do not have. The next edition will carry it.

What can be said without it: the afternoon round will be set on a market that is lower than the one this round was set on, and it will be the first round to contain the surveys. Unlike the rest of this week, today gives a borrower a genuine choice between the two rounds — and on the morning’s evidence, waiting has a case.

THE WEEK ON ONE RATE

The 10-year maturity rate, round by round:

  • 315/26, Monday 09:05 — 6.07%
  • 316/26, Monday 12:22 — 6.08%
  • 317/26, Tuesday 09:09 — 6.15%
  • 318/26, Tuesday 12:32 — 6.13%
  • 319/26, Wednesday 09:04 — 6.10%
  • 320/26, Wednesday 12:16 — 6.11%
  • 321/26, Thursday 09:10 — 6.10%
  • 322/26, Thursday 12:22 — 6.11%
  • 323/26, Friday 09:06 — 6.11%

Nine rounds inside eight basis points, and the week 4bp dearer than it opened. Tuesday morning was the high and nothing since has come back to Monday’s level. The 50-year tells a slightly different story: 6.52% yesterday morning, 6.53% yesterday afternoon, 6.54% now, creeping up while the 10-year sits still.

Bank Rate is 3.75% and the path still shows a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%, unchanged by either of this morning’s releases. The lunchtime round is the last of the week.

Plain-English key: bp = basis point, 0.01% · fix / fixing = the twice-daily setting of PWLB borrowing rates · implied next fix = our model's estimate of where the next fixing would land if markets held · gilts = UK government bonds, the base PWLB rates are built on · OIS / Bank Rate path = what markets currently expect the Bank of England to do.
09:19PULSEpulse

AM fixing call — a big euro area growth surprise has pulled longer-dated borrowing costs back up. The case for this round has halved at 50 years since 08:16 and held at 2 years

PWLB 10y — in force6.11%PWLB 10y — certainty5.91%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.099% (-1.1bp)1y SONIA swap4.141% (-1.1bp)

This morning's rates have not reached us. Notice 322/26, struck yesterday at 12:22, is still the standing price — 6.11% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.91% with the certainty discount.

More

08:30 — euro area flash manufacturing survey came in at 54.1, against 52.0 expected and 52.2 last month. That is a two-point beat on forecast and the strongest reading in this series for some time. A growth surprise on the continent lifts government borrowing costs across Europe, and gilts go with them.

The market turned within minutes of it. The 10-year gilt against yesterday's close: 08:16 0.3bp below, 08:35 0.7bp below — the low — then 0.1bp below at 09:00 and level at 09:14. The 30-year has swung furthest, from 0.3bp below at 08:35 to 0.9bp above now, a 1.2bp move in forty minutes. We report the sequence and note it is consistent with the euro area figure; we are not claiming more than that.

At the last prints to reach us: 2-year 4.350% (1.3bp below yesterday), 5-year 4.589% (0.4bp), 10-year 5.064% (level), 20-year 5.731% (0.5bp above), 30-year 5.809% (0.9bp above), 50-year 5.362% (0.6bp above).

What that does to the round, and it is uneven:

- 2-year about 5.296% — 2.4bp below the rate in force, from 2.3bp at 08:16 - 5-year about 5.600% — 2.0bp below, from 2.3bp - 10-year about 6.099% — 1.1bp below, from 1.5bp - 20-year about 6.643% — 0.7bp below, from 1.3bp - 50-year about 6.524% — 0.6bp below, from 1.3bp

The long-dated case has halved in an hour; the short-dated case has held. For a borrower placing short-dated money this round still carries a real advantage. At 20 and 50 years it is now down to sub-basis-point noise of the kind we have spent the week declining to act on.

The 1-year SONIA swap has fallen further to 4.141%, 1.1bp below yesterday — rate expectations continue to take the retail sales message even as longer-dated costs go the other way.

09:30 — the UK flash purchasing managers' surveys, forecast 51.5 manufacturing and 51.8 services. They land after this round strikes and reach the afternoon one. On the euro area reading just seen, the risk to those forecasts is to the upside.

08:20PULSEpulse

The open took the retail sales message at shorter maturities and ignored it at longer ones — the 2-year is 1.2bp lower and the 30-year is higher. This morning's round now looks 2.3bp below the rate in force at 2 and 5 years, 1.3bp at 50

PWLB 10y — in force6.11%PWLB 10y — certainty5.91%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.095% (-1.5bp)1y SONIA swap4.145% (-0.7bp)

The market has answered the retail sales figure, and it has answered it selectively. Against yesterday's close at the last prints to reach us: 2-year 4.351% (1.2bp below), 5-year 4.587% (0.7bp), 10-year 5.061% (0.4bp), 20-year 5.725% (0.1bp), 30-year 5.803% — 0.2bp above, 50-year 5.355% (0.1bp below).

More

The 2-year and the 30-year moved in opposite directions this morning, and that is the whole picture in one line. Shorter maturities respond to what the Bank of England is expected to do, and a weak consumer argues for cheaper money; the 1-year SONIA swap has fallen 0.7bp to 4.145% with them. Longer-dated borrowing costs respond to government supply — and this morning also brought an unexpected £1.8bn deficit in the public finances, reported as a pre-Budget challenge for the new Chancellor. The two releases pull the curve apart rather than together.

This reverses the week's pattern. Since Wednesday the gap between the rate in force and the next round has widened the longer the borrowing. On the market at 08:16 it is the other way round: the morning round would come in about 5.297% at 2 years and 5.597% at 5 — 2.3bp below 322/26 in both cases — against 6.095% at 10 years (1.5bp), 6.637% at 20 (1.3bp) and 6.517% at 50 (1.3bp).

For a borrower that inverts where the case for this round is strongest. Short-dated drawdowns have the better of it this morning; long-dated ones have about the same basis point they had last night.

09:30 — the flash purchasing managers' surveys, forecast 51.5 manufacturing and 51.8 services. As set out this morning, they land after the round strikes and reach the afternoon one only.

07:24STORYbrief

Retail sales matched forecast on the headline and missed on everything underneath — annual growth more than halved to 1.6%, ex-fuel sales fell 0.9% against 0.5% expected. The first UK release this week that argues clearly for cheaper borrowing

PWLB 10y — in force6.11%PWLB 10y — certainty5.91%PWLB 10y — est (last night)6.099% (-1.1bp)1y SONIA swap4.152%

Correction to yesterday's end-of-day edition. It said both of today's UK releases land before the morning round. That is right for retail sales at 07:00 and wrong for the purchasing managers' surveys at 09:30, which come after it — every round this week has struck between 09:04 and 09:10. The surveys can reach the afternoon round only. Today therefore offers a real choice between the two rounds, which this week has not otherwise provided.

More

Retail sales — actual / forecast / previous:

- Monthly −0.5% / −0.5% / 0.7% - Annual 1.6% / 2.2% / 3.8% - Monthly excluding fuel −0.9% / −0.5% / 0.9% - Annual excluding fuel 2.3% / 3.3% / 5.0%

Only the first line matched. Annual growth came in more than half a point below forecast and at less than half the previous month's rate. Excluding fuel — the cleaner read on whether households are buying more — sales fell nearly twice as much as expected on the month and the annual rate more than halved. Last month was also revised down, from a 1.0% monthly rise to 0.7%.

Alongside it, consumer confidence improved to −14 from −17, where −18 was expected. Households report feeling better and are spending less; the spending is the harder number.

Why it matters to a borrower. Weaker consumer spending is a disinflationary signal, which argues for cheaper borrowing across the curve. It is the first UK release this week to point that way. Set against it: Monday to Thursday produced inflation exactly on forecast, a labour market softening on every measure and a CBI orders survey beating by fifteen points — and ten-year borrowing still ended Thursday 4bp above where it opened Monday, because the direction has been set abroad. The gilt market opens at 08:00 and we will not infer a reaction before it does.

Overnight is still going the wrong way. Japanese inflation came in at 1.9% against 1.7% expected and Japanese 10-year yields tracked US yields higher, after a Thursday on which US yields gave back the whole of Wednesday's buyback relief and the German 10-year held at a 15-year high.

Notice 322/26 stands at 6.11% on the 10-year, 5.91% certainty, 6.53% at 50 years. On last night's close the morning round would come in about a basis point below across the curve: 2-year 5.309%, 5-year 5.604%, 10-year 6.099%, 20-year 6.638%, 50-year 6.518%. That estimate contains none of this morning's retail sales. And yesterday is worth carrying: the advantage stood at about 3bp at 16:20 and closed at about 1bp, because yields rose through the final hour. A gap measured at a close is not a gap a borrower can bank.

08:30 euro area flash manufacturing survey, forecast 52.0. 09:30 UK flash surveys, forecast 51.5 manufacturing, 51.8 services, 51.6 composite — all forecast to slow while staying above the 50 line that separates growth from contraction. Bank Rate 3.75%, the path still showing 25bp in November.

The surveys can reach the afternoon round only. Today therefore offers a real choice between the two rounds, which is not something this week has otherwise provided.
Retail sales matched forecast on the headline and were weaker than forecast on every measure underneath it. Annual growth more than halved to 1.6%, sales excluding fuel fell 0.9% against 0.5% expected, and last month was revised down. It is the first UK release this week that argues clearly for cheaper borrowing — and it lands before this morning’s round.
RETAIL SALES — THE HEADLINE HELD AND NOTHING ELSE DID

Actual, forecast and previous:

  • Monthly −0.5% / −0.5% / 0.7%
  • Annual 1.6% / 2.2% / 3.8%
  • Monthly excluding fuel −0.9% / −0.5% / 0.9%
  • Annual excluding fuel 2.3% / 3.3% / 5.0%

Only the first line matched. Annual growth came in more than half a point below forecast and less than half what it was the month before. Stripping out fuel — the cleaner read on whether households are actually buying more — sales fell nearly twice as much as expected on the month, and the annual rate more than halved from 5.0% to 2.3%.

And last month was revised down, from a 1.0% monthly rise to 0.7%. So the starting point was lower than we thought as well.

Alongside it, consumer confidence improved to −14 from −17, where −18 was expected — a four-point beat. Households report feeling better and are spending less. Of the two, the spending is the harder number.

WHY THIS ONE MATTERS TO A BORROWER

Weaker consumer spending is a disinflationary signal. It argues for the Bank of England to move sooner or further towards cutting, and therefore for cheaper borrowing across the curve. It is the first UK release this week that points clearly in the borrower’s favour.

Set against that, the same caution that has applied all week. Monday to Thursday produced an inflation figure exactly on forecast, a labour market that softened on every measure, and a CBI orders survey that beat forecast by fifteen points — and ten-year borrowing ended Thursday 4bp above where it opened Monday, because the direction has been set by government borrowing costs abroad rather than by anything domestic.

So the honest position is this. Today’s figure gives the market a domestic reason to price cheaper borrowing. Whether it takes it is a different question, and this week’s evidence says not to assume it. The gilt market opens at 08:00 and we will not infer a reaction before it does.

OVERNIGHT: STILL GOING THE WRONG WAY

Japanese inflation came in at 1.9% against 1.7% expected, up from 1.6%, and Japanese 10-year yields have tracked US yields higher. That follows Thursday, on which US government bond yields gave back the whole of Wednesday’s buyback relief and the German 10-year held at a 15-year high.

The picture reaching us this morning is of the global sell-off resuming rather than pausing — higher oil and bond-market stress are both being cited as reasons for caution in Asian trading.

The question this sets up for today is the one yesterday’s close left open: gilts finished Thursday only 2bp higher on a day US borrowing costs deteriorated a great deal more, so the read-across that drove the whole week stopped operating. Today shows whether that was resilience or a lag.

WHERE BORROWING STARTS

Notice 322/26 stands until the morning round replaces it — 6.11% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.91% with the certainty discount for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast, and 6.53% on the 50-year. On last night’s close the morning round would come in about a basis point below it, evenly across the curve:

  • 2-year about 5.309% against 5.32% — 1.1bp lower
  • 5-year about 5.604% against 5.62% — 1.6bp lower
  • 10-year about 6.099% against 6.11% — 1.1bp lower
  • 20-year about 6.638% against 6.65% — 1.2bp lower
  • 50-year about 6.518% against 6.53% — 1.2bp lower

That estimate contains none of this morning’s retail sales, which reached us an hour after those levels were set. It is last night’s market, not this morning’s.

Yesterday’s pattern is worth carrying: the advantage stood at about 3bp at 16:20 and closed at about 1bp, because gilt yields rose through the final hour. A gap measured at a close is not a gap a borrower can bank.

The 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year — closed at 4.152%, 1.3bp above Wednesday. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the path still shows a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%.

THE REST OF TODAY
  • 08:30 — euro area flash manufacturing survey, forecast 52.0 against 52.2
  • 09:30 — UK flash purchasing managers’ surveys, forecast 51.5 manufacturing, 51.8 services, 51.6 composite, against 51.9, 52.1 and 52.2. Above 50 means growth; all three are forecast to slow while staying in growth. These reach the afternoon round, not the morning one.

Also reported this morning: the public finances came in at a £1.8bn shortfall against balance expected, described on the wires as an unexpected deficit in the new Chancellor’s first month. It carries little weight for today’s rates but it is the backdrop to the gilt supply that does.

It is the last trading day of the week, and the week’s remaining domestic risk is all in the next three hours.

Thursday 20 August 2026

17:22STORYend of day

End of day — Wednesday's intervention bought exactly one day. US yields have given back the whole buyback relief and the Treasury Secretary is talking about intervening again. Ten-year PWLB ends where it began at 6.11%

PWLB 10y — in force6.11%PWLB 10y — certainty5.91%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.100% (-1.0bp)1y SONIA swap4.151% (+1.3bp)

The day: 08:06 10-year gilt 1.3bp below yesterday, the low · 09:10 321/26, 10-year 6.10% down 1bp, 50-year 6.52% down 3bp · 11:00 CBI industrial trends orders −25, forecast −40, previously −45 · 12:22 322/26, 10-year 6.11%, up 1bp across every line · 13:38 10-year gilt 4.2bp above yesterday, the day's high · 16:16 0.1bp above · close 10-year gilt 5.065%, 2.0bp above.

More

One note of record: no edition was published between 10:17 and 16:20, so 322/26 and the CBI figure were reported hours after they reached us. Disclosed in the 16:20 edition and repeated here because a day's record should carry it. Nothing in the archive has been altered.

The relief lasted one day. Wednesday afternoon's fall in borrowing costs — the best move of the week — came from the US Treasury announcing bond buybacks. By this evening the market it started in had given all of it back: US yields surging again, the sell-off described as restarting, the German 10-year holding at a 15-year high, and the Treasury Secretary suggesting he could intervene again — 'we have a big tool kit'. An intervention that has to be repeated within a day is information about the strength of what it is pushing against. Wednesday's 3bp at long maturities was worth taking, and 321/26 this morning was the round that carried it.

Two rounds of opposite character, and the morning won. 321/26 split the sheet — 3bp off borrowing over twenty years and more, 1bp on at two years, the first tilted round of the week. 322/26 put a basis point back on every line without distinction. The morning round was the better of the two at every maturity, and both were struck before the day's 13:38 high. Tonight the sheet stands at 5.32% / 5.62% / 6.11% / 6.65% / 6.73% / 6.53% at 2, 5, 10, 20, 25 and 50 years, 20bp lower on each with the certainty discount.

The strongest UK number in weeks, and the market ignored it. CBI orders at −25 against −40 expected is a fifteen-point beat and a twenty-point improvement on the month. A stronger economy ordinarily argues for higher rates; yields eased in the quarter-hour after it, from 1.4bp above yesterday at 11:00 to 0.5bp at 11:15. We report the figure and the price separately rather than joining them. It is the second UK release this week to argue one way while borrowing costs went the other — the clearest evidence yet that UK rates are not currently being set by UK data.

The last hour changed tomorrow's arithmetic. At 16:16 the estimate for tomorrow's round was about 3bp below the rate in force. Yields then rose into the close — 2.2bp above yesterday at 17:00 — and the estimate is now about 6.100% on the 10-year, 1.0bp lower, with 5.605% at 5 years, 6.638% at 20 and 6.520% at 50. A basis point across the curve where three stood an hour earlier.

Tomorrow 07:00 retail sales, forecast −0.5% against a 1% rise, and 09:30 the flash purchasing managers' surveys, 51.5 and 51.8 against 51.9 and 52.1. Both land before the morning round and both can reach it: a one-basis-point advantage measured at the close is worth very little in front of two releases. Bank Rate 3.75%, the path still showing 25bp in November.

The larger question for tomorrow's open is whether gilts keep holding while US borrowing costs deteriorate. They did today — the read-across that drove every move we reported this week did not operate. Whether that is resilience or a lag is the thing to watch.

US government bond yields have given back the whole of the buyback relief, the Treasury Secretary is talking about intervening again, and the German 10-year is back at a 15-year high.   • 09:10 — notice 321/26, 10-year 6.10%, down 1bp; 50-year 6.52%, down 3bp
  • 11:00 — CBI industrial trends orders −25, forecast −40, previously −45
  • 12:22 — notice 322/26, 10-year 6.11%, up 1bp across every line

One note of record. No edition was published between 10:17 and 16:20, so notice 322/26 and the CBI figure were reported hours after they reached us. That was disclosed in the 16:20 edition and is repeated here because a day’s record should carry it. Nothing in the archive has been altered.

THE RELIEF LASTED ONE DAY

Wednesday afternoon’s fall in borrowing costs — the best move of the week, and the first thing in a fortnight to push against the global sell-off — came from the US Treasury announcing bond buybacks. By this evening the market it started in had given all of it back.

Reaching us through the afternoon and evening: US yields surging again a day after the buyback plan, the sell-off in US government bonds described as restarting, the German 10-year holding at a 15-year high, and the US Treasury Secretary suggesting the Treasury could intervene again — ‘we have a big tool kit’. Gold has risen to a two-month high.

What a treasurer should take from that. An intervention that has to be repeated within a day is information about the strength of the thing it is pushing against. The forces that took ten-year borrowing from 6.07% on Monday to 6.15% on Tuesday have not been dealt with; they were interrupted. Wednesday’s 3bp of relief at long maturities was worth taking, and 321/26 this morning was the round that carried it.

TWO ROUNDS OF OPPOSITE CHARACTER, AND THE MORNING WON

Standard maturity rates as they stand tonight, certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside:

  • 2-year 5.32% standard — 5.12% certainty
  • 5-year 5.62% standard — 5.42% certainty
  • 10-year 6.11% standard — 5.91% certainty
  • 20-year 6.65% standard — 6.45% certainty
  • 25-year 6.73% standard — 6.53% certainty
  • 50-year 6.53% standard — 6.33% certainty

321/26 split the sheet and 322/26 moved it as a block. The morning round took 3bp off borrowing over twenty years and more while adding one at two years — the first tilted round of the week, and the one on which Wednesday’s long-dated relief finally reached the sheet. The lunchtime round put a basis point back on every line without distinction.

The result is that the morning round was the better of the two at every maturity, by that basis point, and by 3bp at the long maturities against yesterday afternoon. Ten-year borrowing ends the day exactly where it started it.

Both rounds were struck before the day’s high at 13:38 and both look well placed against it. A borrower waiting through the early afternoon for something better did not get it.

THE STRONGEST UK NUMBER IN WEEKS, AND THE MARKET IGNORED IT

CBI industrial trends orders came in at −25 against −40 expected and −45 the month before. That is a fifteen-point beat on forecast and a twenty-point improvement on the month — large for this survey, which measures the balance of manufacturers reporting order books above or below normal.

A stronger economy ordinarily argues for higher rates. We will not tell you it moved the market, because the market went the other way — yields eased in the quarter-hour after it, from 1.4bp above yesterday at 11:00 to 0.5bp at 11:15. We report the figure and the price separately rather than joining them into a story neither supports.

It matters for a different reason. It is the second UK release this week to argue one way while borrowing costs went the other, and it is the clearest evidence yet that UK rates are not currently being set by UK data.

THE LAST HOUR CHANGED TOMORROW’S ARITHMETIC

At 16:16 the 10-year gilt was 0.1bp above yesterday’s close and tomorrow morning’s round looked about 3bp below the rate in force. Yields then rose through the final hour — 2.2bp above at 17:00, 2.0bp at the last prints to reach us.

Against yesterday’s close at the close: 2-year 4.363% (1.4bp above), 5-year 4.594% (1.9bp), 10-year 5.065% (2.0bp), 20-year 5.726% (1.8bp), 30-year 5.802% (1.7bp), 50-year 5.358% (2.0bp).

On that market, tomorrow morning’s round would come in below 322/26 but only just: about 6.100% on the 10-year, 1.0bp lower, 5.605% on the 5-year (1.5bp), 6.638% on the 20-year (1.2bp) and 6.520% on the 50-year (1.0bp). A basis point across the curve, where three stood an hour earlier.

The 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year — ends at 4.151%, 1.3bp above yesterday, having spent the morning below it. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the path still shows a 25bp rise in November to 4.00%.

TOMORROW IS THE WEEK’S REMAINING DOMESTIC RISK
  • 07:00 — retail sales, forecast −0.5% against a 1% rise the month before
  • 09:30 — flash purchasing managers’ surveys, forecast 51.5 manufacturing and 51.8 services, against 51.9 and 52.1, both above the 50 line separating growth from contraction

Both land before the morning round and both can reach it. That is the difference between tonight and last night: a one-basis-point advantage measured at the close is not one a borrower can rely on at 09:00, and on a Friday with two releases in front of the round it is worth very little.

The larger question tomorrow is whether gilts keep holding while US borrowing costs deteriorate. They did today — the read-across that drove every move we reported this week simply did not operate, and gilts finished 2bp higher on a day US yields gave back a great deal more. Whether that is resilience or a lag is the thing to watch at tomorrow’s open.

No edition was published between 10:17 and now, so the lunchtime round, the 11:00 CBI figure and the whole afternoon went uncovered. Nothing in the record has been altered and no earlier edition was wrong; the gap is a gap. Every figure below is current as at 16:16.
Notice 322/26 struck at 12:22 and added a basis point across the whole sheet, putting the 10-year maturity rate back to 6.11%, 5.91% with the certainty discount. Ten-year borrowing therefore ends the day exactly where it started it. The market did not: it rose to the day’s high at 13:38 and has fallen back through the whole afternoon.

THE AFTERNOON ROUND — NOTICE 322/26

Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against this morning’s round:

  • 2-year 5.32% standard — 5.12% certainty — up 1bp
  • 5-year 5.62% standard — 5.42% certainty — up 1bp
  • 10-year 6.11% standard — 5.91% certainty — up 1bp
  • 20-year 6.65% standard — 6.45% certainty — up 1bp
  • 25-year 6.73% standard — 6.53% certainty — up 1bp
  • 50-year 6.53% standard — 6.33% certainty — up 1bp

Annuity and equal-instalment sheets moved with it, up a basis point almost throughout. 322/26 is the standing price and today’s borrowing is finished.

Today’s two rounds are a study in contrast. This morning’s 321/26 split the sheet four basis points between the shortest and longest maturities; this one moved every line the same way. The morning round was the better of the two at every maturity, by that single basis point.

THE DAY IN ONE LINE, AND WHERE THE ROUNDS LANDED IN IT

The 10-year gilt yield against yesterday’s close:

  • 08:06 — 1.3bp below, the day’s low
  • 09:10 — level, as 321/26 struck
  • 12:22 — 1.3bp above, as 322/26 struck
  • 13:38 — 4.2bp above, the day’s high
  • 16:16 — 0.1bp above

Both rounds were struck before the day’s high and both look well-placed for it. A borrower who drew this morning did best; one who drew at lunchtime paid a basis point more and still avoided the worst of the afternoon. Anyone waiting for a better moment during the early afternoon did not get one — the market spent an hour and a quarter after the second round getting steadily worse.

The whole of that rise has since come back. At the last prints to reach us: 2-year 4.353%, 5-year 4.582%, 10-year 5.046%, 20-year 5.712%, 30-year 5.787%, 50-year 5.339% — all within 0.6bp of yesterday’s close, and the 10-year and 50-year within a tenth of it.

TOMORROW MORNING WOULD COME IN ABOUT 3bp LOWER

Because 322/26 was set on a market near the top of the day’s range and the market has since returned to where it began, the standing price now sits above the market across the whole curve. On the levels at 16:16, tomorrow morning’s round would come in at:

  • 2-year about 5.299% against 5.32% — 2.1bp lower
  • 5-year about 5.593% against 5.62% — 2.7bp lower
  • 10-year about 6.080% against 6.11% — 3.0bp lower
  • 20-year about 6.624% against 6.65% — 2.6bp lower
  • 50-year about 6.501% against 6.53% — 2.9bp lower

Note that this is even across the curve, unlike yesterday, when the gap widened the longer the borrowing. The tilt that produced this morning’s unusual round has flattened out again.

The caution is larger than usual tonight, and it is data. Tomorrow at 07:00 brings retail sales, forecast at −0.5% against a 1% rise the month before, and at 09:30 the flash purchasing managers’ surveys, forecast 51.5 for manufacturing and 51.8 for services. Both land before the morning round and both can reach it. A 3bp advantage measured tonight is not a 3bp advantage a borrower can rely on at 09:00.

TWO THINGS THAT HAPPENED WHILE WE WERE QUIET

11:00 — CBI industrial trends orders came in at −25, against −40 expected and −45 the month before. The measure is the balance of manufacturers reporting order books above normal against those reporting below, so a number closer to zero means fewer firms short of work. A fifteen-point improvement on the forecast and twenty on the month is a large move for this survey.

It is a stronger reading, and a stronger economy is ordinarily an argument for higher rates rather than lower. We will not tell you it moved the market, because the market went the other way — gilt yields eased in the quarter-hour after it. Either the survey was read as backward-looking or something else was moving at the same time. We report the figure and the price separately rather than joining them.

US government bond yields have given back all of the buyback relief. The move that drove Wednesday afternoon — the US Treasury announcing bond buybacks, later reported as a doubling of the programme — has now fully unwound in the market it started in. Wires this afternoon also carry US equities lower on rising bond yields and a Federal Reserve official describing the bond market as a policy signal.

That gilts finished the day close to unchanged while the source of the week’s relief unwound is the more notable half of it. The read-across that has driven every move we have reported this week did not operate today.

THE WEEK ON ONE RATE

The 10-year maturity rate, round by round:

  • 315/26, Monday 09:05 — 6.07%
  • 316/26, Monday 12:22 — 6.08%
  • 317/26, Tuesday 09:09 — 6.15%
  • 318/26, Tuesday 12:32 — 6.13%
  • 319/26, Wednesday 09:04 — 6.10%
  • 320/26, Wednesday 12:16 — 6.11%
  • 321/26, Thursday 09:10 — 6.10%
  • 322/26, Thursday 12:22 — 6.11%

Ten-year borrowing has spent the entire week inside eight basis points and ends today 4bp above where it opened Monday. The 50-year has done the moving: 6.55% on Wednesday afternoon, 6.53% now, having touched 6.52% this morning.

Bank Rate is 3.75% and the expected path still shows a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%, unmoved by today. The 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year — is 4.145%, 0.7bp above yesterday.

THE MORNING ROUND — NOTICE 321/26

Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against yesterday’s final round:

  • 2-year 5.31% standard — 5.11% certainty — up 1bp
  • 5-year 5.61% standard — 5.41% certainty — unchanged
  • 10-year 6.10% standard — 5.90% certainty — down 1bp
  • 20-year 6.64% standard — 6.44% certainty — down 3bp
  • 25-year 6.72% standard — 6.52% certainty — down 3bp
  • 50-year 6.52% standard — 6.32% certainty — down 3bp

Annuity and equal-instalment sheets are tilted the same way, up 1bp at 2 and 5 years and down 1 to 3bp from 10 years out.

A FOUR-BASIS-POINT SPREAD ACROSS ONE SHEET

Every other round this week moved as a block. Monday added a basis point across the curve, yesterday morning took two to three off across the curve, yesterday afternoon put one back across the curve. Today the sheet has split: 4bp between the 2-year and the 20-, 25- and 50-year lines.

That split is not new. It is what the market has been showing since Wednesday lunchtime, when the US Treasury’s bond buyback announcement pushed government borrowing costs down and the relief stayed at long maturities while shorter ones gave theirs back. Wires this morning report global yields retreating from multi-decade peaks on the back of it.

Today is the round on which that reached the sheet. For an authority borrowing over twenty years or more it is worth 3bp against yesterday afternoon. For one borrowing over two, it costs a basis point.

THE MARKET HAS RUN AGAINST THE BORROWER ALL MORNING

The 10-year gilt yield against yesterday’s close, through the morning:

  • 08:06 — 1.3bp below, the low
  • 09:10 — level, as the round struck
  • 09:44 — 1.6bp above

The overnight relief was given back inside the first hour of trading, and the rise has continued since the round was set. At the last prints to reach us: 2-year 4.360%, 5-year 4.591%, 10-year 5.061%, 20-year 5.723%, 30-year 5.801%, 50-year 5.354%, all 1.2 to 1.6bp above yesterday.

The practical consequence is straightforward. A borrower who drew on this round has the better of the day so far. One who waits for lunchtime is, on the market as it stands, waiting for nothing.

WHAT IS PUSHING IT — OIL HAS A PRICE NOW

Brent crude has jumped above $93 a barrel on the Iran impasse. That is the first hard number on a story that has been building all week: crude rising session after session on Strait of Hormuz developments, European gas prices reported to have doubled, and the US President threatening a ‘crushing economic operation’ against Iran.

To be precise about what it explains and what it does not: gilt yields had been rising since 08:06, before the crude headline reached us, so it is not the cause of the whole morning. The acceleration after 09:14 is consistent with it. We are not claiming more than that.

Why a treasurer should care about the oil price this week specifically. Yesterday’s UK inflation figure rose from 2.6% to 2.9% and energy is what pushed it there. An energy shock feeds the next figure directly, and it is the one thing that could put the expected path for Bank Rate back into question. As of now it has not: the path still shows a 25bp rise in November to 4.00%, and the 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank to do over the coming year — is 4.144%, 0.6bp above yesterday.

THE WEEK ON ONE RATE, AND WHAT IS LEFT TODAY

The 10-year maturity rate, round by round:

  • 315/26, Monday 09:05 — 6.07%
  • 316/26, Monday 12:22 — 6.08%
  • 317/26, Tuesday 09:09 — 6.15%
  • 318/26, Tuesday 12:32 — 6.13%
  • 319/26, Wednesday 09:04 — 6.10%
  • 320/26, Wednesday 12:16 — 6.11%
  • 321/26, Thursday 09:10 — 6.10%

Ten-year borrowing has been within four basis points all week and is 3bp above where it opened Monday. The 50-year is the series that has actually moved: 6.55% yesterday afternoon, 6.52% now.

11:00 — CBI industrial trends orders, forecast −40 against −45 last month, a survey of manufacturers’ order books. Medium importance and the only UK release today; it lands before the lunchtime round.

Tomorrow at 07:00 brings retail sales, forecast −0.5% against a 1% rise, and at 09:30 the flash purchasing managers’ surveys — the week’s remaining domestic risk.

More

The morning has gone one way and it is not the borrower's. The 10-year gilt made its low at 08:06, 1.3bp below yesterday's close, and has risen steadily every quarter-hour since. Against yesterday's close: 08:18 −0.8bp, 08:30 −0.1bp, 09:00 −0.1bp, and at 09:14 +0.3bp — the day's high, in the fixing window.

At the last prints to reach us: 2-year 4.349% (level with yesterday), 5-year 4.580% (0.4bp above), 10-year 5.048% (0.3bp above), 20-year 5.710% (0.2bp), 30-year 5.789% (0.4bp), 50-year 5.342% (0.4bp). The whole of the overnight relief has been given back within UK hours.

What that does to the round. On the market at 09:14 it would still come in below the rate in force at longer maturities, but by less than it looked an hour ago:

- 5-year about 5.606% — 0.4bp below, from 1.6bp at 08:18 - 10-year about 6.094% — 1.6bp below, from 2.8bp - 20-year about 6.643% — 2.7bp below, from 3.9bp - 50-year about 6.518% — 3.2bp below, from 4.3bp - 2-year about 5.307% — now 0.7bp *above*

The long-dated case survives the morning; the short-dated one has gone. A borrower drawing 50-year money should still be better off on this round than on yesterday's, by about 3bp rather than the 4.3bp on the screen at the open.

Nothing on our wires explains the reversal. No UK release before 11:00, nothing overnight that has come back into view. We report the move and not a reason for it.

The pattern from yesterday afternoon persists: the gap widens the longer the borrowing, and it is at long maturities that the case for waiting for this round has any weight.

One item on the wires deserves flagging. US federal debt has reached $40tn for the first time. It arrives the morning after the US Treasury announced the buybacks that drove yesterday's fall, and it is the structural fact those buybacks sit against. Nothing in the price this morning suggests the market is treating it as news — but it is the counterweight to yesterday's relief, and it is now a number rather than a theme. Gas is what pushed yesterday's UK inflation figure from 2.6% to 2.9%, so this is the direct route into next month's — but it is an inflation risk, not yet a rate risk. For a long-dated drawdown with any flexibility, 3.6bp is a real number and this morning's round is the one to watch; at shorter maturities the choice barely matters. ✓ The starting position favours waiting for this morning’s round. On last night’s close it would come in about 2.0bp below the rate in force on the 10-year and 3.6bp below on the 50-year. The longer the borrowing, the bigger the gap. That estimate contains nothing that has happened since 18:00 last night, and the gilt market does not open until 08:00.
The UK calendar is all but empty today, so both of today’s rounds will be set by what happens abroad — and abroad is sending two opposite signals. Overnight, yesterday’s relief carried through Asia; at the same time the energy story that drove this week’s inflation figure has escalated. Borrowing starts the day at 6.11% on the 10-year, and on last night’s close this morning’s round would come in below it.
TODAY’S CALENDAR IS NEARLY BARE
  • 11:00 — CBI industrial trends orders, forecast −40 against −45 last month. A survey of manufacturers’ order books; a less negative number means fewer firms reporting orders below normal. Medium importance, and it lands between the two rounds.

That is the whole UK list. There is nothing before the morning round and nothing after the afternoon one. Overnight, Japan’s trade deficit came in at ¥634.5bn against ¥680bn expected — better than forecast but wider than the ¥409.9bn before it.

An empty domestic calendar does not mean a quiet day for rates. It means today’s rates are made somewhere else, and this week that has been true even on the days with data.

OVERNIGHT: THE RELIEF CARRIED

Yesterday afternoon’s fall in government borrowing costs came from Washington — the US Treasury announcing bond buybacks, later reported as a doubling of the existing programme, with the Treasury Secretary intervening publicly. The question overnight was whether that held or drained away. It held.

Reaching us from the Asian session: Japanese yields followed US yields lower, and China’s 10-year yield is sitting near a one-year low. The offshore yuan is at its strongest since 2023.

Why this is the most useful thing on the page. Every significant move this week has arrived overnight rather than during UK hours — Tuesday’s 7bp rise in ten-year borrowing came that way, and so did most of the week’s direction. An overnight session that extends yesterday’s relief rather than reversing it is the single best piece of news a borrower could have had before this morning’s round.

One gap to be straight about: the Federal Reserve minutes were due at 19:00 last night and no reporting on them has reached us. We will not characterise a document we have not seen covered. If it moves anything, it will show in the opening prints.

AND THE OTHER WAY: ENERGY HAS ESCALATED

Two items overnight, and they are the same story.

  • European gas prices are reported to have doubled, with the worst described as still to come.
  • The US President has threatened a ‘crushing economic operation’ against Iran and ‘tremendous economic consequences’ for any country assisting it. Crude had risen for four straight sessions into last night on Strait of Hormuz developments.

This is not background colour, it is the mechanism. Yesterday’s UK inflation figure rose from 2.6% to 2.9% and gas is what pushed it there. A further escalation in gas is the direct route into next month’s figure, and it has arrived inside a day.

The distinction that matters for today: this is an inflation risk, not yet a rate risk. Nothing in it has moved the expected path for Bank Rate, which still shows a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%. It is a reason to be careful about how much comfort to take from a good overnight session, not a reason to expect anything from it this morning.

WHERE BORROWING STARTS

Notice 320/26 stands until the morning round replaces it — 6.11% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.91% with the certainty discount for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast. On last night’s close, this morning’s round would come in below it right along the curve:

  • 5-year about 5.602% against 5.61% — 0.8bp lower
  • 10-year about 6.090% against 6.11% — 2.0bp lower
  • 20-year about 6.641% against 6.67% — 2.9bp lower
  • 50-year about 6.514% against 6.55% — 3.6bp lower

The gap widens the longer the borrowing, and that is not an accident. A buyback programme buys long-dated government debt, so long-dated borrowing costs are where yesterday’s relief settled and stayed — shorter maturities gave back four-fifths of the afternoon move by the close, the longest gave back a third.

What to do with that. For a long-dated drawdown with any flexibility, 3.6bp is a real number and this morning’s round is the one to watch. For shorter maturities there is next to nothing in it and the choice barely matters. As always, the estimate is a read on last night’s market and not a forecast of the round; the gilt market opens at 08:00 and we will not infer a reaction before it does.

The 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year — closed last night at 4.139%, 1.8bp below the night before.

AND TOMORROW

Friday 07:00 — retail sales, forecast at −0.5% against a 1% rise the month before. 09:30 — the flash purchasing managers’ surveys, forecast 51.5 for manufacturing and 51.8 for services, both a shade below last month and both above the 50 line that separates growth from contraction.

That is the week’s remaining domestic risk, and it prints before Friday’s morning round.

More

Both rounds were struck in the flattest stretch of the day, and the single basis point between them is all that stretch produced. At 09:04 the 10-year gilt stood 2.7bp below yesterday; by 12:16 the morning's fall had drained to 1.5bp. What today rewarded was having waited since Tuesday afternoon, not having picked between this morning and lunchtime — against yesterday's final round, ten-year borrowing is 2bp lower tonight, the first down day of the week.

The move came after both rounds had struck, and we saw it fifty minutes before we saw the reason. Yields fell across the curve from 13:30; at 13:44 the whole curve was 5.6 to 6.4bp below yesterday and we reported it without a cause because we did not have one. At 14:19 the explanation reached us: the US Treasury has announced bond buybacks, with the Treasury Secretary intervening publicly, later reported as a doubling of the existing programme. After a fortnight in which government borrowing costs at multi-decade highs abroad drove every rise we reported, this is the first thing pushing the other way.

Half the fall went back, and it went back at the shorter maturities. At the close, against yesterday, with the 13:44 low alongside: 2-year 4.348% (1.1bp below, from 5.9bp), 5-year 4.577% (2.5bp, from 6.2bp), 10-year 5.045% (3.1bp, from 5.6bp), 20-year 5.709% (3.7bp, from 5.8bp), 30-year 5.785% (4.1bp, from 6.0bp), 50-year 5.340% (4.1bp, from 6.4bp). Shorter maturities gave back four-fifths of the move; the longest gave back a third. A buyback programme buys long-dated debt, and long-dated borrowing costs are where the benefit has stayed.

320/26 stands until tomorrow morning. On the market at the close, tomorrow's round would come in about 6.090% on the 10-year (2.0bp lower) and 6.516% on the 50-year, 3.4bp lower — a real number for a long-dated drawdown with a day of flexibility, and next to nothing at shorter maturities. Two things stand in between: the Federal Reserve minutes at 19:00, and an overnight session, which on this week's evidence is where the moves have actually happened.

One thing we still cannot tell you, because we have not established it: whether an application made late in the day prices at the round in force or rolls into the next one. With a 3.4bp gap open on 50-year money that is worth settling once, and it is a question for the lender.

Nothing on the UK calendar tomorrow. Friday brings retail sales at 07:00, forecast −0.5% against a 1% rise previously, and the flash purchasing managers' surveys at 09:30 — 51.5 manufacturing, 51.8 services, both a shade below last month and both above the 50 line. Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise in November to 4.00%; today's in-line inflation figure changed nothing in it.

THE TWO ROUNDS, AND THE ONE BASIS POINT BETWEEN THEM

Standard maturity rates as they stand tonight, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside:

  • 2-year 5.30% standard — 5.10% certainty
  • 5-year 5.61% standard — 5.41% certainty
  • 10-year 6.11% standard — 5.91% certainty
  • 20-year 6.67% standard — 6.47% certainty
  • 25-year 6.75% standard — 6.55% certainty
  • 50-year 6.55% standard — 6.35% certainty

The morning round was the better of the two, by a single basis point on every maturity. The reason is that both rounds were struck in the flattest stretch of the day. At 09:04 the 10-year gilt stood 2.7bp below yesterday; by 12:16 the morning’s fall had drained away to 1.5bp. A basis point and a bit on the market, a basis point on the sheet.

Neither round captured what happened next, and no borrower could have positioned for it. What today rewarded was having waited since yesterday afternoon, not having picked between this morning and lunchtime: against Tuesday’s final round, ten-year borrowing is 2bp cheaper tonight.

THE MOVE CAME AFTER BOTH ROUNDS HAD STRUCK

At 13:30 gilt yields began falling across every maturity at once, and by 13:44 the whole curve stood 5.6 to 6.4bp below yesterday’s close. We reported that move without a cause, because we did not have one. Nothing on the UK calendar, nothing on our wires.

The explanation reached us at 14:19: the US Treasury has announced bond buybacks, with the Treasury Secretary intervening publicly to steady the market. Later reports put it as a doubling of the existing programme rather than a new one. US yields fell hard and gilts went with them.

That is a fifty-minute gap between a price moving and the reason arriving, and it is worth stating plainly: the market had the information and we did not. We describe when a price reached us rather than when it traded, and we do not fill the gap with a guess.

Why it matters beyond today. Every rise we have reported since Monday traced back to government borrowing costs at multi-decade highs across the major markets — the German 10-year at its highest since 2011, the French since 2008, the US 30-year since 2007. This is the first thing in a fortnight to push the other way.

HALF THE FALL WENT BACK, AND IT WENT BACK AT THE SHORTER MATURITIES

Against yesterday’s close, at the last prints to reach us, with the 13:44 low alongside:

  • 2-year 4.348% — 1.1bp below, from 5.9bp
  • 5-year 4.577% — 2.5bp below, from 6.2bp
  • 10-year 5.045% — 3.1bp below, from 5.6bp
  • 20-year 5.709% — 3.7bp below, from 5.8bp
  • 30-year 5.785% — 4.1bp below, from 6.0bp
  • 50-year 5.340% — 4.1bp below, from 6.4bp

Shorter maturities gave back four-fifths of the move; the longest gave back a third. That asymmetry held for three and a half hours, and it is the most informative thing on the screen tonight. A buyback programme buys long-dated debt, and it is long-dated borrowing costs that have kept the benefit. The retracement is the market thinning out a first reaction, not rejecting it.

The 1-year SONIA swap — the clearest read on what markets expect the Bank of England to do over the coming year — ends at 4.139%, 1.8bp below yesterday, holding about half the fall it made on this morning’s inflation figure.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR TOMORROW’S BORROWING

Notice 320/26 is the standing price until tomorrow morning’s round replaces it. On the market at the close, tomorrow’s round would come in below it right along the curve:

  • 5-year about 5.603%, 0.7bp lower
  • 10-year about 6.090%, 2.0bp lower than 6.11%
  • 20-year about 6.641%, 2.9bp lower
  • 50-year about 6.516%, 3.4bp lower than 6.55%

For a borrower with a long-dated drawdown to place and a day of flexibility, 3.4bp is a real number rather than the sub-basis-point noise we have been declining to act on all week. For shorter maturities there is next to nothing in it.

Two things stand between that estimate and the round. The Federal Reserve minutes at 19:00 tonight, and an overnight session — which on this week’s evidence is where the moves have actually happened. Tuesday’s 7bp rise arrived overnight, and so did most of this week’s direction.

One thing we still cannot tell you, because we have not established it: whether an application made late in the day prices at the round in force or rolls into the next one. That is the lender’s operating practice. With a 3.4bp gap open on 50-year money it is worth settling once, and it is a question for the lender rather than for us.

TONIGHT, AND THE REST OF THE WEEK

19:00 — Federal Reserve minutes, the only scheduled release left. They land between today’s rounds and tomorrow’s, on the same afternoon the US Treasury moved to steady its own bond market. On a week when US borrowing costs have set the direction for everyone, they are the thing to read tonight.

Nothing on the UK calendar tomorrow. Friday brings retail sales at 07:00, forecast at −0.5% against a 1% rise previously, and the flash purchasing managers’ surveys at 09:30, forecast at 51.5 for manufacturing and 51.8 for services — both a shade below last month, both still above the 50 line that separates growth from contraction.

Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%. Today’s inflation figure landing exactly on forecast changed nothing in that path.

Two cautions to carry overnight. An intervention that calms a market is not a problem solved — the same wires carrying the buyback also carry America’s debt pile as the week’s preoccupation. And UK gas prices are reported at a three-year high: gas is what drove this morning’s inflation figure up from 2.6%, so a fresh high in it is the mechanism to watch into next month’s.

It was a slide, not a jump. The prints run smoothly from 2.5bp below at 13:30 to 6.0bp below at 13:43, every tenor moving together minute by minute. Gilts have rallied hard in the last quarter of an hour, and the whole curve is now 5.6 to 6.4bp below yesterday’s close. Today’s borrowing is already done at 6.11%, but tomorrow morning’s round would now come in about 4.5bp below that — the widest gap between the standing rate and the next estimate we have reported this week.
WHAT MOVED

Against yesterday’s close, at the last prints to reach us, with where each stood at 13:21 for comparison:

  • 2-year 4.300% — 5.9bp below, from 2.8bp
  • 5-year 4.540% — 6.2bp below, from 2.8bp
  • 10-year 5.019% — 5.6bp below, from 2.0bp
