  • 30-year 5.766% — 6.0bp below, from 1.9bp
  • 50-year 5.317% — 6.4bp below, from 2.1bp

It was a slide, not a jump. The prints reaching us run smoothly from 2.5bp below at 13:30 to 6.0bp below at 13:43, every tenor moving together minute by minute, easing very slightly at 13:44. We checked it print by print before reporting it: this is a real move in the market, not a stale reading correcting itself.

The 1-year SONIA swap has gone with it, back to 4.120% and 3.6bp below yesterday — matching the low it made on this morning’s inflation print.

WHAT IT MEANS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

It does not change today. Both of today’s rounds have struck. Notice 320/26 at 12:16 set the 10-year maturity rate at 6.11%, 5.91% with the certainty discount, and that is the standing price.

It changes tomorrow. On the market at 13:44, tomorrow morning’s round would come in about 4.5bp below today’s afternoon rate — 6.065% on the 10-year, 5.566% on the 5-year, 6.620% on the 20-year and 6.493% on the 50-year, the last of those 5.7bp below. For a borrower with a drawdown to place and the flexibility to wait a day, that is a real number rather than the sub-basis-point noise we have been declining to act on all week.

One thing we will not tell you, because we have not established it: whether an application made this afternoon still prices at 320/26 or rolls into tomorrow’s round. That is the lender’s operating practice and we have never verified it. If the distinction matters to a decision, it is a question for the lender rather than for us.

The usual caveat carries more weight than usual today: an overnight session sits between this and tomorrow’s round, and on this week’s evidence the overnight session is where the moves have actually happened. Tuesday’s 7bp rise arrived that way.

TONIGHT

19:00 — Federal Reserve minutes, the only scheduled release left. They land after today’s rounds and before tomorrow’s, so they are an input to tomorrow morning’s rates. On a week when US long yields have set the direction for everyone, and on an afternoon when something has moved the curve without announcing itself, they are worth reading.

Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise at the November meeting.

THE DAY, AND THE WEEK IT SITS IN

Today has taken 2bp off the cost of ten-year borrowing — the first down day of the week, and the reason is an inflation figure that arrived exactly where it was forecast rather than above it.

Set against Tuesday morning’s 6.15% peak, four basis points of that overnight spike have come back. Set against Monday’s open, the week is still 4bp dearer. The gap that opened on Tuesday has been partly closed, not undone.

A full afternoon and an overnight session stand in front of that, and on this week’s evidence an overnight session is where the moves have actually happened.

Nothing on the UK calendar until Friday, which brings retail sales and the flash PMIs.

Two things to carry forward. And UK gas prices are reported at a three-year high: gas drove this morning’s inflation figure, so a fresh high in it is the mechanism to watch into next month’s print.

Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise in November to 4.00%. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.129%, 2.7bp below yesterday and holding most of the fall it made on the print.

On the market at 12:16 it would come in 1.5bp above that: 6.115% on the 10-year, 5.612% on the 5-year, 6.669% on the 20-year, 6.551% on the 50-year. Across the curve, 0.9 to 1.5bp above the rates in force.

That is narrower than the 2.3bp we reported at midday — gilts have recovered part of the late-morning give-back, with the 10-year back to 5.061%, 1.5bp below yesterday's close. But the direction of the comparison is unchanged: this morning's round is still the better of the two, and has been since 09:50.

The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.131%, holding 2.5bp of the fall it made on the inflation print.

Nothing is scheduled between now and the close of business except the Federal Reserve minutes at 19:00, which land after both rounds and shape tomorrow morning. Crude has risen for a fourth session.

It was gas, which is the point. Yesterday we logged two readings pulling opposite ways — grocery inflation at a two-year low arguing against a rise of this size, the energy price cap arguing for. ⚠ Every estimate below is anchored to last night’s close and contains none of this morning’s figures. The gilt market opens at 08:00. Until it does we have no read on how the print has been taken, and we will not infer one — the first honest number comes in the 08:15 edition.
The week’s event has passed and it landed exactly on forecast: inflation 2.9%, against 2.9% expected and 2.6% last. No headline surprise, which removes the single biggest scheduled risk to this morning’s round. But the detail cuts both ways — core inflation came in a tenth hot and has now held at 2.6% for a third month, while producer input costs fell far faster than anyone expected.
THE INFLATION FIGURES, 07:00

Actual, then forecast, then last:

  • Headline CPI 2.9% — 2.9% expected, 2.6% last
  • Core CPI 2.6% — 2.5% expected, 2.6% last
  • CPI monthly 0.3% — 0.3% expected, 0.1% last
  • Producer input prices 4.9% — 6.6% expected, 7.4% last
  • Producer output prices 3.1% — 3.2% expected, 3.5% last
  • RPI 3.2% — 3.3% expected, 3.0% last

The headline is the number that matters this morning, and it is the one that behaved. A three-tenths jump was expected and a three-tenths jump arrived. There is no surprise for the market to price, which is the best available outcome for a borrower on a day when the round strikes two hours after the print.

Underneath, two things pull against each other. Core inflation — the measure that strips out energy and food, and the one the Bank watches — came in a tenth above forecast and has not moved in three months. Sticky core is the argument against rate cuts. But producer input costs, which feed consumer prices with a lag, came in at 4.9% where 6.6% was expected and 7.4% was last. That is the pipeline cooling hard, and it is the more forward-looking of the two.

IT WAS GAS, WHICH IS THE POINT

The rise is being attributed this morning to a surge in gas costs. That matters because it settles a question we set out yesterday afternoon rather than leaving it open.

We logged two readings pulling opposite ways: grocery price inflation at a two-year low of 2.1%, arguing against a rise of this size, and the energy price cap increase, arguing for it. The energy side won, and it won for the reason given. We said we would not call the print and we did not; the mechanism, at least, was the one to watch.

The distinction is worth holding on to. An energy-driven rise is a level effect that washes out of the annual comparison in time. A core-driven rise would not. This morning was the first kind, which is why a headline at 2.9% is less alarming than 2.9% sounds — and why the sticky 2.6% core is the number to keep watching.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR TODAY’S ROUND

The 07:00 release lands roughly two hours before the morning round strikes, so it is an input to today’s rates, not tomorrow’s — as is whatever the market does between the 08:00 open and the strike.

Until then notice 318/26 is the standing price: 6.13% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.93% with the certainty discount, struck at 12:32 yesterday. On last night’s close alone the round would have come in fractionally below it, at 6.127%. That number contains none of this morning’s news and is the starting point today moves from, not a forecast of where it ends.

Yesterday is the reason to hold that lightly. The domestic data argued one way all day and the global long end pushed the other, and the global side won by enough to add 5bp to ten-year borrowing. An in-line inflation print removes a domestic reason to sell gilts; it does nothing about the reason they have actually been selling.

THE REST OF TODAY

19:00 — the Federal Reserve’s meeting minutes. They land after both of today’s rounds, so they shape tomorrow morning rather than anything available today. On a week when US long yields have set the direction, they are worth reading.

Nothing else is scheduled. Oil is reported higher again this morning on Strait of Hormuz developments, which is the same driver that has run all week.

Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%. Neither this morning’s figures nor yesterday’s labour market has shifted it.

Later this week: retail sales and the flash PMIs on Friday.

18:45STORYend of day

End of day — every domestic number argued for cheaper borrowing, and borrowing got dearer anyway. Ten-year PWLB ends 5bp higher at 6.13%

PWLB 10y — in force6.13%PWLB 10y — certainty5.93%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.127% (-0.3bp)1y SONIA swap4.155% (+1.3bp)

This edition replaces those issued at 17:22 and 18:05. No market figure has changed. The 17:22 version stated each event twice — once in an interpreted timeline, again in a section explaining the same event. Both earlier versions also carried a council-sector section, which does not belong in the market pulse and has been removed; that material lives on the councils stream.

More

The day: 07:00 unemployment 4.9% (4.8% expected), employment +83,000 (+200,000), payrolls −13,000 · 08:00 gilts open 2.0–3.3bp higher · 09:09 317/26, 10-year 6.15%, up 7bp · 09:30 productivity −0.8% · 10:00 gilt 2036 auction clears 5.155% (5.040% previously) · 12:32 318/26, 10-year 6.13%, down 2bp · 13:30 US permits 1.443M, starts 1.239M · close 10-year gilt 5.076%, up 2.6bp.

Where each round landed in the day's 4bp range is the whole difference between them. At 09:09 the 10-year yield stood 4.3bp above yesterday, peaking at 4.7bp minutes later; by 12:32 it was 3.3bp. A basis point lower on the curve, two lower on the round. A borrower who drew this morning paid the day's high, one who drew after lunch paid 2bp less, neither with any way of knowing in advance.

The auction didn't bite. A higher clearing yield than last time is what a market at these levels produces; what mattered is that yields fell afterwards, giving back more than half the morning's rise within the hour. German 10-year at its highest since 2011, French since 2008, US 30-year since 2007 — and UK supply absorbed into that without difficulty.

318/26 stands until tomorrow morning — 6.13% on the 10-year, 5.93% certainty. Bank Rate 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise in November, unmoved by a labour market that softened on every measure that matters to it.

Tomorrow 07:00: inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%, printing before the round and able to reach it. Grocery inflation at a two-year low argues against; the energy price cap argues for. We are not calling it.

WHERE GILTS FINISHED, AND WHY THE TWO ROUNDS DIFFERED

At the last prints to reach us, against yesterday’s close: 2-year 4.359% (+1.4bp), 5-year 4.601% (+1.7bp), 10-year 5.076% (+2.6bp), 20-year 5.744% (+1.6bp), 30-year 5.826% (+1.3bp), 50-year 5.382% (+0.5bp). The 1-year SONIA swap firmed late to 4.155%.

The 10-year traded a range of about 4bp through the day, and where each round landed in that range is the whole difference between them. At 09:09 the yield stood 4.3bp above yesterday, going on to peak at 4.7bp minutes later. By 12:32 it was 3.3bp. A basis point lower on the curve, two lower on the round.

So a borrower who drew this morning paid the day’s high and one who drew after lunch paid 2bp less — neither with any way of knowing in advance. It is a clean illustration of why the standing rate and the estimate for the next round are worth comparing, rather than treating whatever fixing is current as simply the price of the day.

318/26 is the standing price until tomorrow morning: 6.13% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.93% with the certainty discount. Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise in November — unmoved by a labour market that softened on every measure that matters to it.

THE AUCTION THAT DIDN’T BITE

The auction was the day’s largest scheduled risk and we flagged it three times before it landed: supply into a long end at multi-decade highs is where stress surfaces first.

A higher clearing yield than last time is simply what a market at these levels produces. What mattered was what happened next, and what happened next was that yields fell — the morning’s rise was more than half given back within the hour.

That is the reassuring datum to carry forward. The German 10-year is at its highest since 2011, the French since 2008, the US 30-year since 2007 — and UK supply was absorbed into that without difficulty.

TOMORROW — THE WEEK’S EVENT

07:00 — inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. It prints before the morning round and can therefore reach it, exactly as today’s labour figures did.

Two readings surfaced today and they cut opposite ways. Grocery price inflation slowed to 2.1%, a two-year low, arguing against a rise of that size; the energy price cap increase is reported as set to push July inflation higher, and a cap increase is the mechanism most often behind a step of this magnitude. We are not calling it.

What today established is the asymmetry. The global long end has overridden domestic data all week, so a soft print may not help much, while a hot one would push the same way the world is already pushing.

On the market at 17:15 tomorrow’s round would come in fractionally below today’s, at 6.127% on the 10-year, with an overnight session and the inflation figure in front of it. Friday brings retail sales and the flash PMIs.

The six authorities whose reviews were published are East Sussex, Gloucester, Halton, Peterborough, Worcestershire and Worthing, alongside updated Exceptional Financial Support guidance for 2025-26 and 2026-27. All six are already on the support list, so this is one coordinated release rather than six events.

Support of this kind lets an authority meet revenue costs from capital resources — in practice by borrowing against them. It converts a revenue problem into a debt position, which makes that list the authorities whose borrowing requirement is least discretionary, on a day the cost of it rose 5bp.

Largest agreed in principle for 2026-27, as stated on the guidance page: Shropshire £121.0m, Croydon £119.0m, Warrington £92.047m. Among today’s six, East Sussex £70.0m and Worcestershire £59.933m. Every domestic number today argued for cheaper borrowing, and borrowing got dearer anyway. Ten-year PWLB ends 5bp above where it started: 6.13%, or 5.93% with the certainty discount. The labour market softened, productivity fell, and none of it mattered against a global long end at multi-decade highs.

THE DAY IN ONE LINE

A gap higher overnight, a round struck on the gap, and a slow walk back that never quite undid it.

  • 07:00 — the labour market came in weak. Unemployment 4.9% against 4.8% expected, employment +83,000 against +200,000, payrolls down 13,000.
  • 08:00 — gilts opened 2.0 to 3.3bp higher regardless, on an overnight move in global bonds.
  • 09:09 — notice 317/26, the 10-year up 7bp to 6.15%, struck within minutes of the day’s high.
  • 10:00 — the gilt 2036 auction cleared at 5.155% and was absorbed without stress. Yields fell afterwards.
  • 12:32 — notice 318/26, the 10-year down 2bp to 6.13%.
  • 13:30 — US housing mixed: permits beat at 1.443M, starts missed at 1.239M.
  • 15:11 — the department published six 2026-27 external assurance reviews, all for councils already receiving support.

Net: 5bp on the cost of ten-year borrowing, in a day when the domestic data pointed the other way throughout.

WHERE GILTS FINISHED

At the last prints to reach us, against yesterday’s close:

  • 2-year 4.359% — up 1.4bp
  • 5-year 4.601% — up 1.7bp
  • 10-year 5.076% — up 2.6bp
  • 20-year 5.744% — up 1.6bp
  • 30-year 5.826% — up 1.3bp
  • 50-year 5.382% — up 0.5bp

The 10-year traded a range of about 4bp — from 0.5bp above yesterday at its lowest to 4.7bp at its highest, shortly after the morning round was struck — and closed nearer the middle. Higher yields mean a higher cost of borrowing, so the day ended against the borrower, though by less than it threatened at half past nine.

The 1-year SONIA swap firmed late to 4.155%, 1.3bp above yesterday. Bank Rate is 3.75%, and the path still shows a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00% — unmoved by a labour market that softened on every measure that matters to it.

THE TWO ROUNDS, AND WHY TIMING DECIDED THEM

The difference between this morning’s round and this afternoon’s was not a change of view. It was where each one caught the market.

At 09:09 the 10-year gilt yield stood 4.3bp above yesterday’s close, and went on to peak at 4.7bp minutes later. By 12:32 it was 3.3bp. A basis point lower on the curve, and the round came in two lower.

A borrower who drew on the morning round paid the day’s high; one who drew after lunch paid 2bp less. Neither had a way of knowing in advance, and we would not pretend otherwise — but it is a clean illustration of why the standing rate and the estimate for the next round are worth comparing rather than treating a fixing as simply the price of the day.

318/26 is the standing price until tomorrow morning — 6.13% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.93% with the certainty discount.

THE AUCTION THAT DIDN’T BITE

The 10:00 gilt 2036 auction was the day’s single largest scheduled risk, and we flagged it three times before it landed: an auction into a long end at multi-decade highs is where stress shows up first.

It cleared at 5.155%, against 5.040% at the previous one. A higher clearing yield is what a market at these levels produces; the part that mattered was what happened next, and what happened next was that yields fell. The morning’s rise was more than half given back within the hour.

That is worth carrying into tomorrow. The long end is at levels not seen in decades — the German 10-year at its highest since 2011, the French since 2008, the US 30-year since 2007 — and UK supply was absorbed into it without difficulty.

COUNCIL SIDE

The department published 2026-27 external assurance reviews for six authorities this afternoon — East Sussex, Gloucester, Halton, Peterborough, Worcestershire and Worthing — alongside updates to its Exceptional Financial Support guidance for both 2025-26 and 2026-27. All six are already on the support list, so this is one coordinated release.

Support agreed in principle for 2026-27, as stated on the guidance page: the largest include Shropshire at £121.0m, Croydon at £119.0m and Warrington at £92.047m. Among today’s six, East Sussex £70.0m and Worcestershire £59.933m.

Support of this kind converts a revenue problem into a debt position, which makes that list the authorities whose borrowing requirement is least discretionary — on a day the cost of it rose 5bp. We have not read the reviews and will report their content properly rather than from the announcement. Pension scheme fund statistics for England and Wales were also published.

TOMORROW — THE WEEK’S EVENT

07:00 — inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. It prints before the morning round and can therefore reach it, exactly as this morning’s labour figures did.

Two readings surfaced today and they cut opposite ways. Grocery price inflation slowed to 2.1%, its lowest in two years, which argues against a rise of that size. The energy price cap increase is reported as set to push July inflation higher, which argues for it — and a cap increase is the mechanism most often behind a step of this magnitude. We are not calling it.

What today established is the asymmetry: the global long end has been overriding domestic data all week. A soft print may not help much; a hot one would push the same way the world is already pushing.

On the market at 17:15 tomorrow morning’s round would come in fractionally below today’s, at 6.127% on the 10-year. An overnight session and the inflation figure sit in front of it. Later this week: retail sales and flash PMIs on Friday.

i We have not read the reviews. This edition reports what was published and what the support page states, both of which are checkable. The reviews themselves are substantial documents and we will report on their content properly rather than from the announcement — the same discipline we applied to the Slough papers yesterday.
The department published its 2026-27 external assurance reviews this afternoon, for six councils, and every one of them is already on the Exceptional Financial Support list. Markets meanwhile have gone quiet: gilts have given back most of the afternoon’s firmness and tomorrow’s round would come in a shade below today’s.
WHAT WAS PUBLISHED

Between 15:11 and 15:12 the department published 2026-27 external assurance reviews for six authorities, alongside updates to its Exceptional Financial Support guidance for both 2025-26 and 2026-27. The guidance page records the change as “2026-27 external assurance reviews added”.

The six:

  • East Sussex County Council
  • Gloucester City Council
  • Halton Borough Council
  • Peterborough City Council
  • Worcestershire County Council
  • Worthing Borough Council

All six already appear on the support list. The review is the independent diagnostic that accompanies a request for support, so this is a coordinated release rather than six separate events, and it tells you where the department’s attention currently sits.

WHY THIS IS A TREASURY STORY, NOT A GOVERNANCE ONE

Exceptional Financial Support is the mechanism by which an authority that cannot balance its budget is permitted to meet revenue costs from capital resources — in practice, by borrowing against them. It converts a revenue problem into a debt position.

That makes the support list a list of the authorities whose borrowing requirement is least discretionary, on a day when the cost of that borrowing rose 5bp and the ten-year PWLB maturity rate sits at 6.13%. An authority capitalising a deficit is not choosing whether to borrow, only when and at what maturity.

The support amounts agreed in principle for 2026-27, as stated on the guidance page, run from under a million to well over a hundred million. The largest include Shropshire at £121.0m, Croydon at £119.0m and Warrington at £92.047m, with Warrington also carrying £87.029m agreed for 2025-26 and Shropshire £71.4m. Among today’s six: East Sussex £70.0m, Worcestershire £59.933m, Halton £35.0m, Gloucester £9.05m, Peterborough £5.68m and Worthing £5.0m.

The page does not state an aggregate total, and we are not going to add one up and present it as official.

THE MARKET, QUIETLY

Gilts have given back the afternoon’s firmness. At the last prints to reach us: 10-year 5.070%, 2.0bp above yesterday’s close, having been 3.2bp at 14:18; the 20-year 1.3bp up, the 30-year 1.0bp and the 50-year 0.3bp. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.145%.

Notice 318/26 stands — 6.13% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.93% with the certainty discount. On the market at 15:17 tomorrow morning’s round would come in a shade below it, at 6.121% on the 10-year and 6.668% on the 20-year.

That small discount has now appeared and vanished four times today. At this size it is not a signal, and we would not act on it in either direction.

TOMORROW

07:00 — inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. It prints before the morning round and can therefore reach it, exactly as this morning’s labour figures did. It is the week’s event.

Today has shown what that means in practice: the domestic release argued one way, the global long end argued the other, and the global side won by enough to add 5bp to the cost of ten-year borrowing. A hot inflation print would push the same direction as the global move rather than against it.

The counterpoint logged this morning still stands: grocery price inflation slowed to 2.1%, its lowest in two years. Bank Rate is 3.75% with a 25bp rise still expected in November.

13:48PULSEupdate

US housing data mixed — permits beat, starts missed; gilts have drifted up 0.6bp since, which is drift rather than a reaction

PWLB 10y — in force6.13%PWLB 10y — certainty5.93%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.128% (-0.2bp)1y SONIA swap4.145% (+0.2bp)

The 13:30 US releases have printed, and they point both ways.

More

- Building permits 1.443M, against 1.37M expected and 1.374M last — a clear beat, and the forward-looking half of the pair. - Housing starts 1.239M, against 1.35M expected and 1.415M last — a sizeable miss on current activity.

Permits are the leading indicator and they came in strong; starts are the here-and-now and they were weak. Taken together this is not a clean signal in either direction.

Gilts have drifted up about six tenths of a basis point in the prints reaching us since. The 10-year is 5.077%, 2.7bp above yesterday's close, having been 2.1bp at 13:19. The 20-year is 1.9bp up. That is drift rather than a reaction, and we would not read a direction into it yet: our newest print is timed 13:44 against a 13:46 clock, so our view is close to current but the releases are only sixteen minutes old.

Today's borrowing is finished, so nothing here reaches a rate available now. Notice 318/26 stands — 6.13% on the 10-year, 5.93% with the certainty discount — and these figures feed tomorrow morning's round instead. On the market at 13:44 that round would come in fractionally below today's, at 6.128%.

The wider picture has not shifted: bond markets from the US to Japan are reported under pressure on inflation and fiscal worries, which is the same story that set today's direction overnight.

Tomorrow at 07:00 is the week's event: inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%.

THE AFTERNOON ROUND — NOTICE 318/26

Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against this morning’s round:

  • 2-year 5.32% standard — 5.12% certainty — down 1bp
  • 5-year 5.63% standard — 5.43% certainty — down 2bp
  • 10-year 6.13% standard — 5.93% certainty — down 2bp
  • 20-year 6.68% standard — 6.48% certainty — down 2bp
  • 25-year 6.77% standard — 6.57% certainty — down 2bp
  • 50-year 6.57% standard — 6.37% certainty — down 2bp

The annuity and equal-instalment sheets moved the same way, 1 to 2bp lower across the curve. As uniform on the way down as this morning’s was on the way up.

318/26 is now the standing price and today’s borrowing is finished. It holds until tomorrow morning’s round replaces it.

WHY THE ROUND CAME DOWN

Because of where each round caught the market, not because anything changed its mind.

At 09:09, when the morning round was struck, the 10-year gilt yield was 4.3bp above yesterday’s close — and it went on to peak at 4.7bp a few minutes later, the high of the day so far. By 12:32, when the afternoon round was struck, it was 3.3bp. A basis point lower on the curve, and the round came in two lower.

In between, the gilt auction at 10:00 was absorbed without stress — it cleared at 5.155% against 5.040% at the previous one, and yields fell rather than rose afterwards. That was the day’s single largest risk and it passed quietly.

So the shape of the day is a gap higher overnight, a morning round struck on that gap, and a gradual walk back through the session. The overnight move was the event; London has spent the day partially undoing it.

THE DAY IN FULL

Three rounds now sit in the recent record, and the 10-year maturity rate tells the story:

  • 316/26, 12:22 yesterday — 6.08%
  • 317/26, 09:09 today — 6.15%, up 7bp
  • 318/26, 12:32 today — 6.13%, down 2bp

Net, today has added 5bp to the cost of ten-year borrowing. That is a real move on a day when the domestic data argued the other way: unemployment came in at 4.9% against 4.8% expected, employment rose 83,000 against a forecast 200,000, payrolls fell, and productivity missed. None of it mattered next to a global long end at multi-decade highs.

Gilt yields have eased further since the round: the 10-year is 5.071%, 2.2bp above yesterday’s close, and the 50-year is back to 0.2bp. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.147%, 0.4bp up. Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path unchanged with a 25bp rise still expected in November.

TOMORROW

On the market at 13:19, tomorrow morning’s round would come in a shade below today’s close of business — 6.122% on the 10-year against the 6.13% in force, and 6.563% on the 50-year against 6.57%. Under a basis point, and a full afternoon and overnight session sit in front of it.

Tomorrow at 07:00 is the week’s event: inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. It prints before the morning round and can therefore reach it, exactly as this morning’s labour figures did. A rise of that size on a curve already at these levels is the risk worth planning around, and it is the one number this week most likely to move a borrowing decision.

One counterpoint logged this morning and worth carrying into it: grocery price inflation slowed to 2.1%, its lowest in two years.

Still to come today: US building permits and housing starts at 13:30. Both land after today’s final round, so they shape tomorrow morning rather than anything still available now.

12:20PULSEupdate

PM fixing call — the morning's small discount has closed; the lunchtime round now looks level with this morning's

PWLB 10y — in force6.15%PWLB 10y — certainty5.95%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.150% (level)1y SONIA swap4.145% (+0.3bp)

The lunchtime round has not reached us. On recent sessions it strikes shortly after 12:25; the rates in force remain notice 317/26 from 09:09 — 6.15% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.95% with the certainty discount.

More

On the market at 12:17 it would come in level with this morning's. The 10-year at 6.150% against 6.15%, the 20-year 6.699% against 6.70%, the 2-year unchanged at 5.33%. An hour ago the same estimate sat about a basis point below the round in force; that discount has closed, and anyone who held off this morning expecting a cheaper lunchtime round no longer has one.

The exception is the long end. The 50-year would come in at 6.568% against 6.59% in force — 2.2bp below, and the only line on the sheet with a real gap. It was 2.8bp at 10:18, so it is narrowing too.

Gilts have drifted back up through the late morning after the auction rally faded: 10-year 5.082%, now 3.3bp above yesterday's close having been 2.3bp at 10:14. The 20-year is 2.9bp up and the 30-year 2.4bp. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.145%, back above yesterday.

The reason is the same one that has run all day and is now re-asserting: oil extended its gains as peace prospects dimmed, European bond yields are reported at multi-year highs on Iran-related inflation fears, and US 30-year Treasury yields are again at their highest since 2007.

US building permits and housing starts at 13:30 land after the lunchtime round, so they shape tomorrow morning — as does tomorrow's 07:00 inflation figure, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%, which remains the week's event.

10:18PULSEupdate

The gilt auction passed without stress — cleared 5.155%, and yields eased after it. The morning's rise is more than half given back

PWLB 10y — in force6.15%PWLB 10y — certainty5.95%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.141% (-0.9bp)1y SONIA swap4.144% (+0.2bp)

The Treasury gilt 2036 auction cleared at 5.155%, against 5.040% at the previous one. That is the number the market was waiting on, and we flagged it twice this morning as the single event most likely to move the lunchtime round.

More

It did not. Gilts firmed slightly into the auction — the 10-year yield at 3.3bp above yesterday's close as it opened — and have eased steadily since, reaching us at 2.3bp by 10:14. A higher clearing yield than the last auction is what a market at multi-decade highs produces; being absorbed without a sell-off afterwards is the part that matters, and it was.

The morning's rise is now more than half given back. Against yesterday's close: 2-year 4.350% (+0.5bp), 5-year 4.592% (+0.7bp), 10-year 5.073% (+2.4bp), 20-year 5.746% (+1.9bp), 30-year 5.827% (+1.5bp), 50-year 5.379% (+0.2bp). The 10-year peaked at 4.7bp shortly after this morning's round struck.

317/26 remains the standing price — 6.15% on the 10-year, 5.95% with the certainty discount. On the market at 10:14 the lunchtime round would come in a little below it: 6.141% on the 10-year, 6.562% on the 50-year. Still under a basis point at the 10-year and we would not act on that, though the long end has drifted further: the 50-year estimate is 2.8bp below the rate in force.

Elsewhere the global story has not gone away — the French 10-year yield is reported at its highest since 2008, following the German and US markers earlier. Euro area ZEW sentiment beat sharply at 34.2 against a forecast 30.

Still to come: US building permits and housing starts at 13:30, after the lunchtime round, so they shape tomorrow morning. Tomorrow at 07:00 is inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%.

Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against yesterday’s final round:

  • 2-year 5.33% standard — 5.13% certainty — up 5bp

The annuity and equal-instalment sheets moved with it, 4 to 8bp across the curve. Nothing was spared and nothing fell: this is a uniform repricing, not a rotation.

317/26 is now the standing price, and remains so until the lunchtime round replaces it.

WHY, AND IT IS NOT THE LABOUR MARKET

This morning’s UK labour figures were weak — unemployment at 4.9% against 4.8% expected, employment up 83,000 against a forecast 200,000, payrolls down 13,000. On their own those argue for lower rates and lower yields.

They were outvoted overnight. Long-dated government borrowing costs are at multi-decade highs across the major economies: the German 10-year bund yield is reported at its highest since March 2011, and US 30-year yields at their highest since 2007. A US-Iran ceasefire expired, oil rose, and a vessel was reported hit in the Strait of Hormuz before the London open.

The gilt market gapped on that overnight, and this round was struck on the gap. Sterling has fallen from a three-month high and the 10-year gilt yield reached a three-week high this morning. Productivity, published at 09:30, fell 0.8% against a forecast 0.5% — another soft domestic number that has not touched the direction of travel.

WHERE THAT LEAVES A BORROWER

Yesterday’s standing price, 316/26 at 6.08% on the 10-year, was available until 09:09 this morning. It has been replaced by one 7bp higher. Anyone who drew on it yesterday afternoon or first thing has that price; the comparison from here is a different one.

From here, the question is 317/26 against the lunchtime round. On the market at 09:44 the lunchtime round would come in fractionally below this morning’s — the 10-year at 6.142% against 6.15%, the 50-year 6.567% against 6.59%. That is under a basis point on the 10-year and we would not describe it as an opportunity: it is inside the noise, and three hours of a volatile market sit in front of it.

What would make it a real question is the auction below.

THE AUCTION, IN MINUTES

10:00 — the Treasury gilt 2036 auction, last cleared at 5.040%. It lands between this morning’s round and the lunchtime one, into a long end that has been at multi-decade highs overnight.

An auction into a market like this is where stress shows up first, and it is the single thing today most likely to move the lunchtime round in either direction. We will report the outcome when it reaches us.

Also today: euro area ZEW sentiment at 10:00, and US building permits and housing starts at 13:30 — the latter after the lunchtime round, so they shape tomorrow morning.

Tomorrow at 07:00 is the week’s event: inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. One counterpoint logged this morning: grocery price inflation slowed to 2.1%, a two-year low. Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise in November.

We will report the new figures when they arrive, and we will not characterise the lender's timing from the moment we happen to see them.

More

On the market at 09:15, the round would come in about 7.3bp above those. The 10-year maturity rate would be 6.153%, or 5.953% with the certainty discount; the 20-year 6.707%; the 5-year 5.645%; the 50-year 6.570%. At 08:15 that same estimate was 6.1bp — the market has added roughly another basis point through the first hour of trading, and it has been in one direction all morning.

Gilts have edged further from the open rather than settling back: 10-year 5.096%, now 4.7bp above yesterday's close, the 20-year 4.3bp and the 30-year 3.8bp. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.155%, 1.3bp up.

The global driver is still running — US 30-year yields are reported at their highest since 2007, with war and oil the cited reasons, and oil rose again after the US–Iran ceasefire expired.

One counterpoint worth logging for tomorrow. Grocery price inflation slowed to 2.1%, its lowest in two years. Tomorrow's headline CPI is forecast at 2.9% against 2.6% last, and this is the first read this week arguing the other way.

10:00 — the Treasury gilt 2036 auction, last cleared 5.040%. It lands in roughly forty minutes into a long end that has risen every hour since it opened.

✖ Notice 316/26 stands at 6.08% on the 10-year — 5.88% with the certainty discount — until this morning’s round replaces it, which on recent sessions is between 09:00 and 09:15. On the market at 08:15 its replacement would come in at 6.141%, or 5.941% certainty. That is a standing price roughly 6bp below where the next one is estimated, with a known expiry. This is the clearest draw-now case we have reported in a fortnight — but it is an estimate of an unstruck round, not a rate, and the market has forty-five minutes left to change its mind.
The global bond move won, and it was not close. Gilts gapped higher at the open despite the weak labour figures — the 10-year yield is 5.085%, 3.5bp above yesterday’s close. This morning’s round now looks about 6bp above the one in force, and the one in force is still available until it strikes.
HOW GILTS OPENED

Against yesterday’s close, at the last prints to reach us:

  • 2-year 4.367% — up 2.1bp
  • 5-year 4.604% — up 2.0bp
  • 10-year 5.085% — up 3.5bp
  • 20-year 5.758% — up 3.0bp
  • 30-year 5.842% — up 2.9bp
  • 50-year 5.400% — up 2.3bp

The move was a gap, not a drift. Yields opened between 2.0 and 3.3bp above yesterday’s close and have moved very little since — a few tenths either way in the first quarter-hour. So this was decided overnight, before London could trade it.

The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.149%, 0.7bp above yesterday.

THE LABOUR FIGURES DID NOT HOLD IT BACK

At 07:25 we set out two forces pulling in opposite directions and said we would not guess which won. The answer is now in: the global one, comfortably.

A softening jobs market with cooling pay would ordinarily argue for lower yields. It did not get the chance. Overnight the wires carried long-term government borrowing costs at their highest in decades across the major economies; a US-Iran ceasefire expired and oil rose; and before the London open a vessel was reported hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. Against that, a domestic labour release is a second-order input.

The labour data has not been ignored so much as outvoted. Economists quoted this morning read the cooling labour market as supporting rate cuts; the gilt market has priced the opposite, because what is moving it is not the Bank of England.

WHAT IT DOES TO THIS MORNING’S ROUND

On the market at 08:15, the round striking shortly would come in above the one in force across the whole curve. Standard maturity rates, certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside:

  • 2-year 5.321% — 5.121% certainty — about 4.1bp above the round in force
  • 5-year 5.637% — 5.437% certainty — about 5.7bp above
  • 10-year 6.141% — 5.941% certainty — about 6.1bp above
  • 20-year 6.694% — 6.494% certainty — about 6.4bp above
  • 50-year 6.571% — 6.371% certainty — about 6.1bp above

For scale: last night’s close implied about 2.6bp on the 10-year. The overnight move has added roughly three and a half basis points to that estimate before the market opened.

These are estimates of a round whose rates have not reached us. They move with the market until they do, and we will report the actual figures when they arrive — not before, and without characterising the lender’s timing from the moment we happen to see them.

THE REST OF TODAY

10:00 — the Treasury gilt 2036 auction, last cleared at 5.040%. This now matters more than it did at 07:00: an auction into a long end that has gapped higher overnight is where stress shows up first, and it lands between this morning’s round and the lunchtime one.

Also: euro area ZEW sentiment at 10:00 (forecast 30 against 26.3), and US building permits and housing starts at 13:30, which land after the lunchtime round and therefore shape tomorrow morning.

Tomorrow at 07:00 is the week’s event: inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. On a curve that has just gapped higher, a rise of that size is the risk worth planning around.

Bank Rate is 3.75%, the path still showing a 25bp rise at the November meeting to 4.00%. Nothing this morning has changed it — which is rather the point: this is a gilt story, not a Bank Rate story.

07:25STORYbrief

Labour market weaker than forecast at 07:00 — and it prints before this morning's round, but the global long end sold off overnight

PWLB 10y — in force6.08%PWLB 10y — certainty5.88%PWLB 10y — est (stale)6.106%1y SONIA swap4.142%

Six labour market figures at 07:00, and the direction of travel is a softening jobs market with pay easing. Unemployment held at 4.9% where 4.8% was expected. Employment rose 83,000 against a forecast of 200,000 — the largest miss on the sheet. HMRC payrolls fell 13,000 against an expected +5,000. Two cut the other way: the claimant count fell 11,000 where a rise was expected, and earnings excluding bonuses came in a tenth hot at 3.5%. Earnings including bonuses were in line at 4.1%, down from a revised 4.4%.

More

It prints roughly two hours before the morning round strikes, so it is an input to today's rates, not tomorrow's.

But overnight the global long end sold off hard. Wires report long-term government borrowing costs at their highest in decades across the major economies, with bond investors described as "in revolt", and oil up after a US–Iran ceasefire expired. That is the standing story of the past fortnight escalating, not settling.

So two forces pull the round in opposite directions: a domestic release arguing for lower yields, a global move pushing them higher. The gilt market opens at 08:00 and we do not know which wins until it does.

Notice 316/26 is the standing price until the round replaces it — 6.08% on the 10-year, 5.88% with the certainty discount. On last night's close alone the round would have come in about 2.6bp above it, but that number contains none of this morning's news and is shown only as a starting point.

Also today: a Treasury gilt 2036 auction at 10:00 (last cleared 5.040%), which is where stress shows up first on a morning like this. Tomorrow 07:00 is the week's event — inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%.

⚠ The estimates below are anchored to last night’s close and do not contain either of this morning’s two events. They carry neither the labour market figures nor the overnight move in global bonds. Treat them as where yesterday finished, not as a forecast of today’s round. The first honest read comes after the market opens at 08:00, in the 08:15 edition.
The labour market came in weaker than forecast at 07:00, and it prints before this morning’s round — so it can reach it. Unemployment held at 4.9% where 4.8% was expected, and employment rose 83,000 against a forecast of 200,000. But overnight the global long end sold off hard, and those two pull the round in opposite directions. The gilt market opens at 08:00; until it does we do not know which wins.
THE LABOUR MARKET, 07:00

Six figures landed together. Forecast in brackets:

  • Unemployment rate 4.9% (4.8% expected, 4.9% last) — the headline, and higher than expected
  • Employment change +83,000 (+200,000 expected, +147,000 last) — the largest miss on the sheet
  • HMRC payrolls -13,000 (+5,000 expected) — payrolls fell
  • Claimant count -11,000 (+11,200 expected) — fewer claimants, the one figure that came in better
  • Average earnings including bonus 4.1% (4.1% expected, revised 4.4% last) — in line, and cooling
  • Average earnings excluding bonus 3.5% (3.4% expected) — a tenth hotter

The direction of travel is a softening labour market with pay growth easing. Jobs growth well below forecast, payrolls falling outright, unemployment refusing to come down. Two figures cut the other way — the claimant count fell, and earnings excluding bonuses were a shade above forecast — so this is not a clean read, and early press comment notes public sector pay as the reason headline wage growth held up.

On its own, softer jobs and cooling pay is the combination that argues for lower rates: gilt yields would fall, so borrowing would get cheaper. On its own.

THE OTHER THING THAT HAPPENED OVERNIGHT

While that was being prepared, the global bond market moved against borrowers, and hard. Wires overnight report long-term government borrowing costs at their highest in decades across the major economies, with one describing bond investors as being “in revolt”. Oil is up after the expiry of a US-Iran ceasefire, with Iran threatening to go, in the reporting’s words, “fully offensive” in the Strait of Hormuz.

This is the standing story this publication has carried for a fortnight — the one that reached a marker yesterday afternoon at “highest since the 2008 crisis” — and it has escalated overnight rather than settled.

So the morning sets two forces against each other: a domestic release arguing for lower yields, and a global move pushing them higher. We are not going to pretend to know which wins, and anyone who tells you before 08:00 is guessing.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR TODAY’S ROUND

The 07:00 release lands roughly two hours before the morning round strikes, so it is an input to today’s rates, not tomorrow’s. So is anything the market does between the 08:00 open and the strike.

Until then, notice 316/26 is the standing price — 6.08% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.88% with the certainty discount, struck at 12:22 yesterday. It remains available until this morning’s round replaces it. That is the comparison worth holding: a price you can have now, against a round whose direction is genuinely uncertain for the first time in several sessions.

On last night’s close alone, before any of this morning’s news, the round would have come in about 2.6bp above yesterday’s on the 10-year. That number is already out of date and is shown only as the starting point this morning moves from.

THE REST OF TODAY

Still to come:

  • 09:30 — labour productivity, forecast -0.5% against 0.9% last. Lands after the morning round.
  • 10:00 — euro area ZEW economic sentiment, forecast 30 against 26.3. High impact for the bloc.
  • 10:00 — a Treasury gilt 2036 auction, with the last one clearing at 5.040%. Worth watching on a morning when the long end is under this much pressure: an auction into a weak market is where stress shows up first.
  • 13:30 — US building permits and housing starts. After the lunchtime round, so they shape tomorrow morning.

Tomorrow at 07:00 is the week’s event: inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. A rise of that size, on a curve already at these levels and with the global long end selling off, is the thing to have in view all week.

Bank Rate is 3.75%. The path still has the next move as a 25bp rise at the November meeting, to 4.00% — and this morning’s labour figures are the first data in a while to argue against it.

THE DAY IN ONE LINE

A day that did almost nothing for eight hours and then moved in the last ninety minutes.

Both rounds were quiet. Notice 315/26 at 09:05 set the 10-year maturity rate at 6.07%, up 4bp on Friday, and 316/26 at 12:22 moved it a single basis point to 6.08%. Between them the market drifted slightly in the borrower’s favour: for most of the afternoon the long end sat below Friday’s close and the 10-year barely above it.

From 16:00 that reversed, steadily and across every tenor at once, and it held into the close.

WHERE GILTS FINISHED

Yields at the settled close, against Friday’s close:

  • 2-year 4.346% — up 0.1bp, effectively unchanged
  • 5-year 4.584% — up 3.7bp, the day’s biggest move
  • 10-year 5.049% — up 3.1bp
  • 20-year 5.728% — up 2.6bp
  • 30-year 5.813% — up 2.5bp
  • 50-year 5.377% — up 2.0bp

The 10-year traded a range of about 5bp: 1.4bp below Friday at its lowest, 3.5bp above at its highest, and it finished near the top of that range. Higher yields mean a higher cost of borrowing, so the day ended against the borrower after spending most of it mildly in their favour.

The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.142%, 1.5bp above Friday, having been level with it at lunchtime. Bank Rate is 3.75%, and the path still has the next move as a 25bp rise at the November meeting, to 4.00% — untouched by any of today.

WHAT WE SAID AT 16:20, AND WHAT WE KNOW NOW

At 16:20 we reported the move and said plainly that we could not explain it: there had been no UK release, and nothing on the wires accounted for a curve-wide rise. We said that if a reason emerged we would say so.

Something did, and it is context rather than an explanation. At 16:13 a wire item reported that borrowing costs across the leading economies have reached their highest since the 2008 crisis — France, Germany, the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom together. That is the standing global story this publication has been carrying for a fortnight, reaching a marker worth naming.

It fits, and we will not claim more than that. The item reached us during the move rather than before it, and a headline restating a backdrop is not the same as a trigger. What can be said honestly is that gilts rose into the close on a day when the global long end was the only story running, and that the two are consistent.

TOMORROW MORNING’S ROUND

On the closing market, tomorrow’s first round would come in above today’s across the curve. Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside:

  • 2-year 5.299% standard — 5.099% certainty — about 1.9bp above today
  • 5-year 5.617% standard — 5.417% certainty — about 3.7bp above
  • 10-year 6.106% standard — 5.906% certainty — about 2.6bp above
  • 20-year 6.664% standard — 6.464% certainty — about 3.4bp above
  • 50-year 6.548% standard — 6.348% certainty — about 3.8bp above

Treat these as where the market closed, not as where the round will land. A whole overnight session sits in front of them, and so does a UK labour market release.

Today’s borrowing is finished. Notice 316/26 — 6.08% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.88% with the certainty discount — is the standing price until tomorrow morning’s round replaces it. It is a standing price with an expiry, not a past event: it can be acted on until it is replaced, and on tonight’s market its replacement looks dearer.

TOMORROW AND THE WEEK

Tomorrow, 07:00 — unemployment rate, forecast 4.8% against 4.9% last. It prints three hours before the morning round and can therefore reach it. The rest of the labour market release lands with it: average earnings including bonus, forecast 4.1% against 4.3%, and employment change, forecast +200.0K against +147K.

Wednesday, 07:00 — inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. This is the week’s event, and a forecast rise of that size on a curve already at these levels is the thing to watch.

Friday, 07:00 — retail sales, forecast -0.3% against 1.0%.

Also tomorrow: a Treasury gilt 2036 auction at 09:00, which sits between the unemployment print and the morning round.

ELSEWHERE

Slough. The department published correspondence this evening on the appointment of a Managing Director Commissioner at Slough Borough Council, with an updated explanatory memorandum. Filed for the council shelf; we have not yet read the papers and will report on them properly rather than from the announcement.

Oil and the Gulf. Iran threatened to go on the offensive in the Strait of Hormuz if diplomacy with the United States fails. Crude swung through the session without settling in a direction. This is the standing inflation risk behind Wednesday’s figure and the reason it stays in view.

China. Industrial output (4.5% against 5.0% forecast) and retail sales (0.6%) both came in below forecast this morning, and the reporting since suggests the slowdown is extending.

Japan. Preliminary quarterly growth of 0.3% against a 0.5% forecast, and the 10-year yield reached a 30-year high. Japan is the sharpest edge of the long-end story and it moved again today.

EVERY INPUT READING NORMALLY

All of it, for the first time since lunchtime: the economic calendar, the PWLB fixing feed, gilt benchmarks, SONIA and the Bank Rate path. Twenty-three of twenty-four news sources reachable.

Gilt levels in this edition are the settled close, timed 17:59. Our sight of the market runs behind it; where we give a time, it is when a price reached us, not when it traded.

Gilts sold off into the close, and the whole curve finished above Friday. The 5-year ended 3.8bp higher and the 10-year 3.3bp, almost all of it after 16:00. Tomorrow morning’s round would come in around 2.8bp above today’s on the 10-year — but tomorrow opens with the unemployment figure at 07:00, which prints before the round and can reach it.
THE DAY IN ONE LINE

A day that did almost nothing for eight hours and then moved in the last ninety minutes.

Both rounds were quiet. Notice 315/26 at 09:05 set the 10-year maturity rate at 6.07%, up 4bp on Friday, and 316/26 at 12:22 moved it a single basis point to 6.08%. Between them the market drifted slightly in the borrower’s favour: for most of the afternoon the long end sat below Friday’s close and the 10-year barely above it.

From 16:00 that reversed, steadily and across every tenor at once, and it held into the close.

WHERE GILTS FINISHED

Yields at the last prints to reach us, against Friday’s close:

  • 2-year 4.346% — up 0.1bp, effectively unchanged
  • 5-year 4.585% — up 3.8bp, the day’s biggest move
  • 10-year 5.051% — up 3.3bp
  • 20-year 5.726% — up 2.5bp
  • 30-year 5.812% — up 2.4bp
  • 50-year 5.376% — up 2.0bp

The 10-year traded a range of about 5bp: 1.4bp below Friday at its lowest, 3.5bp above at its highest, and it finished within a whisker of the high. Higher yields mean a higher cost of borrowing, so the day ended against the borrower after spending most of it mildly in their favour.

The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.143%, 1.6bp above Friday, having been level with it at lunchtime. Bank Rate is 3.75%, and the path still has the next move as a 25bp rise at the November meeting, to 4.00% — untouched by any of today.

WHAT WE SAID AT 16:20, AND WHAT WE KNOW NOW

At 16:20 we reported the move and said plainly that we could not explain it: there had been no UK release, and nothing on the wires accounted for a curve-wide rise. We said that if a reason emerged we would say so.

Something did, and it is context rather than an explanation. At 16:13 a wire item reported that borrowing costs across the leading economies have reached their highest since the 2008 crisis — France, Germany, the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom together. That is the standing global story this publication has been carrying for a fortnight, reaching a marker worth naming.

It fits, and we will not claim more than that. The item reached us during the move rather than before it, and a headline restating a backdrop is not the same as a trigger. What can be said honestly is that gilts rose into the close on a day when the global long end was the only story running, and that the two are consistent.

TOMORROW MORNING’S ROUND

On the closing market, tomorrow’s first round would come in above today’s across the curve. Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside:

  • 2-year 5.300% standard — 5.100% certainty — about 2.0bp above today
  • 5-year 5.617% standard — 5.417% certainty — about 3.7bp above
  • 10-year 6.108% standard — 5.908% certainty — about 2.8bp above
  • 20-year 6.663% standard — 6.463% certainty — about 3.3bp above
  • 50-year 6.547% standard — 6.347% certainty — about 3.7bp above

Treat these as where the market closed, not as where the round will land. A whole overnight session sits in front of them, and so does a UK labour market release.

Today’s borrowing is finished. Notice 316/26 — 6.08% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.88% with the certainty discount — is the standing price until tomorrow morning’s round replaces it. It is a standing price with an expiry, not a past event: it can be acted on until it is replaced, and on tonight’s market its replacement looks dearer.

TOMORROW AND THE WEEK

Tomorrow, 07:00 — unemployment rate, forecast 4.8% against 4.9% last. It prints three hours before the morning round and can therefore reach it. The rest of the labour market release lands with it: average earnings including bonus, forecast 4.1% against 4.3%, and employment change, forecast +200.0K against +147K.

Wednesday, 07:00 — inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%. This is the week’s event, and a forecast rise of that size on a curve already at these levels is the thing to watch.

Friday, 07:00 — retail sales, forecast -0.3% against 1.0%.

Also tomorrow: a Treasury gilt 2036 auction at 09:00, which sits between the unemployment print and the morning round.

ELSEWHERE

Slough. The department published correspondence this evening on the appointment of a Managing Director Commissioner at Slough Borough Council, with an updated explanatory memorandum. Filed for the council shelf; we have not yet read the papers and will report on them properly rather than from the announcement.

Oil and the Gulf. Iran threatened to go on the offensive in the Strait of Hormuz if diplomacy with the United States fails. Crude swung through the session without settling in a direction. This is the standing inflation risk behind Wednesday’s figure and the reason it stays in view.

China. Industrial output (4.5% against 5.0% forecast) and retail sales (0.6%) both came in below forecast this morning, and the reporting since suggests the slowdown is extending.

Japan. Preliminary quarterly growth of 0.3% against a 0.5% forecast, and the 10-year yield reached a 30-year high. Japan is the sharpest edge of the long-end story and it moved again today.

A NOTE ON WHAT REACHED US

The economic calendar’s usual source has been unreachable since about 13:40 and remains so. The agenda above comes by an alternative route to the same publisher, carrying the same identifiers, and we have verified the figures line up. Rates, gilt yields, SONIA and the Bank Rate path all read normally throughout.

Gilt levels in this edition are the last prints to reach us, timed 17:16. Our sight of the market runs behind it; where we give a time, it is when a price reached us, not when it traded.

16:20PULSEupdate

A late push higher: the whole curve is above Friday for the first time today, and tomorrow's round would come in about 2.4bp above today's

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.08%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.104% (+2.4bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.607% (+2.7bp)1y SONIA swap4.140% (+1.2bp)

The afternoon did nothing for two hours and then moved. From 14:00 to 16:00 the curve sat still. In the prints reaching us since, it has risen steadily — every tenor together, minute after minute to about 16:13, easing slightly into the last reading at 16:16.

More

That has taken the whole curve above Friday's close for the first time today. The long end had been below it all session:

- 2-year 4.348%, +0.3bp on Friday — was 1.0bp below it at 16:00 - 5-year 4.574%, +2.7bp - 10-year 5.047%, +2.8bp - 20-year 5.718%, +1.7bp - 30-year 5.803%, +1.5bp — was 0.1bp above it at 16:00 - 50-year 5.364%, +0.7bp — was a shade below

What that does to tomorrow morning's round. On the market at 16:16 it would come in about 2.4bp above today's on the 10-year — 6.104% against the 6.08% in force, 5.904% against 5.88% with the certainty discount. At 15:27 we put that at 1.5bp. The estimate has moved and this is the number that matters: a whole overnight session and the unemployment print still sit in front of it, so treat it as where the market stands, not where the round will land.

The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.140%, 1.2bp above Friday, having been level with it at lunchtime.

We cannot tell you why. There was no UK release today, and nothing on the wires in that window accounts for a curve-wide move — the last market note to reach us was on crude oil. A late move on a quiet Monday with no visible trigger is worth reporting and not worth explaining. If a reason emerges we will say so.

One caveat on timing: these are the last prints we have, not a close. Our sight of the market runs behind it, and if further prints arrive the shape may yet change.

Tomorrow the domestic week starts. Unemployment at 07:00, forecast 4.8% against 4.9% last — it prints before the morning round and can therefore reach it. Then Wednesday's inflation figure, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%, which is the week's event.

Today's borrowing is done. Notice 316/26 — 6.08% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.88% with the certainty discount — is the standing price until tomorrow morning's round replaces it.

THE AFTERNOON ROUND — NOTICE 316/26

Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against this morning’s round:

  • 2-year 5.28% standard — 5.08% certainty — unchanged
  • 5-year 5.58% standard — 5.38% certainty — up 1bp
  • 10-year 6.08% standard — 5.88% certainty — up 1bp
  • 20-year 6.63% standard — 6.43% certainty — up 1bp
  • 25-year 6.71% standard — 6.51% certainty — up 1bp
  • 50-year 6.51% standard — 6.31% certainty — up 1bp

As quiet a round as this publication has reported. The equal-instalment 2-year is the only line on the whole sheet that fell, by a single basis point; the 50-year annuity rate is the only one that rose by more than one, by two.

That matches what the estimates said all morning: from the 09:33 fixing report onwards, the afternoon round looked level with the morning, and it was.

A CORRECTION ABOUT TIMING — AND WHY IT KEEPS HAPPENING

Our 12:46 note said the round had not struck and was running late. It had struck at 12:22. The figures did not reach us until shortly before 12:50.

This is the third time in three sessions that the same gap has caught us out, in three different disguises: on Friday we called a market move “delayed” when our view of it was; this morning we announced a round as “striking about now” nineteen minutes after it had struck; and this afternoon we called a round late when it was not.

The rule we set on Friday was to describe when a price reached us rather than when it traded. That plainly has to cover the lender as well as the market. We do not know when a round strikes until its rates arrive, and the interval between those two moments is ours, not theirs.

THE DAY IN FULL

Two rounds, and between them almost nothing happened:

  • 315/26, 09:05 — 10-year 6.07%, up 4bp on Friday’s close. The middle of the curve moved most.
  • 316/26, 12:22 — 10-year 6.08%, up 1bp on the morning.

So the whole of today’s increase, 5bp on the 10-year against Friday, was set at 09:05 on a market that had already moved over the weekend. The London session itself was almost inert.

Gilt yields say the same. They opened below Friday’s close, drifted sideways for four hours and are still below it at the short and long ends — the 2-year down 2.1bp, the 30-year down 1.5bp — while the 10-year has edged 0.4bp above. Falling yields mean cheaper borrowing, so the day’s drift has been mildly in the borrower’s favour without being enough to show up in a rate. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.116%, down 1.2bp, still unwinding Friday afternoon’s rise.

Bank Rate is 3.75%, next move expected November 2026 — untouched by any of it.

TOMORROW

Today’s borrowing is finished; 316/26 is the standing price until tomorrow morning’s round replaces it. On the market at 12:49 that round would come in about a basis point above today’s — 6.081% on the 10-year, 6.634% on the 20-year — but a whole afternoon and an overnight session sit in front of it.

Tomorrow the domestic week begins. Unemployment at 07:00, forecast 4.8% against 4.9% last, printing before that morning’s round and therefore able to reach it. Then Wednesday’s inflation figure, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%, which is the week’s event.

The standing global risk is unchanged and worth keeping in view: long-dated government borrowing has been getting dearer across the major economies, with Japan’s 10-year yield reaching a 30-year high this morning after the United States sold 30-year bonds at a 25-year high cost last week.

THE MORNING ROUND — NOTICE 315/26

The round struck at 09:05. Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against Friday’s lunchtime round:

  • 2-year 5.28% standard — 5.08% certainty — up 2bp
  • 5-year 5.57% standard — 5.37% certainty — up 3bp
  • 10-year 6.07% standard — 5.87% certainty — up 4bp
  • 20-year 6.62% standard — 6.42% certainty — up 4bp
  • 25-year 6.70% standard — 6.50% certainty — up 4bp
  • 50-year 6.50% standard — 6.30% certainty — up 3bp

The shape is worth a moment. Friday’s move was led by the very long end; this round is led by the middle — the 10-, 20- and 25-year all up 4bp, with the 2-year and the 50-year up less. Annuity and equal-instalment rates moved 2 to 4bp on the same pattern.

WHAT IT COST TO WAIT

Friday’s round, notice 314/26, was the rate in force from 12:23 on Friday until this morning — through Friday afternoon, the weekend, and the first hour of trading today. It is now gone.

The difference, in money rather than basis points. On £10m over 20 years at the certainty rate, the 4bp step from 6.38% to 6.42% is roughly £4,000 a year, about £80,000 over the life of the loan. On the 10-year, 4bp is around £4,000 a year as well.

That is the practical content of this morning’s correction: the window in which Friday’s rate was available and the market had already moved past it lasted from Friday lunchtime until 09:05 today. It is closed now.

WHERE THE MARKET IS

Gilt yields are slightly below Friday’s close and have barely moved through the morning. At 09:30:

  • 2-year yield 4.325%, down 2.0bp on Friday
  • 10-year yield 5.016%, down 0.2bp
  • 20-year yield 5.685%, down 1.6bp
  • 30-year yield 5.765%, down 2.3bp
  • 50-year yield 5.330%, down 2.6bp

Falling yields mean cheaper borrowing, so the direction of travel this morning is mildly helpful — it simply arrived too late to spare this round from Friday’s damage. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.115%, down 1.3bp, so the front end has given back a little of what it picked up on Friday afternoon.

Bank Rate is 3.75% and the next move markets expect is still a rise in November 2026.

THE AFTERNOON ROUND, AND THE WEEK

On the market at 09:30 the afternoon round would come in level with the one that has just struck — 6.07% on the 10-year, 5.57% on the 5-year, 6.62% on the 20-year. No advantage either way as things stand, which means there is nothing to be gained or lost by choosing between the two rounds at this moment. It is worth checking again before committing: it has taken very little to move these estimates several basis points in a morning.

No UK data today. Tomorrow the domestic week starts — unemployment at 07:00, forecast 4.8% against 4.9% last, printing before that morning’s round. Then Wednesday’s inflation figure, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%, which is the week’s event and also lands before the round it can affect.

08:42PULSEcorrection

CORRECTION — we wrote that gilts 'opened cheaper' this morning. In market language that means the opposite of what we meant: gilt YIELDS fell, so borrowing got cheaper

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.03%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.069% (+3.9bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.567% (+2.7bp)1y SONIA swap4.119% (-0.9bp)

A bond's price and its yield move in opposite directions, so "cheap" and "dear" mean one thing about a gilt and the reverse about borrowing. "Gilts got cheaper" conventionally means prices fell and yields rose — borrowing got dearer. We used it to mean the opposite.

More

To be unambiguous about this morning: gilt yields have fallen, and that makes borrowing cheaper. At 08:39 the 10-year yield is 5.009%, down 1.0bp on Friday's close; the 30-year is 5.757%, down 3.1bp; the 50-year 5.322%, down 3.5bp. The estimate for this morning's round has come down with them, to 6.069% on the 10-year from 6.079% at 07:49.

The same error ran in reverse in Friday's end-of-day wrap, which said gilts "closed dearer" of a day when yields rose. The numbers and directions in both editions were right; the adjective was attached to the wrong thing. From here we will say what moved — yields, or the cost of borrowing — and let the direction carry it.

WHAT WE GOT WRONG

Four times since Friday afternoon — in Friday’s afternoon edition, Friday’s end-of-day wrap, the weekend read and this morning’s brief — we described the gap between a struck round and a market that moved afterwards as something councils could do nothing about. This morning’s brief put it as a gap “they had no chance to act on”.

That confuses two different things. It is true that a release landing after a round cannot change that round’s rates — it shapes the next one. It does not follow that a borrower is a spectator. PWLB rates are not a moment, they are a standing price with an expiry. The rate struck at 12:23 on Friday remained the rate in force through Friday afternoon, the weekend, and this morning until the next round replaces it.

So the correct reading of Friday is close to the opposite of ours. As the market sold off through Friday afternoon and our own estimates for the next round climbed, the already-struck 6.03% was becoming a better price by the hour — and it stayed on the table.

THE USEFUL VERSION OF THIS

Stated properly, it is the most actionable thing this publication can tell you, and it cuts both ways:

  • When the market moves against you after a round strikes, the standing rate is now below the market. It is an option with a known expiry — the next round. That is the moment to draw, not to wait.
  • When the market rallies after a round strikes, the standing rate is above the market. Waiting for the next round is what pays.

Which is the whole point of an estimate for the next round: not as a forecast for its own sake, but as a comparison against the price you can have right now.

Where that leaves the five headline maturities at 08:36, in force against estimated:

  • 2-year — in force 5.26%, next round estimated 5.291% (+3.1bp)
  • 5-year — in force 5.54%, estimated 5.576% (+3.6bp)
  • 10-year — in force 6.03%, estimated 6.075% (+4.5bp)
  • 20-year — in force 6.58%, estimated 6.622% (+4.2bp)
  • 50-year — in force 6.47%, estimated 6.492% (+2.2bp)

Certainty rates are 20bp below each of those standard rates.

WHAT WE HAVE NOT VERIFIED

One limit, stated plainly rather than glossed. We have not established PWLB’s cut-off for applications within a window — whether an application late in a window is priced at the rate then in force, or rolls to the next round. That determines how much of the window is genuinely usable, and it is a question of the lender’s operating practice rather than of the market.

So take the principle as sound and the timing as needing your own confirmation with the lender before you rely on the last minutes of a window. We would rather say that than repeat the mistake of asserting a mechanism we have not checked.

Everything else in this morning’s brief and in Friday’s editions — the rates, the moves, the estimates — stands. It is the conclusion drawn from them that was wrong.

 -2.7bp5.33%
✓ The gap councils inherited this morning has narrowed, and narrowed most where it was widest. At 07:49 the 50-year estimate stood 5.5bp above Friday’s round; it now stands 2.8bp above. The 20-year has come in from 5.9bp to 4.4bp. The round has not struck, and this can move back.
Chinese retail sales and industrial production both missed this morning, and gilts opened cheaper. The long end has given back the most: the 50-year estimate for today’s round has improved 2.7bp since our 07:49 brief, and unusually, this is data that can reach today’s rates.
THE FIGURES — AND WHY THEY COUNT TODAY

Two high-impact Chinese releases landed at 08:00, and both disappointed:

  • Retail sales — 0.6% on the year, against a 1.5% forecast and 1% last. A miss of nearly a full percentage point, and a slowdown rather than the expected pick-up.
  • Industrial production — 4.5%, against a 5.0% forecast and 5.3% last.

Reporting this morning also has China’s property downturn deepening on fresh data.

The timing is what makes this unusual. Nearly everything that moved borrowing costs last week arrived after the rounds had struck and could only reach the following day. These landed at 08:00, before this morning’s round — so for once, a non-UK release can reach a rate councils borrow at today.

WHERE THE MARKET OPENED

Gilts opened cheaper than Friday’s close — the first move in the borrower’s favour in three sessions. Levels at 08:34, against Friday:

  • 2-year gilt 4.327%, down 1.8bp
  • 5-year gilt 4.542%, down 0.5bp
  • 10-year gilt 5.015%, down 0.3bp
  • 20-year gilt 5.685%, down 1.6bp
  • 30-year gilt 5.764%, down 2.4bp
  • 50-year gilt 5.330%, down 2.7bp

Note the shape, because it is the exact mirror of Friday. Then, the further out you looked the worse it got; this morning, the further out you look the more has come back. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.119%, down 0.9bp.

We are not going to tell you the market fell because of China. The releases landed at 08:00 and these are readings taken 34 minutes later, which is not long enough to separate a response from the ordinary business of a Monday open — and our own view of prices carries a lag we cannot measure. What can be said is that the figures and the direction are consistent, and that weak Chinese demand is the kind of news that usually helps a bond market.

WHAT THE MORNING ROUND WOULD COME IN NEAR

Nothing has fixed today. The rate in force is still Friday’s lunchtime round, notice 314/26, at 6.03% on the 10-year. On the market at 08:34, the round striking shortly would come in near:

  • 2-year 5.286% standard — 5.086% certainty — up 2.6bp on Friday
  • 5-year 5.575% standard — 5.375% certainty — up 3.5bp
  • 10-year 6.076% standard — 5.876% certainty — up 4.6bp
  • 20-year 6.624% standard — 6.424% certainty — up 4.4bp
  • 50-year 6.498% standard — 6.298% certainty — up 2.8bp

Every one of those is still above Friday’s round — the week did not open cheap, it opened less expensive than it looked at breakfast. Set against our 07:49 estimates, the 50-year has improved 2.7bp, the 20-year 1.5bp and the 10-year 0.3bp.

These remain estimates of a round that has not struck. Rates publish at about 09:30.

THE REST OF THE DAY

No UK data today at all. After this morning’s round the only scheduled event of consequence is the lunchtime round itself, which on recent sessions has struck shortly after noon.

Tomorrow is where the domestic week starts — unemployment at 07:00, forecast 4.8% against 4.9% last, printing before that morning’s round. Then Wednesday’s inflation figure, forecast 2.9% against 2.6%, which is the week’s event.

The standing risks are unchanged from the brief: American long-dated supply, which set last week’s tone, and the oil price, which moved a morning round 10bp a week ago today.

WHERE THE WEEK STARTS

Nothing has fixed today. The rate in force is still Friday’s lunchtime round, notice 314/26, at 6.03% on the 10-year maturity rate.

These estimates are anchored on Friday’s close because the market has not opened yet. On that basis the round striking this morning would come in near:

  • 2-year 5.304% standard — 5.104% certainty — up 4.4bp on Friday
  • 5-year 5.579% standard — 5.379% certainty — up 3.9bp
  • 10-year 6.079% standard — 5.879% certainty — up 4.9bp
  • 20-year 6.639% standard — 6.439% certainty — up 5.9bp
  • 50-year 6.525% standard — 6.325% certainty — up 5.5bp

That gap exists because of when Friday’s rounds struck rather than anything that happened since. Both fixed before the American afternoon; gilts then finished the day 5.1 to 9.3bp dearer than Thursday, with the 30-year worst at 5.788%. None of that reached a borrowable rate on Friday. It reaches one this morning.

WEDNESDAY’S INFLATION FORECAST HAS BEEN CUT

Worth flagging early, because we have called it the month’s largest scheduled risk every day for a week. The forecast for Wednesday’s inflation figure has moved from 3.0% to 2.9%, against 2.6% last.

That is a smaller expected jump, not a smaller risk. A tenth off the forecast does not change the shape of the event: a reading meaningfully above 2.9% would still be the week’s worst outcome for borrowing costs, and it prints at 07:00, before that morning’s round rather than after it. Unlike most of last week’s news, it can reach a rate the same day.

Tuesday’s unemployment forecast has also moved, to 4.8% from 4.9%, against 4.9% last — so a fall is now expected rather than a hold. Friday’s retail sales forecast is −0.3%.

TODAY — AND WHICH ROUND IT REACHES

No UK data today. The morning’s releases are Chinese and they land at 08:00 — retail sales, forecast 1.5% against 1% last, and industrial production, forecast 5.0% against 5.3%. That is before this morning’s round strikes, so unusually for a non-UK release, it can reach today’s rates.

Overnight, Japanese growth missed: GDP rose 0.3% in the quarter against a 0.5% forecast and 0.5% previously.

Two threads from the weekend press bear watching, neither of them settled:

  • The American long end is now a UK story. Weekend coverage ties US bond-market strain to warnings about the UK economy. Goldman Sachs is arguing markets are too hawkish on the odds of the Federal Reserve raising rates — a view that, if it takes hold, would pull yields down rather than up.
  • Oil and the Strait of Hormuz. Renewed talk of the United States declaring the Strait its own territory. Oil is what moved the morning round 10bp on Tuesday last week, so this is the live risk to watch rather than a background story.

Also on the fiscal side, Jamie Dimon has publicly warned the Chancellor against higher bank taxes. Budget-adjacent noise rather than a rates event today, but the fiscal argument is what sets gilt supply, and supply is felt at the long end.

THE WEEK AHEAD

All three UK releases land at 07:00, before that morning’s round:

  • Tuesday — unemployment, forecast 4.8% against 4.9% last
  • Wednesday — inflation, forecast 2.9% against 2.6% last. The week’s event.
  • Friday — retail sales, forecast −0.3%

Bank Rate is 3.75% and the next move markets expect remains a rise in November 2026 — unchanged through all of last week’s movement. The 1-year SONIA swap ended Friday at 4.127%, up 2.6bp on the day, having been below Thursday’s close at lunchtime. The front end joined the move late on Friday, and whether it stays joined is the thing to watch this week.
