i The week's best domestic news changed nothing. Britain grew faster than any other G7 economy in the first half of the year, confirmed on Wednesday. Gilt yields rose anyway. When the price of long-dated borrowing is being set by American deficits and the oil price, good UK growth figures do not get a vote.
The 10-year maturity rate ended the week at 6.03%, 5bp above where it closed the week before — but that number hides the week rather than describing it. Borrowing costs were shoved twice by things that happened outside the United Kingdom, and both shoves landed at the long end.
THE WEEK

Ten rounds struck this week, and for most of them nothing much happened. The week was made by two days.

Tuesday was the shock. The morning round, notice 307/26, fixed the 10-year maturity rate at 6.09% — up 10bp on the previous afternoon, and the highest point of the week. The cause was oil: a repricing that pushed inflation expectations up across the curve. It was the single largest one-round move of the week and it happened before most people had read their email.

Wednesday and Thursday gave it back. 309/26 came in at 6.02%, five below Tuesday lunchtime; 310/26 at 6.00%. Thursday sat still at 6.01% for both rounds. By Thursday evening the week looked like a scare that had passed — the 10-year was a single basis point above where it had started on Monday morning.

Then Friday. The United States sold 30-year bonds at 5.216%, the highest cost since around 2001, and a 10-year auction the day before had drawn the steepest financing cost since 2007. That reached London overnight. Friday's rounds fixed at 6.03% both times — modest enough — but after the second round struck at 12:23, two weak American consumer readings landed and gilt yields kept climbing all afternoon. The market finished the day 4.4 to 9.2bp dearer depending on maturity, with none of it reaching a rate anyone could borrow at.

That is the week's shape: the rounds moved 1 to 3bp on Friday while the market moved two to five times as much. Anyone who drew down on Friday got a price set before the day got expensive. Monday inherits the difference.

Certainty rates are 20bp lower throughout, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast. Dashes are maturities not recorded at that round rather than rates that did not move.

  • 10-year, week on week — 5.98% to 6.03%, up 5bp. High 6.09% Tuesday morning, low 5.97% Monday morning: a 12bp range.
  • 5-year — 5.49% to 5.54%, up 5bp. 20-year — 6.52% to 6.58%, up 6bp. 50-year — 6.47% at the close, up 3bp on Thursday alone.
  • 1-year SONIA swap — 4.127%, up 2.6bp on Friday alone, having been below Thursday's close at lunchtime.
  • Bank Rate — 3.75%, unchanged. Next move markets expect: a rise of 25bp in November 2026, also unchanged on the week.

Worth holding those last two together. Nothing this week changed what anyone expects the Bank of England to do. Everything this week changed what it costs to borrow for twenty or fifty years. Those are different markets, and this week only one of them moved.

WORTH YOUR TIME

We read five candidates this week and two earned your time. Both are free, both were published during the week under review, and between them they cover the two ends of the thing that actually drove your borrowing costs.

1. “Treasury Auction Yield Hits Highest in 25 Years”
Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, 14 August 2026 — crfb.org

Short, and the closest thing to a primary account of Friday's cause. It reports the $25bn 30-year auction clearing at 5.216% and goes past the headline to the demand detail that matters: a bid-to-cover of 2.39 and primary dealers left holding 11.5% of the issue, both weaker than their twelve-month averages, and an awarded yield above the when-issued level — the technical signature of a sale that struggled.

Why it earns your time: this is the event that made your Friday afternoon more expensive, described by people who follow the arithmetic rather than the drama. It is also a useful corrective to reading one auction as a crisis: the piece argues the pressure is structural — a debt path, not a bad day — which is precisely why the effect on the gilt long end did not reverse by the close. Read it for the mechanism, and hold the advocacy at arm's length; the CRFB campaigns for deficit reduction and the conclusion follows the campaign.

2. “Economy slows but doesn’t stall as the UK leads the G7 on growth”
Resolution Foundation, 13 August 2026 — resolutionfoundation.org

The domestic half. UK output grew 0.4% in the second quarter after 0.6% in the first, making Britain the fastest-growing G7 economy in the first half of the year, with 15 of 20 subsectors expanding and information and communications up 2.7% on AI investment. GDP per head rose 0.4%, close to its long-run average — though still 6.6% below the pre-pandemic trend.

Why it earns your time: for the sting in the tail, which is a borrowing story. The Foundation estimates that if the Office for Budget Responsibility marks down its forecasts on the war's energy and supply-chain effects, the hit could absorb around £6bn — roughly a quarter — of the Chancellor's fiscal headroom. Less headroom means more gilt issuance, and more issuance is felt at the long end, which is where councils borrow. It also explains something odd about this week: strong growth figures arrived on Wednesday and did nothing to borrowing costs, because the market is pricing supply and inflation rather than activity.

Three candidates were rejected on date alone — a gilt expected-returns piece from 4 August, a Bank of England decomposition of 2025 long rates from January, and an NIESR note on shortening gilt maturities from March. All three are worth reading; none of them is this week's news, and this section does not pad.

THE WEEK AHEAD

Monday’s round would come in near 6.079% on the 10-year maturity rate (5.879% certainty), 5.579% on the 5-year and 6.639% on the 20-year — 3.9 to 5.9bp above the rounds that struck on Friday. That is a close-anchored estimate of a round that has not struck, with a weekend in front of it.

Three UK releases, all at 07:00, all landing before that morning’s round rather than after it — so unlike most of last week's news, each one can reach a rate the same day:

  • Tuesday — unemployment, forecast 4.9%, unchanged on last.
  • Wednesday — inflation, forecast 3.0% against 2.6% last. The month’s largest scheduled risk to borrowing costs, and on this week’s evidence a surprise would be felt at the long end first.
  • Friday — retail sales, forecast −0.6%.

Globally, the thing most likely to move UK rates is the same one that moved them on Friday: American long-dated supply, and whether the weak consumer readings that closed last week turn into a growth story or stay a deficit story. The oil price is the other watch item, and it has already moved this month’s rates once.

WHAT COUNCILS ACTUALLY BORROWED AT

Two rounds, both struck, both now history:

  • 313/26, 09:25 — up 2bp across every maturity and every repayment type. A clean parallel shift.
  • 314/26, 12:23 — a twist: 1bp lower at the short end, unchanged in the middle, 1bp higher at 50 years.

Where the day left the standard maturity rates, against yesterday:

  • 2-year 5.26% — 5.06% certainty — up 1bp
  • 5-year 5.54% — 5.34% certainty — up 1bp
  • 10-year 6.03% — 5.83% certainty — up 2bp
  • 20-year 6.58% — 6.38% certainty — up 2bp
  • 50-year 6.47% — 6.27% certainty — up 3bp
WHAT THE MARKET DID AROUND THEM

Rather more. Gilts closed dearer right across the curve, and the further out you look the worse it got:

  • 2-year gilt 4.337%, up 4.4bp
  • 5-year gilt 4.555%, up 7.2bp
  • 10-year gilt 5.019%, up 6.9bp — through 5% and staying there
  • 20-year gilt 5.702%, up 8.3bp
  • 30-year gilt 5.781%, up 8.6bp
  • 50-year gilt 5.357%, up 8.9bp

That gap is the story of the day. It is not an inconsistency: the two rounds are photographs, taken at 09:25 and 12:23, and most of the day’s move showed up after the second one. The rates councils borrowed at today were set before the market got expensive.

Splitting where the move came from, using the minute-by-minute path: roughly a third of it was already in the price before London opened — between 2.1 and 3.6bp depending on maturity — carried in overnight from the United States, which sold 30-year bonds at the highest cost since around 2001. The remainder built up through the afternoon.

THE CHARACTER CHANGED DURING THE DAY

This is worth carrying into next week, because it is not the same market that opened this morning.

Through the morning the move was confined to the long end — the classic signature of investors demanding more to lend far into the future, while expectations for the next year or two sat still. At lunchtime the 1-year SONIA swap was 4.100%, marginally below yesterday.

It finished at 4.127%, up 2.6bp. The front end joined, and kept going. The rate-cut path itself did not move — Bank Rate 3.75%, next change markets expect still a rise in November 2026 — but the price of everything around it did.

Two American consumer readings missed badly today: retail sales at −0.6% against a +0.1% forecast, and Michigan sentiment at 51.0 against 54.5. Ordinarily weak consumer data argues for lower rates and cheaper borrowing. It went the other way. We are not going to invent a mechanism for that at the end of a Friday; we are recording it as the fact of the day.

A CORRECTION TO THIS AFTERNOON'S CORRECTION

At 13:51 we said gilts had “barely acknowledged” the retail sales miss, and corrected that at 14:18 when they plainly had. That correction stands.

The explanation attached to it does not. We wrote that a London reaction to a Washington release “can take the better part of an hour to arrive” — presenting the market as slow. We have no way of knowing that. This publication does not watch the live market: our own view of prices trails real time, and by how much is not something we can measure from where we sit. Only participants trading in it see it as it is.

So the honest account is narrower, and less flattering to us: the reading we published at 13:51 was already out of date when we published it. The market may well have moved at 13:30, on time, and simply not reached us. From here, times in this publication describe when a price reached us, not when it traded — and we will not characterise a market’s reaction until we have seen enough of it to be sure we are describing the market rather than our own delay.

MONDAY, AND THE WEEK

On the close, Monday morning’s round would come in near:

  • 2-year 5.296% — 5.096% certainty — up 3.6bp on today
  • 5-year 5.587% — 5.387% certainty — up 4.7bp
  • 10-year 6.079% — 5.879% certainty — up 4.9bp
  • 20-year 6.640% — 6.440% certainty — up 6.0bp
  • 50-year 6.526% — 6.326% certainty — up 5.6bp

These are close-anchored estimates of a round that has not struck, with a weekend in front of them — the market has two days to reconsider today before anyone can act on it.

Next week is where the domestic risk sits, and all three land at 07:00, before that morning’s round rather than after it:

  • Tuesday — unemployment, 4.9% forecast, 4.9% last
  • Wednesday — inflation, 3.0% forecast against 2.6% last. The month’s largest scheduled risk to borrowing costs.
  • Friday — retail sales, −0.6% forecast

On this week’s evidence, the long end is where a surprise would be felt. Have a good weekend.

⚠ Everything that has moved this afternoon lands on Monday, not today. Both of today’s rounds are struck and safe. But an authority that was planning to draw down on Monday has watched the estimate move against it three times since lunch — and there is a weekend in between, during which nothing can be done about it.
The verdict we held back at 15:02 is now in: the market did react, and it has kept going. The 10-year gilt has crossed 5% for the first time today and Monday morning’s round would now come in 4.1bp above the one that struck at lunchtime.
THE REACTION, NOW THAT THERE IS ONE

At 15:02 this publication reported the Michigan sentiment figure and explicitly declined to say what the market had made of it, on the grounds that two minutes is not long enough to know. Fifty minutes on, it is.

The market reacted, and the reaction did not stop:

  • 15:00 — 10-year gilt 4.996%, up 4.6bp on yesterday
  • 15:16 — 4.997%, up 4.7bp
  • 15:53 — 5.011%, up 6.1bp

Three readings across nearly an hour, all pointing the same way. That is a move, not noise, and it is now safe to call it one.

The whole curve is dearer than it was at yesterday’s close: the 2-year up 3.2bp, the 5-year 5.5bp, the 20-year 6.1bp, the 30-year 6.5bp and the 50-year 6.3bp.

THE CHARACTER OF THE MOVE HAS CHANGED

This matters, and it is a correction to the picture we drew at lunchtime.

Through the morning this was a pure long-end story: the far end of the curve got dearer while the short end sat still or eased, which is what a term-premium move looks like. At 12:50 the 1-year SONIA swap was 4.100%, marginally below yesterday.

It is now 4.115%, up 1.4bp. The front end has joined. What was a move in the price of lending far into the future has broadened into the whole curve repricing together.

Worth noting plainly: two weak American consumer readings would ordinarily push expectations towards lower interest rates, which would pull the front end down rather than up. It has gone the other way. We are not going to invent a reason for that on a Friday afternoon — we are recording that it happened.

WHAT MONDAY LOOKS LIKE FROM HERE

On the market at 15:53, Monday morning’s round would come in near:

  • 2-year 5.284% standard — 5.084% certainty — up 2.4bp on today’s afternoon round
  • 5-year 5.571% standard — 5.371% certainty — up 3.1bp
  • 10-year 6.071% standard — 5.871% certainty — up 4.1bp
  • 20-year 6.618% standard — 6.418% certainty — up 3.8bp
  • 50-year 6.500% standard — 6.300% certainty — up 3.0bp

The drift through the afternoon, on the 10-year: near 6.035% when we published at 13:51, 6.049% at 14:18, 6.056% at 15:02, and 6.071% now. Rather more than 3bp against the borrower in two hours, all of it after both of today’s rounds had struck.

These are estimates of a round that has not struck, and a weekend sits in front of it.

WHY TODAY'S ROUNDS LOOK CHEAP IN HINDSIGHT

One number is worth holding on to over the weekend. Gilts have moved 3.2 to 6.5bp today depending on maturity. The two PWLB rounds that actually struck moved 1 to 3bp.

That is not an inconsistency. The rounds are two photographs, taken at 09:25 and 12:23, and most of the day’s move happened after the second one. Anyone who borrowed today caught the cheaper half of it. The rest is sitting in the market waiting for Monday morning.

Next week carries the domestic risk: unemployment Tuesday, forecast 4.9%, and inflation Wednesday, forecast 3.0% against 2.6% last — which prints at 07:00, before that morning’s round rather than after it.

i We are reporting the figure, not the reaction. This printed at 15:00 and it is now 15:02. Two minutes is not long enough to know what a bond market has decided — as this afternoon demonstrated, when the response to the 13:30 release took the better part of an hour to arrive. Levels below are stated with their timestamp. The verdict follows when there is one.
American consumer sentiment fell to 51.0, against a 54.5 forecast and 55.2 last. That is the second consumer reading to miss badly this afternoon, after retail sales contracted 0.6%. Both land after today’s rounds, so both are Monday’s problem.
THE FIGURE

The University of Michigan’s preliminary consumer sentiment index for the month came in at 51.0, against a 54.5 forecast and 55.2 the month before. That is a miss of three and a half points and a fall of more than four from last month.

It is the second American consumer reading of the afternoon to disappoint, and by some margin the larger of the two. Retail sales at 13:30 came in at −0.6% against a +0.1% forecast. One measures what households actually spent; the other measures how they feel about spending. Both went the same way within ninety minutes.

WHERE THE MARKET IS — AS AT 15:00

These are levels, not conclusions. Gilt yields at 15:00, against yesterday’s close:

  • 2-year gilt 4.323%, up 2.9bp
  • 5-year gilt 4.533%, up 5.0bp
  • 10-year gilt 4.996%, up 4.6bp
  • 20-year gilt 5.666%, up 4.7bp
  • 30-year gilt 5.748%, up 5.3bp
  • 50-year gilt 5.320%, up 5.1bp

The whole curve is now more expensive than it was at yesterday’s close, and by more than at any point today. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.110%, up 0.9bp.

What we will not do is tell you yet whether that is a response to this release, a continuation of the move that began after 13:30, or the ordinary drift of a Friday afternoon. Those are different claims and none of them is established two minutes in.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR MONDAY

Today’s borrowing is long finished. Both rounds struck before either American figure printed, and nothing this afternoon can change a rate struck this morning or at lunchtime.

On the market as it stands at 15:00, Monday morning’s round would come in near:

  • 2-year 5.282% standard — 5.082% certainty — up 2.2bp on today’s afternoon round
  • 5-year 5.566% standard — 5.366% certainty — up 2.6bp
  • 10-year 6.056% standard — 5.856% certainty — up 2.6bp
  • 20-year 6.604% standard — 6.404% certainty — up 2.4bp
  • 50-year 6.489% standard — 6.289% certainty — up 1.9bp

An authority planning to draw down on Monday should know that the estimate has moved against it twice this afternoon: near 6.035% on the 10-year when we published at 13:51, near 6.049% at 14:18, and near 6.056% now. That is a drift of about 2bp in a little over an hour, and there is a weekend still to come before the round strikes.

These remain estimates of a round that has not struck.

AND THEN NEXT WEEK

The American data is done for the week. The domestic risk starts on Tuesday with unemployment (4.9% forecast), and the week turns on Wednesday’s inflation figure, forecast at 3.0% against 2.6% last.

That one prints at 07:00, before the morning round rather than after it — so unlike everything that has landed this afternoon, it will reach a rate councils can borrow at the same day. On this week’s evidence, the long end is where a surprise would be felt.

✖ What we got wrong, plainly. We characterised the market’s reaction to a high-impact release seventeen minutes after it printed, and called a small move in an unexpected direction “noise”. It was not noise. It was the leading edge of a real move, and we explained it away instead of waiting for it. The direction we noted was right; the conclusion we drew from it was wrong.
Correction. At 13:51 we said gilts had “barely acknowledged” the American retail sales miss. That was wrong. The sell-off came — it was simply delayed. Gilt yields have risen sharply since, and Monday’s round would now come in 1.4bp more expensive than when we published.
WHAT WE SAID, AND WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED

At 13:51 this publication said that American retail sales had missed badly and that “gilts have barely acknowledged it”. It described the move at the long end as “four-tenths of a basis point” and “comfortably inside the range a market wanders through on a quiet Friday afternoon”.

That reading was taken at 13:47, seventeen minutes after the release. It was accurate as a snapshot and wrong as a conclusion. Here is the same curve then and now:

  • 10-year gilt 4.975% then, 4.989% now — up 3.9bp on yesterday, against 2.5bp when we published
  • 30-year gilt 5.725% then, 5.738% now — up 4.2bp, against 3.0bp
  • 50-year gilt 5.293% then, 5.312% now — up 4.3bp, against 2.5bp
  • 2-year gilt 4.301% then, 4.316% now — up 2.3bp, against 0.7bp

The front end, which we described as sitting still through the release, has since joined the move. This is a whole-curve sell-off, not the non-event we reported.

WHAT IT COSTS

Today’s two rounds are struck and unaffected — 313/26 at 09:25 and 314/26 at 12:23 stand as fixed. That part of the earlier edition holds.

The cost lands on Monday morning. On the market as it stands, Monday’s round would come in near:

  • 2-year 5.275% standard — 5.075% certainty — up 1.5bp on today’s afternoon round
  • 5-year 5.554% standard — 5.354% certainty — up 1.4bp
  • 10-year 6.049% standard — 5.849% certainty — up 1.9bp
  • 20-year 6.595% standard — 6.395% certainty — up 1.5bp
  • 50-year 6.481% standard — 6.281% certainty — up 1.1bp

When we published at 13:51, the same 10-year estimate was 6.035%. It is now 6.049%. An authority reading that earlier edition would have been told Monday looked broadly level with today. It no longer does.

These remain estimates of a round that has not struck, and there is a weekend before it does.

WHY THE DELAY, AND WHY IT MATTERS

A large release does not reprice a bond market instantly. Dealers wait for the detail beneath the headline figure, for the American cash market to open properly, and for each other. A London afternoon reaction to a Washington number can take the better part of an hour to arrive, and the long end — thinner, slower, and where councils borrow — is usually last to move.

That is the lesson, and it is a process one. Reporting a release quickly is useful. Characterising the market’s response to it quickly is not, because at seventeen minutes there is not yet a response to characterise. From today this publication will report the figure on the fast window and hold any verdict on the market’s reaction until it can be confirmed by more than one reading.

STILL TO COME

Michigan consumer sentiment at 15:00, forecast 54.5 against 55.2 last. On this afternoon’s evidence, the reaction to it should be judged well after it prints rather than in the minutes following.

Next week: unemployment Tuesday (4.9% forecast), and inflation Wednesday, forecast 3.0% against 2.6% last — the month’s largest scheduled risk, and one that lands before that morning’s round rather than after it.

i Nothing in this release can reach a rate you borrow at today. The morning round struck at 09:25 and the afternoon round at 12:23. This figure landed at 13:30, after both — so it feeds into Monday morning’s round, with a weekend in between for the market to think about it.
American retail sales fell 0.6% in the month, against forecasts of a 0.1% rise. A seven-tenths miss and an outright contraction — and gilts have barely acknowledged it. Both of today’s PWLB rounds have already struck, so this one is for Monday.
THE NUMBER

US retail sales for the month came in at −0.6%, against a +0.1% forecast and +0.2% the month before. That is a miss of seven-tenths of a percentage point, and it turns modest growth into a contraction.

On the face of it this is a weak-consumer signal from the world’s largest economy, and the textbook response in government bond markets is for yields to fall — a softer economy argues for lower interest rates, and lower expected rates make existing bonds more attractive.

THE REACTION — OR THE LACK OF ONE

That is not what has happened. Twenty minutes after the release, gilt yields are slightly higher than they were before it:

  • 10-year gilt 4.975%, up 2.5bp on yesterday — it was up 2.1bp just before the print
  • 30-year gilt 5.725%, up 3.0bp — it was up 2.6bp
  • 2-year gilt 4.301%, up 0.7bp — essentially unchanged through the release

Two things are worth saying carefully here. The first is that these moves are small — four-tenths of a basis point at the long end — and comfortably inside the range a market wanders through on a quiet Friday afternoon. It would be wrong to present this as a decisive verdict on the release.

The second is that the direction is still notable, because it is the opposite of the textbook one, and it is the third time this week the long end has drifted the way that costs borrowers money while the short end has sat still.

WHY A WEAK CONSUMER MIGHT NOT HELP

This week’s driver has not been growth expectations. It has been the price investors demand for lending far into the future — term premium — after the United States sold 30-year bonds at the highest cost since around 2001.

A soft month of retail sales does not answer that. It speaks to how fast the economy is growing, not to how much compensation a buyer wants for holding a fifty-year bond. If anything, a weaker economy raises the prospect of more government borrowing to support it, which points the same way as the term-premium story rather than against it.

The domestic rate path is unchanged: Bank Rate 3.75%, next move expected a rise in November 2026, and the 1-year SONIA swap is 4.104%, within a rounding error of yesterday.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR MONDAY

Today’s borrowing is finished. The next PWLB rate anyone can strike is Monday morning’s round, and it will be set by whatever the market has made of this by then.

One more American figure is still to come today — Michigan consumer sentiment at 15:00, forecast at 54.5 against 55.2 last, so already expected to soften. If it also disappoints, that is two consumer readings pointing the same way in a single afternoon, and a weekend for the market to decide whether that changes the picture or merely confirms it.

Beyond that, next week is where the domestic risk sits: unemployment on Tuesday (4.9% forecast), and inflation on Wednesday, forecast at 3.0% against 2.6% last — the month’s largest scheduled risk to borrowing costs, and on this week’s evidence the long end is where a surprise would land.

THE AFTERNOON ROUND — NOTICE 314/26

The round struck at 12:23. Standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted a borrowing forecast — alongside, and the change against this morning’s round:

  • 2-year 5.26% standard — 5.06% certainty — down 1bp
  • 5-year 5.54% standard — 5.34% certainty — down 1bp
  • 10-year 6.03% standard — 5.83% certainty — unchanged
  • 20-year 6.58% standard — 6.38% certainty — unchanged
  • 25-year 6.66% standard — 6.46% certainty — unchanged
  • 50-year 6.47% standard — 6.27% certainty — up 1bp

This is a different shape from the morning. The 09:25 round was a clean parallel shift — every maturity up 2bp together. This one is a twist: the short end down, the middle flat, the long end up. When the two ends of the curve move in opposite directions, the story is rarely the same story at both.

THE DAY AS A WHOLE

Two rounds are now on the board, and against yesterday’s close the whole curve is more expensive — but not evenly:

  • 2-year 5.26%, up 1bp on the day
  • 5-year 5.54%, up 1bp
  • 10-year 6.03%, up 2bp
  • 20-year 6.58%, up 2bp
  • 25-year 6.66%, up 2bp
  • 50-year 6.47%, up 3bp

The cost of borrowing rose with the length of the loan, every step of the way. That is the signature of a term-premium move — investors asking to be paid more for lending far into the future — rather than a change in what anyone expects the Bank of England to do.

The rest of the market agrees. The 1-year SONIA swap has slipped to 4.100%, marginally below yesterday, and Bank Rate is 3.75% with the next move markets expect still a rise in November 2026. Expectations for the near term eased slightly today. It was the far end that got dearer.

WHY THE LONG END

The cause was set overnight and has not gone away. The United States sold 30-year bonds at the highest borrowing cost since around 2001. Long-dated government debt is priced globally, and when the largest issuer pays more for 30-year money, the effect reaches the gilt curve.

Gilts have drifted back through the session without unwinding it. The 10-year is up 2.1bp on yesterday, having been up 3.0bp at the open; the 30-year is up 2.6bp, having been up 3.4bp. The move faded at the front and held at the back — which is exactly the shape the two fixings took.

Oil is the second thread. It moved higher this morning, and the United States has since threatened an indefinite blockade against Iran. That is a live risk to the oil price rather than a settled fact, and no part of today’s move should be pinned on it — but it points the same way as everything else that has driven this week, which is towards higher inflation expectations and a dearer long end.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT — AND WHEN IT REACHES YOU

Today’s borrowing is done. Both rounds have struck and there is no third. Anything that happens from here reaches a rate on Monday morning, not today.

That matters this afternoon, because two American releases are still to come and both are now irrelevant to today’s rates: US retail sales at 13:30 (0.1% forecast) and Michigan consumer sentiment at 15:00 (54.5 forecast). Whatever they print, they bear on Monday’s morning round — and with a weekend in between for the market to reconsider them.

Next week carries the domestic risk. Wednesday’s inflation figure is forecast at 3.0% against 2.6% last, and on this week’s evidence the long end is where a surprise would be felt. Unemployment lands Tuesday (4.9% forecast) and retail sales Friday.

Gilts have eased back from the highs they set at the open. The 10-year is now up 2.4bp on yesterday against 3.0bp an hour ago, and the 2-year has given up most of its move, up 1.1bp against 2.4bp first thing. Nothing has caused it — there has been no UK or European data this morning — so this reads as the overnight American move settling rather than reversing.

More

On that basis the lunchtime round would come in near 6.028% on the 10-year maturity rate and 5.546% on the 5-year, a shade below the morning round at 6.03% and 5.55%. The difference is a fraction of a basis point and well inside the noise of a round that has not struck; treat the two rounds as level rather than expecting the afternoon to be cheaper. The round strikes around the middle of the day, and on each of the last two sessions it has done so shortly after noon.

THE MORNING ROUND — NOTICE 313/26

The round struck at 09:25. These are the standard maturity rates, with the certainty rate — 20bp lower, for authorities that have submitted their borrowing forecast — alongside:

  • 2-year 5.27% standard — 5.07% certainty — up 2bp
  • 5-year 5.55% standard — 5.35% certainty — up 2bp
  • 10-year 6.03% standard — 5.83% certainty — up 2bp
  • 20-year 6.58% standard — 6.38% certainty — up 2bp
  • 25-year 6.66% standard — 6.46% certainty — up 2bp
  • 50-year 6.46% standard — 6.26% certainty — up 2bp

Annuity and equal-instalment rates moved with them, almost all by the same 2bp. The exceptions are the 25-year annuity, the 20-year EIP and the 50-year EIP, each up 1bp.

A uniform move of this kind — every maturity, every repayment type, the same amount — is a clean parallel shift. It tells you the whole curve repriced together rather than one part of it moving on its own.

WHAT MOVED IT

The cause was set before London opened. The United States sold 30-year bonds overnight at the highest borrowing cost since around 2001, and long-dated government borrowing costs do not stay inside national borders. Gilts opened higher across the board and have stayed there:

  • 2-year gilt 4.316%, up 2.3bp
  • 5-year gilt 4.519%, up 3.6bp
  • 10-year gilt 4.980%, up 3.0bp
  • 20-year gilt 5.646%, up 2.8bp
  • 30-year gilt 5.726%, up 3.0bp
  • 50-year gilt 5.298%, up 2.9bp

Oil moving higher this morning added a second push in the same direction, through inflation expectations rather than through the long end.

The rate-cut path did not move: Bank Rate is 3.75%, and the next change markets expect is still a rise in November 2026. Nothing this morning was about what the Bank does next.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR A BORROWER

Two basis points is a small move in isolation. On £10m of 20-year borrowing it is roughly £2,000 a year, and about £40,000 over the life of the loan — real, but not the kind of number that changes a decision on its own.

What matters more is the direction and the reason. This is the second consecutive session in which the long end has moved against borrowers, and the cause sits outside the United Kingdom. That makes it harder to argue it reverses on a domestic data point.

The 5-year remains the maturity to watch. It is the largest gilt mover on the day at 3.6bp, and the medium part of the curve is where an inflation-expectations story shows up first — with Wednesday’s inflation print forecast at 3.0% against 2.6% last.

THE REST OF TODAY

One round left. The afternoon round strikes around the middle of the day — on each of the last two sessions it has done so shortly after noon — with rates following shortly after.

Today’s only scheduled releases are American and both come too late to reach it: US retail sales at 13:30 (0.1% forecast) and Michigan consumer sentiment at 15:00 (54.5 forecast). Neither will reach a rate you can borrow at today. They bear on Monday morning.

So the afternoon round will be decided by what London does with this morning’s move, and by nothing that is scheduled.

WHAT THE OPEN DID

The market has been trading about fifty minutes. It opened higher — meaning more expensive to borrow — and it did so everywhere, not in one corner of the curve:

  • 2-year gilt 4.318%, up 2.4bp
  • 5-year gilt 4.518%, up 3.5bp — the biggest move on the curve
  • 10-year gilt 4.978%, up 2.8bp
  • 20-year gilt 5.647%, up 2.8bp
  • 30-year gilt 5.725%, up 2.9bp
  • 50-year gilt 5.297%, up 2.8bp

A parallel move of this shape — everything up by roughly the same amount — is the signature of a global repricing arriving overnight rather than a domestic story. There was no UK data this morning to cause it.

THE MORNING ROUND — WHAT IT WOULD COME IN NEAR

Nothing has fixed yet. The rate in force is still yesterday’s lunchtime round, notice 312/26, at 6.01% on the 10-year. On the market as it stands at 08:50, the round striking at about 09:00–09:15 would come in near:

  • 2-year 5.275% standard — 5.075% certainty — up 2.5bp
  • 5-year 5.545% standard — 5.345% certainty — up 1.5bp
  • 10-year 6.027% standard — 5.827% certainty — up 1.7bp
  • 20-year 6.578% standard — 6.378% certainty — up 1.8bp
  • 50-year 6.459% standard — 6.259% certainty — up 1.9bp

These are estimates of a round that has not struck. They move with the market until it does, and the rates publish at about 09:30.

Worth holding the two sets side by side. At 07:59 this morning, anchored to last night’s close, the same five estimates read 5.250%, 5.510%, 5.999%, 6.551% and 6.430% — four of the five below yesterday. Every one of them is now above. The open cost roughly 2.5 to 3.5bp across the board.

WHY — AMERICA OVERNIGHT, OIL THIS MORNING

Two things, and they push the same way.

The overnight leg was American. The United States sold 30-year bonds at the highest borrowing cost since around 2001 — a 25-year high at the long end. Long-dated government borrowing costs are not a closed national market; when the largest issuer in the world pays more for 30-year money, the repricing reaches Westminster by morning. This was the risk flagged in today’s earlier brief, and it has arrived.

The morning leg is oil. Crude is moving higher, which feeds directly into inflation expectations — and inflation expectations are what the medium part of the curve prices. That is the most plausible reason the 5-year is the day’s biggest mover rather than the 50-year, which is where a pure long-end story would have concentrated.

The rate-cut path is unchanged: Bank Rate 3.75%, with the next move markets expect still a rise in November 2026. This morning is a term-premium and inflation-expectations move, not a change in what anyone thinks the Bank does next.

WHAT TO WATCH FROM HERE

Today’s two scheduled releases are both American and both late — US retail sales at 13:30 and Michigan consumer sentiment at 15:00. Both land after the lunchtime round strikes, so neither reaches a rate you can borrow at today; they bear on Monday morning.

That leaves the shape of today unusually simple. Two rounds, no domestic data to move them between, and a market taking its direction from abroad. If the American move keeps feeding through, the lunchtime round would be the one that carries it.

Next Wednesday’s inflation print remains the month’s largest scheduled risk — 3.0% forecast against 2.6% last. This morning’s oil move is a small piece of the same argument, arriving early.

WHERE THE DAY STARTS

Nothing has fixed today. The rate in force is still yesterday's lunchtime round, notice 312/26, at 6.01% on the 10-year maturity rate — the same rate both of yesterday's rounds struck at.

On last night's close, the round striking at about 09:00–09:15 would come in near:

  • 2-year maturity: 5.250% (0.0bp — level with yesterday)
  • 5-year maturity: 5.510% (-2.0bp)
  • 10-year maturity: 5.999% (-1.1bp)
  • 20-year maturity: 6.551% (-0.9bp)
  • 50-year maturity: 6.430% (-1.0bp)

Those are estimates anchored to the 17:59 close, not rates, and the market has not opened since. UK government bonds closed lower on the day across the curve — the 10-year at 4.95% (-1.8bp) and the 5-year at 4.483% (-2.1bp) — with the 1-year SONIA swap at 4.102%, -1.3bp.

THE OVERNIGHT STORY IS AMERICAN, AND IT POINTS UP

The overnight story is American, and it points the other way. The United States sold 30-year bonds at the highest borrowing cost since around 2001 — a 25-year high — with the Guardian's live coverage reporting inflation fears behind it. Long-dated government yields move together internationally more closely than short ones, so a heavy US long-end auction is the most likely thing to push UK long yields up this morning.

Separately, Reuters reports the Bank of Japan is eyeing a September rate hike — another central bank moving away from cheap money, and another mild upward pull on global long yields.

Treasurer's read: this is a long-end risk, not a short-end one, and that matters because the estimates above have the 20-year and 50-year among the cheapest on the day. If the overnight move carries into the London session, those are the maturities where the estimate is most likely to be revised away. The 2-year, already level with yesterday, has far less exposure to it.

TODAY — AND WHICH ROUND IT REACHES

No UK data today. The day's releases are both American and both late:

  • 13:30 — US retail sales, forecast 0.1%
  • 15:00 — Michigan consumer sentiment, preliminary, forecast 54.5

Both land after the lunchtime round strikes — which on each of the last two days has been shortly after noon, so neither reaches a rate you can borrow at today. They bear on Monday morning's round.

In UK politics, Nigel Farage has won the Clacton by-election. Front-page news, but with no direct read-through to gilt pricing this morning — we would not attribute any move today to it.

THE WEEK AHEAD

Next week carries the month's real tests, all at 07:00 and all before that day's morning round:

  • Tuesday 18th — unemployment rate, forecast 4.9%
  • Wednesday 19th — inflation, forecast 3.0% against 2.6% last time
  • Friday 21st — retail sales, forecast -0.6%

Bank Rate is 3.75% and the next move markets expect remains a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: Wednesday's inflation figure remains the largest scheduled risk to borrowing costs this month. Today is a quiet UK day whose direction will be set abroad, which usually means the morning round lands as a fair reflection of where things stand and the afternoon drifts on American news.

THE DAY’S BORROWING: ONE NUMBER, TWICE

The day's borrowing came down to one number repeated. The morning round, notice 311/26, struck at 09:05 and fixed the 10-year maturity rate at 6.01%. The lunchtime round, notice 312/26, struck at 12:11 and fixed it at 6.01% — unchanged at every maturity, on all three repayment bases. A borrower who drew at nine and one who drew at half past twelve paid exactly the same.

Both were one to two basis points dearer than yesterday's lunchtime round. The full set as struck: 2-year 5.25%, 5-year 5.53%, 10-year 6.01%, 20-year 6.56%, 25-year 6.64%, 50-year 6.44%.

Treasurer's read: on most days the choice between the two rounds is worth a basis point or two. Today it was worth nothing, which is worth knowing for its own sake — it is the clearest illustration this week that the timing decision is usually small next to the decision to borrow at all.

WHAT MOVED IT, AND WHAT WE GOT WRONG

Three things moved the day, in order.

UK growth, 07:00. The monthly figure beat expectations at 0.3% against 0% forecast, and business investment rose 1.7% against a forecast fall. But quarterly growth slowed to 0.4% from 0.6%, and the production side missed across the board — manufacturing −0.5%, industrial output −0.2%, construction orders −18.1% against +11.8% expected, and all three trade balances worse than forecast. Services carried it.

The morning round published three hours late. It struck on time at 09:05, but its rates did not reach us until after 11:20. Between 10:37 and 11:22 we reported the fixing as missing and told readers the lunchtime round was the day's only chance to borrow. That was wrong — the morning round was there all along — and we corrected it at 12:24. The distinction matters: a round that does not happen removes an option, a round whose rates publish late does not.

US producer prices, 13:30. Softer than expected at 0% against 0.2%, with the previous month revised down to −0.3%. Both of today's rounds were already struck, so it reached neither.

THE RALLY THAT CAME AND WENT

The producer-price figures took about an hour to bite, then drove a proper rally. By 15:19 tomorrow's round was tracking 5.3bp below today's — the first time this week that waiting looked worth real money, about £5,300 a year on a £10m maturity loan.

It did not last. From late afternoon the Middle East reasserted itself — Iran claiming control of the Strait of Hormuz, Oman reporting the oil spill had reached its coastline, warnings of renewed war in Yemen — and the rally unwound almost completely. At the close:

  • 2-year: 4.294% (-1.3bp)
  • 5-year: 4.483% (-2.1bp)
  • 10-year: 4.949% (-1.9bp)
  • 20-year: 5.618% (-1.1bp)
  • 30-year: 5.696% (-1.3bp)
  • 50-year: 5.268% (-1.3bp)

The 1-year SONIA swap closed at 4.102%, -1.3bp, having been 3.2bp lower at the peak. Bank Rate stays 3.75% with the next move markets expect a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: this is the third afternoon this week to give back what it gained. Tuesday's went overnight, this morning's went in an hour, and this one went in ninety minutes. A pattern that repeats three times in four sessions is worth treating as the normal behaviour of this market rather than as bad luck.

TOMORROW, AND THE DATE THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS

Nothing has fixed for tomorrow. On tonight's close its rounds would come in near 5.250% at 2 years (0.0bp — level with today), 5.510% at 5 years (-2.0bp), 5.998% at 10 years (-1.2bp) and 6.550% at 20 years (-1.0bp).

Friday carries no UK release. The next figures that matter are next week, all at 07:00 and all before that day's morning round:

  • Tuesday 18th — unemployment rate, forecast 4.9%
  • Wednesday 19th — inflation, forecast 3.0% against 2.6% last time
  • Friday 21st — retail sales, forecast -0.6%

Treasurer's read: a jump in inflation from 2.6% to 3.0% is the single largest scheduled risk to borrowing costs this month, and today's growth beat makes it harder for the Bank to look through. If you have discretion over when to draw in the next fortnight, Wednesday morning is the date to plan around — not tomorrow.

ALMOST ALL OF IT HANDED BACK

At 15:19 the estimate for tomorrow's round sat 5.3bp below today's, and we said it was the first time this week that waiting looked worth real money. An hour and a half later almost all of that has gone:

  • 10-year: 5.957% → 5.999% (-1.1bp against today, from -5.3bp)
  • 5-year: 5.478% → 5.518% (-1.2bp)
  • 2-year: 5.200% → 5.250% (+-0.0bp — level)
  • 20-year: 6.515% → 6.550% (-1.0bp)

Gilt yields have followed: the 2-year at 4.293% (-1.4bp) against −6.4bp at its best, the 10-year at 4.951% (-1.7bp) against −6.0bp. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.104%, -1.1bp on the day, having been −3.2bp. Whatever repricing of Bank Rate expectations the afternoon delivered has been handed back too.

THE MIDDLE EAST IS THE AFTERNOON’S NEWS

The Middle East has been the afternoon's news, and it points the right way for this move. Iran says the Strait of Hormuz is under its control and rejects President Trump's claims; Oman reports the massive oil spill has reached its coastline; and there are warnings of renewed all-out war in Yemen as Houthi attacks escalate.

Treasurer's read: this is the same thread that drove Tuesday's sell-off. Higher energy risk feeds inflation expectations, and inflation expectations feed the price of long-dated government borrowing. We would not put the whole afternoon on it — the earlier give-back began as Wall Street opened and looked like ordinary risk appetite — but the escalation is the more plausible driver of the last hour.

THE THIRD REVERSAL THIS WEEK

This is the third time this week. Tuesday's improvement reversed entirely before the next morning. This morning's post-growth rise unwound within the hour. And now the afternoon's rally has nearly gone the same way. We flagged the risk at 15:19 and again at 15:44, and on each occasion the caution has been worth more than the number it qualified.

Nothing has fixed for tomorrow. On current pricing its round would be 1.1bp cheaper on the 10-year — about £1,100 a year on a £10m maturity loan, against roughly £5,300 at the peak. On the 2-year there is now no advantage at all.

Treasurer's read: the window we described at quarter past three has closed to roughly a basis point. That is back inside the range where timing is noise rather than a decision. If you deferred a drawdown this afternoon on the strength of it, you have lost very little; if you were planning to defer tomorrow's, the case no longer really exists. The end-of-day edition will close the arc.

THE GIVE-BACK, AND WHERE IT LANDED

The 15:19 edition warned against treating the afternoon's improvement as banked, on the grounds that this week has twice seen exactly that kind of move reverse. It has started to happen, though only in part.

Against that edition, the estimates have moved back up:

  • 2-year: 5.200% → 5.235% (+3.5bp)
  • 5-year: 5.478% → 5.495% (+1.7bp)
  • 10-year: 5.957% → 5.974% (+1.7bp)
  • 20-year: 6.515% → 6.524% (+0.9bp)

The 2-year has given back the most, and it was the maturity leading the fall earlier — which is consistent with this being a partial unwind of the Bank Rate repricing rather than a fresh piece of news. Gilt yields remain below last night's close everywhere, but by less: the 2-year at 4.278% (-2.8bp) against −6.4bp at quarter past three, the 10-year at 4.926% (-4.3bp) against −6.0bp. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.091%, -2.3bp on the day, having been -3.2bp.

WHY — AND IT IS NOT A UK STORY

The likeliest candidate is straightforward, and it is not a UK story. Wall Street opened higher as investors weighed weaker oil alongside the producer-price figures. A firmer risk appetite and a softer oil price pull in opposite directions for gilt yields, and the first hour of American trading has taken some of the morning's safety bid back out.

Treasurer's read: nothing here changes the direction, only the size. Tomorrow's round still looks cheaper than today's, and it is still the better of the two windows you can see. What has changed is the margin, and with it how much conviction the decision deserves.

WHAT TOMORROW IS NOW WORTH

Nothing has fixed for tomorrow. On current pricing its morning round would come in 3.6bp below today's on the 10-year, worth about £3,600 a year on a £10m maturity loan — against roughly £5,300 half an hour ago. The 2-year advantage has narrowed to 1.5bp.

Both of today's rounds are struck and cannot change. The afternoon has an hour and a half left to run, and tomorrow's round is struck on the overnight close, not on this reading. Bank Rate is 3.75% with the next move markets expect still a rise in Nov 2026.

THE MOVE HAS RUN ONE WAY ALL AFTERNOON

The 14:31 edition put tomorrow's round about two basis points below today's. It is now 5.3bp below, and the move has been one-directional all afternoon — a further 3.1bp on the 10-year since that edition.

UK government bond yields have fallen hard against last night's close, with the shorter maturities leading as they have all day:

  • 2-year: 4.243% (-6.4bp)
  • 5-year: 4.451% (-5.2bp)
  • 10-year: 4.909% (-6.0bp)
  • 20-year: 5.583% (-4.6bp)
  • 30-year: 5.663% (-4.5bp)
  • 50-year: 5.235% (-4.6bp)

The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — is 4.083%, -3.2bp on the day and falling through the afternoon. Bank Rate itself is 3.75%, and the next move markets expect is still a rise in Nov 2026 — but the conviction behind that has softened noticeably since this morning.

WHAT TOMORROW’S ROUND WOULD COST

Nothing has fixed for tomorrow. On current pricing the round striking at about 09:00–09:15 tomorrow would come in near:

  • 2-year maturity: 5.200% (-5.0bp against today)
  • 5-year maturity: 5.478% (-5.2bp)
  • 10-year maturity: 5.957% (-5.3bp)
  • 20-year maturity: 6.515% (-4.5bp)

Treasurer's read: on a £10m 10-year maturity loan, 5.3bp is about £5,300 a year, or roughly £53,000 over the life of the loan. That is no longer noise. If your drawdown can wait until the morning, waiting currently looks worth real money — the first time this week that has been true by a margin worth acting on.

WHY NOT TO TREAT IT AS BANKED

The honest caveat, and it has bitten twice this week already. On Tuesday an afternoon improvement of this kind reversed entirely before the next morning, and this morning's post-growth rise unwound inside an hour. Tomorrow's round is the first of the day, struck on wherever the overnight session leaves things, with no UK data before it to anchor expectations.

What is different today is the shape and the persistence: the fall has run in one direction for over two hours, it is led by the short end where Bank Rate expectations sit, and the swap market has moved with it rather than against it. That is a more coherent move than Tuesday's oil-driven lurch. It is still an estimate at quarter past three, not a rate at quarter past nine.

ELSEWHERE, AND THE WEEK AHEAD

Nothing further is scheduled today. For the local-government diary, the annual treasury and current affairs survey opened this afternoon.

Next week brings the two UK releases most likely to move borrowing costs this month: the unemployment rate on Tuesday, and on Wednesday an inflation figure markets expect to jump to 3.0% from 2.6%. Both publish at 07:00, before that day's morning round.

THE MOVE WE DECLINED TO CALL AN HOUR AGO HAS NOW ARRIVED

At 13:37 we reported the softer American producer-price figures and said we would not claim they had caused the small move visible at the time — under a basis point, four minutes after publication, was well inside ordinary drift. That caution was right, and the picture has now changed enough to say something firmer.

In the hour since, the estimate for tomorrow morning's round has fallen 2.7bp on the 10-year and 2.7bp on the 5-year, and gilt yields have dropped across the whole curve:

  • 2-year: 4.275% (-3.1bp)
  • 5-year: 4.48% (-2.4bp)
  • 10-year: 4.939% (-2.9bp)
  • 20-year: 5.606% (-2.4bp)
  • 30-year: 5.688% (-2.0bp)
  • 50-year: 5.259% (-2.1bp)

A move of that size, sustained over an hour and consistent across every maturity, is a different thing from the first flicker. The market wires now carry the read-through explicitly — that the latest inflation readings could keep the US Federal Reserve from raising interest rates. Softer American inflation lowers expected US rates, and UK government bond yields tend to follow.

AND IT REACHES TOMORROW’S ROUND, NOT TODAY’S

This is tomorrow's story, not today's. Both of today's rounds are struck — the morning at 09:05 and the lunchtime at 12:11, both at 6.01% on the 10-year maturity rate. Nothing published after about 12:30 can reach either of them. Every figure below is an estimate for the round that strikes tomorrow at about 09:00–09:15, and nothing has fixed for it:

  • 2-year maturity: 5.232% (-1.8bp against today)
  • 5-year maturity: 5.507% (-2.3bp)
  • 10-year maturity: 5.988% (-2.2bp)
  • 20-year maturity: 6.537% (-2.3bp)

The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — is 4.096%, -1.9bp on the day and its lowest reading of the session. Bank Rate itself is 3.75%, with the next move markets expect still a rise in Nov 2026.

WHAT THAT IS WORTH, AND WHY NOT TO BANK IT

Treasurer's read: if you have flexibility on timing, tomorrow morning currently looks cheaper than today did — a little over two basis points on the 10-year, which on a £10m maturity loan is roughly £2,200 a year. That is a real if modest saving, and it is the first time this week the next round has looked meaningfully better than the last one.

Two cautions against banking it. This week has twice seen an afternoon improvement reverse before the next morning — on Tuesday the entire day's gain was given back after 14:15, and this morning's post-growth rise unwound within the hour. And tomorrow's round is the first of the day, struck on wherever the overnight session leaves things, with no UK data before it. An estimate at half past two is not a rate at quarter past nine.

ELSEWHERE, AND WHAT IS COMING

Elsewhere, Jaguar Land Rover reported sales hit by a fire at a supplier and by Middle East disruption — a reminder that the Gulf situation which drove this week's earlier moves is still working through the real economy as well as the oil price.

Nothing further is scheduled today. Next week brings the two UK releases that matter most this month: the unemployment rate on Tuesday, and on Wednesday an inflation figure markets expect to jump to 3.0% from 2.6%.

THE RELEASE: SOFTER THIS MONTH, AND SOFTER LAST MONTH TOO

US producer prices — what American factories and firms charge each other, and an early read on where consumer inflation heads next — rose 0% on the month against a forecast of 0.2%. The previous month was also revised down, from -0.1% to -0.3%.

So the release was softer than expected on both counts: this month weaker than forecast, and last month weaker than first reported. Coming a day after US consumer inflation landed exactly in line, it points the same way — American price pressure easing rather than building.

WHICH ROUND IT ACTUALLY REACHES

This release cannot reach either of today's rounds. The morning round struck at 09:05 and the lunchtime round at 12:11, both hours before this figure was published. It bears on tomorrow morning's round.

Today's two rounds both fixed the 10-year maturity rate at 6.01%. Nothing has fixed for tomorrow: on current pricing it would come in near 6.015% on the 10-year (+0.5bp against today), 5.534% on the 5-year (+0.4bp) and 5.258% on the 2-year (+0.8bp).

THE FIRST REACTION, AND WHY WE ARE NOT OVER-READING IT

The first reaction is small, and it runs the other way from the textbook. Softer American inflation would ordinarily pull government bond yields down. In the few minutes since the release, UK yields have edged slightly up:

  • 2-year: 4.301% (-0.6bp)
  • 5-year: 4.507% (+0.3bp)
  • 10-year: 4.966% (-0.2bp)
  • 30-year: 5.711% (+0.3bp)

The estimate for tomorrow's round has risen 0.4bp on the 10-year and 0.8bp on the 2-year since just before the release. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.110%, -0.5bp on the day.

Treasurer's read: we would not read much into this yet, and we are not going to claim the release caused it. Under a basis point, four minutes after publication, is well inside ordinary drift, and UK yields have wandered in both directions all day. If anything it echoes yesterday, when an American inflation figure that landed exactly in line was followed within a couple of hours by UK yields turning higher rather than lower. The reading that matters is tomorrow morning's, and the afternoon has time to change it.

WHERE TODAY LEAVES THINGS

Today is done for borrowing: two rounds, both at 6.01% on the 10-year, one to two basis points above yesterday's lunchtime round. Bank Rate is 3.75% with the next move markets expect a rise in Nov 2026.

Next week carries the bigger UK tests: the unemployment rate on Tuesday and, on Wednesday, an inflation figure markets expect to jump to 3.0% from 2.6%.

THE LUNCHTIME FIXING: NOT A BASIS POINT IN IT

Notice 312/26, struck at 12:11, on the standard maturity basis:

  • 2-year maturity: 5.25% (unchanged)
  • 5-year maturity: 5.53% (unchanged)
  • 10-year maturity: 6.01% (unchanged)
  • 20-year maturity: 6.56% (unchanged)
  • 50-year maturity: 6.44% (unchanged)

Not a single basis point of movement at any maturity, on any of the three repayment bases. That is an unusually clean result, and it means today's two rounds priced identically — a borrower who drew down this morning and one who drew down at lunchtime paid the same rate.

Treasurer's read: today turned out to be a day with no timing decision in it at all. The choice between morning and lunchtime, which on most days is worth a basis point or two, was worth nothing. Against yesterday's lunchtime round both of today's are one to two basis points dearer.

CORRECTION, AND A TIMING ASSUMPTION WE ARE DROPPING

Correction. Our 12:24 edition said the lunchtime round would strike “at about 12:25”. It had already struck, at 12:11, thirteen minutes before we published that. We reported it as still to come when it was already done.

This is the second day running we have made that error, and the reason is worth setting out because it now looks less like a slip than a wrong assumption. We describe the lunchtime round as striking at about 12:25–12:30. Yesterday's struck at 12:04. Today's struck at 12:11. Both were well inside the window we tell readers to expect, and on both days that led us to write about a round in the future tense after it had priced.

Two days is not a rule, and we are not going to rewrite the timetable on it. But we will stop asserting that the lunchtime round is still to come simply because the clock says 12:15, and check whether it has struck before saying so.

WHERE THAT LEAVES TOMORROW

Markets barely moved either side of the round. Gilt yields are a little below last night's close at the shorter maturities and close to flat further out — the 2-year at 4.293% (-1.3bp), the 10-year at 4.962% (-0.7bp) and the 30-year at 5.707% (-0.1bp). The next round, tomorrow morning, would on current pricing come in near 6.012% on the 10-year (+0.2bp), 5.533% on the 5-year (+0.3bp) and 5.252% on the 2-year (+0.2bp). Nothing has fixed for tomorrow. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.109%, -0.6bp on the day, with Bank Rate at 3.75% and the next move markets expect a rise in Nov 2026.

THIS AFTERNOON — AND WHAT WE CANNOT SEE

US producer prices are due at 13:30, expected at 0.2% on the month against −0.3% previously. Both of today's rounds are now struck, so this release cannot reach either — it bears on tomorrow morning's round.

One caveat on the agenda, and the banner at the top of this edition says the same: our economic calendar is currently unavailable, so we cannot confirm the day's remaining schedule or pick up release results automatically. The producer prices timing above comes from earlier checks today, when the calendar was working. We would rather tell you the schedule is unverified than present an empty agenda as though the afternoon were clear.

CORRECTION: THE MORNING ROUND WAS HELD, ITS RATES WERE LATE

What we got wrong. At 11:22 we wrote that the lunchtime round was “today's only chance to borrow”. That was wrong, and it is the most important thing to fix before anything else. The morning round was held on time, striking at 09:05, and it priced normally. What failed was the publication of its rates to us: they did not appear until some time after 11:20, roughly three hours later than usual.

The distinction matters because the two situations call for different decisions. A round that does not happen removes an option. A round whose rates publish late does not — it was there all along. Our 10:37 edition described today's morning fixing as “missing”; the accurate word was unpublished, and we should have drawn that line more carefully than we did.

One smaller correction from earlier: the 09:15 edition described the round as “striking now”. It had in fact struck ten minutes before, at 09:05. The earlier editions remain in the archive as published.

THE MORNING FIXING IN FULL

Notice 311/26, struck at 09:05 on the standard maturity basis:

  • 2-year maturity: 5.25% (+1bp on yesterday's lunchtime round, 5.24%)
  • 5-year maturity: 5.53% (+2bp on yesterday's lunchtime round, 5.51%)
  • 10-year maturity: 6.01% (+1bp on yesterday's lunchtime round, 6.00%)
  • 20-year maturity: 6.56% (+2bp on yesterday's lunchtime round, 6.54%)
  • 50-year maturity: 6.44% (+2bp on yesterday's lunchtime round, 6.42%)

So the morning round came in one to two basis points above yesterday's lunchtime round across the curve — a little dearer, and close to what our estimates had been pointing to through the morning. In cash terms, a basis point on a £10m 10-year maturity loan is about £1,000 a year.

Treasurer's read: if you drew down at the morning round you paid roughly a basis point more than yesterday lunchtime, which for most schemes is immaterial. If you held off this morning because our earlier editions suggested there was nothing to draw against, the practical cost is smaller than the error: the lunchtime round striking now would come in at much the same level, as below.

THE LUNCHTIME ROUND, STRIKING NOW

The lunchtime round strikes at about 12:25, with its rates normally published by around 12:30. Nothing has fixed for it yet. On live pricing it would come in near 6.009% on the 10-year maturity rate (-0.1bp against this morning's round), 5.529% on the 5-year (-0.1bp) and 5.247% on the 2-year (-0.3bp) — essentially level with the morning.

Gilt yields remain below last night's close, the short end still leading: the 2-year at 4.289% (-1.8bp) and the 10-year at 4.959% (-0.9bp). The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.105%, -1.0bp on the day; Bank Rate is 3.75% with the next move markets expect still a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: there is no meaningful difference between the two rounds today, so the morning's publication delay has cost nobody anything measurable. Given the rates publish late, though, anyone relying on same-day confirmation should assume it may not arrive promptly.

WHAT IS LEFT TODAY

13:30 — US producer prices (forecast 0.2%, previously −0.3%). This lands after the lunchtime round strikes, so it bears on tomorrow morning's round, not today's. NIESR's monthly growth tracker has slipped to 12:30 and is now also expected after the round.

THE LUNCHTIME ROUND IS NOW THE ONLY ROUND

The morning round's rates have still not been published, and our checks continue to record today's morning fixing as missing. The most recent struck rate remains yesterday's lunchtime round — notice 310/26, 6.00% on the 10-year maturity rate and 5.51% on the 5-year.

The consequence is worth stating plainly, because it changes today's decision rather than just describing it: the lunchtime round, striking at about 12:25, is now the only opportunity to borrow today unless the morning rates appear after the event. A round that would ordinarily be the second choice of the day has become the only one.

THE MORNING’S EASING HAS PARTLY REVERSED

The steady easing of the morning has partly reversed over the last three quarters of an hour. Gilt yields are still below last night's close but by less, and two maturities are now level with it:

  • 2-year: 4.295% (-1.2bp)
  • 5-year: 4.504% (+0.0bp)
  • 10-year: 4.961% (-0.7bp)
  • 20-year: 5.626% (-0.3bp)
  • 30-year: 5.709% (+0.0bp)
  • 50-year: 5.279% (-0.1bp)

The estimate for the lunchtime round has risen with them, by 0.4bp on the 10-year and 0.8bp on the 2-year since 10:36. Nothing has fixed, so these remain estimates: 6.015% on the 10-year (+1.5bp against yesterday lunchtime), 5.524% on the 5-year (+1.4bp) and 5.248% on the 2-year (+0.8bp), the 2-year having crossed back above yesterday's fix after briefly sitting level. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.106%, -0.9bp on the day against -1.4bp an hour ago.

Treasurer's read: the cheapest pricing of the day was around half past ten, and it was not available to borrow at, because no round was open. That is frustrating rather than costly — the give-back is under half a basis point on the 10-year, and the lunchtime round would still come in only modestly above yesterday's.

TWO NEWS THREADS PULLING UPWARD

Two threads from this morning's news bear on where rates go from here.

The European Central Bank. A poll of economists reported this morning points to another ECB rate rise in September. European and UK government bond yields tend to move together, so a European central bank still tightening is a mild upward pull on gilt yields and therefore on PWLB rates — and it sits awkwardly beside this morning's softening in UK Bank Rate expectations.

Energy and shipping risk. The UK has defended its seizure of a shadow-fleet tanker following a threat from President Putin, and Yemeni forces report repelling a Houthi attack at Taiz. Neither is a market event on its own, but both sit on the same thread that drove the oil-led sell-off two days ago.

Treasurer's read: the balance of these is mildly upward for borrowing costs, which argues against assuming the morning's easing continues into the afternoon. If the lunchtime round is your only shot today, the case for taking it rather than holding out for a better level later is a little stronger than it was at ten o'clock.

WHAT IS LEFT TODAY, AND WHICH ROUND IT REACHES

12:00 — NIESR publishes its monthly growth tracker (forecast 0.4%, previously 0.4%), landing about twenty-five minutes before the lunchtime round strikes. Low impact, but the timing means it is the last data the round will see.

13:30 — US producer prices (forecast 0.2%, previously −0.3%). This lands after the lunchtime round, so it reaches tomorrow morning's round, not today's.

WHAT HAS HAPPENED, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN

The morning round is expected to strike at about 09:00–09:15, with its confirmed rates normally reaching us by around 09:30. At 10:36 they have not appeared, and our checks now record today's morning fixing as missing rather than merely late — the notice in the panel above is yesterday's lunchtime round, notice 310/26, struck at 12:04 on 12 August. It is labelled as such throughout, and no figure in this edition is presented as today's fixing.

To be plain about what this does and does not mean. It does not mean rates have moved sharply, or that anything is wrong with the market: gilts are trading normally and our estimates are live. It means the confirmed rates a borrower actually transacts at have not been published for this morning's round, so there is currently no morning rate to draw against.

It is the second consecutive day the timetable has been irregular, after yesterday's lunchtime round struck early at 12:04 — ahead of its usual window, which we corrected in the 12:52 edition.

THE MARKET HAS BEEN QUIET THROUGH THE DELAY

The market itself has been quiet through the delay. Gilt yields remain below last night's close across the curve, with the shorter maturities still leading:

  • 2-year: 4.287% (-2.0bp)
  • 5-year: 4.497% (-0.7bp)
  • 10-year: 4.958% (-1.1bp)
  • 20-year: 5.624% (-0.5bp)
  • 30-year: 5.704% (-0.5bp)
  • 50-year: 5.275% (-0.5bp)

Nothing has fixed, so these remain estimates: on live pricing a round striking now would come in near 6.011% on the 10-year (+1.1bp against yesterday's lunchtime round), 5.517% on the 5-year (+0.7bp) and 5.240% on the 2-year (+0.0bp) — the 2-year now level with where it fixed yesterday. The figures have barely moved since 10:15. The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — is 4.101%, -1.4bp on the day, with Bank Rate at 3.75% and the next move markets expect still a rise in Nov 2026.

WHAT TO DO ABOUT A DRAWDOWN TODAY

Treasurer's read: if you were waiting on this morning's rate to decide, the decision has effectively been made for you — there is nothing to transact against, and the realistic options are the lunchtime round, which strikes at about 12:25, or tomorrow morning. On the numbers that is not a painful place to be: borrowing costs have eased all morning and a round striking now would be little more than a basis point above yesterday lunchtime, with the 2-year level.

Two things to keep in view for the lunchtime round. NIESR publishes its monthly growth tracker at 12:00, shortly before the round strikes. And US producer prices at 13:30 land after it — so they bear on tomorrow morning's round, not today's.

We will publish the morning rates as soon as they appear, however late, and say plainly if the round turns out not to have been held at all.

THE MORNING’S RISE HAS UNWOUND

The 08:15 edition reported gilts higher at every maturity after the growth figures. That has gone into reverse in the hour since, and then some — UK government bond yields are now below last night's close almost across the curve:

  • 2-year: 4.295% (-1.2bp)
  • 5-year: 4.504% (+0.0bp)
  • 10-year: 4.96% (-0.8bp)
  • 20-year: 5.627% (-0.3bp)
  • 30-year: 5.705% (-0.4bp)
  • 50-year: 5.275% (-0.5bp)

The estimate for the round striking now has come down with them — 1.3bp on the 10-year and 1.4bp on the 2-year since the open. The shorter maturities are leading the fall.

AND THE BANK RATE VIEW HAS SOFTENED, NOT FIRMED

The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — is 4.105%, -1.0bp on the day, having been only 0.4bp lower at the open. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the next move markets expect remains a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: this is the opposite of what a growth beat normally does, and the shape of the move is the clue — the front of the curve is leading it, which is where Bank Rate expectations live. The reading that fits is that markets have looked past the headline to the weak production, construction and trade detail underneath it, and concluded the economy is not running hot enough to change the Bank's path. That is interpretation, not an observed fact, and a single morning is thin evidence.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE ROUND STRIKING NOW

Against yesterday's lunchtime round (notice 310/26, 10-year maturity rate 6.00%), the round striking now would come in +1.4bp dearer on the 10-year, +1.4bp on the 5-year and +0.8bp on the 2-year. Only becomes a rate at about 09:15, and the confirmed figures publish by around 09:30.

Treasurer's read: the day-ahead warned that this morning's estimate was stale and that a growth beat argued for a dearer round. Half of that has held — the round does still look dearer than yesterday lunchtime — but the margin has halved since the open and is now inside a basis and a half. For most drawdowns that is noise rather than a reason to wait; if you were holding off this morning on the strength of the growth number, the case for doing so is weaker now than it was at eight o'clock.

The morning round looks like being modestly dearer than yesterday's lunchtime one, not materially so, and the gap is worth about a basis point of hesitation rather than a change of plan.

THE GROWTH FIGURES: SLOWER ON THE QUARTER, BETTER ON THE MONTH

Two readings of the same release, and both are true. On the quarter, growth slowed — 0.4% in the preliminary estimate, exactly as forecast, down from 0.6% in the quarter before. That is the reading the morning's press has led with. On the month, though, the economy did better than anyone expected:

  • Monthly growth: 0.3% (forecast 0%, previously 0%, revised to 0.1%)
  • Quarterly, preliminary: 0.4% (forecast 0.4%, previously 0.6%)
  • Annual, preliminary: 1.2% (forecast 1.1%, previously 0.9%)
  • Business investment, quarterly: 1.7% (forecast -0.5%, previously 0.9%)

Business investment is the eye-catching one: a rise of 1.7% against a forecast fall of -0.5%.

The production side of the economy tells the opposite story, and it is worth seeing before anyone calls this a strong release:

  • Manufacturing output, monthly: -0.5% (forecast -0.2%, previously -0.2%, revised to 0.1%)
  • Industrial output, monthly: -0.2% (forecast 0.1%, previously -0.7%, revised to -0.5%)
  • Construction orders, annual: -18.1% (forecast 11.8%, previously -11.9%)
  • Goods trade balance: £-23.01B (forecast £-20.5B, previously £-21.08B, revised to £-18.66B)

Treasurer's read: the growth came from the services side of the economy, not from factories, building sites or exports. For borrowing costs the headline is what counts in the first hour — an economy growing faster than expected reduces the case for the Bank of England cutting, and rates that markets expect to stay higher for longer feed straight into the price of PWLB borrowing. The weak industrial detail argues the other way, but it usually takes longer to be priced.

WHY THESE ESTIMATES DO NOT YET TELL YOU WHERE THE ROUND LANDS

This is the part that separates today from yesterday. Yesterday's two rounds were both struck before the day's big release. Today the release came first — published at 07:00, with the morning round striking at about 09:00–09:15.

Everything in the panels above was measured at last night's close, at 17:59. That means the estimates you can see are, quite literally, yesterday's answer to a question that changed at seven o'clock this morning. Nothing has fixed today, and no live market reading exists until the 08:00 open.

For the record, where things stood at the close, against yesterday's lunchtime round (notice 310/26, 10-year maturity rate 6.00%):

  • 2-year maturity: 5.260% (+2.0bp)
  • 5-year maturity: 5.524% (+1.4bp)
  • 10-year maturity: 6.022% (+2.2bp)
  • 20-year maturity: 6.565% (+2.5bp)

UK government bonds (gilts — the bonds PWLB rates are built on) closed yesterday with the 10-year at 4.968% (+0.7bp) and the 2-year at 4.307% (+0.9bp) against Tuesday's close. The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — sat at 4.115%. Bank Rate itself is 3.75%, with the next move markets expect being a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: if you are drawing down today, the honest position is that the morning round is less predictable than usual and the estimate on the page is stale by one news cycle. The 08:15 and 09:15 editions will carry live readings. If the certainty matters more than the timing, the lunchtime round gives you a second look with the reaction fully visible.

THE REST OF TODAY — AND WHICH ROUND IT REACHES

Still to come today:

  • 12:00 — NIESR monthly growth tracker (forecast 0.4%, previously 0.4%). Low impact, but it lands between the two rounds.
  • 13:30 — US producer prices, monthly (forecast 0.2%, previously -0.3%). High impact.

The timing rule matters again here, in the other direction. The morning round strikes at about 09:00–09:15 and the lunchtime round at about 12:25–12:30. A 13:30 release therefore reaches neither of today's rounds — it bears on tomorrow morning's. Anyone borrowing today can disregard it; anyone borrowing tomorrow cannot.

THE WEEK AHEAD

Next week carries the two releases most likely to move UK borrowing costs this month:

  • Tue 18 Aug, 07:00 — unemployment rate (forecast 4.9%, previously 4.9%)
  • Wed 19 Aug, 07:00 — UK inflation (forecast 3.0%, previously 2.6%)
  • Fri 21 Aug, 07:00 — retail sales, monthly (forecast -0.6%, previously 1%)

Treasurer's read: the inflation figure is the one to diarise. Markets expect it to jump from 2.6% to 3.0% — and today's growth beat, if it holds up, makes that combination harder for the Bank of England to look through. Both releases land at 07:00, before that day's morning round, exactly as today's did.
