TWO ROUNDS, BOTH CHEAPER — AND BOTH BEFORE THE US FIGURES

Two rounds struck today and both came in cheaper than yesterday. The morning round (notice 309/26) set the 10-year maturity rate at 6.02%, 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round. The lunchtime round (notice 310/26) took it to 6.00% — and it struck at 12:04, earlier than the usual 12:25–12:30 window. Our 12:15 edition wrote about that round as still to come; it had in fact already been struck, and we said so in the 12:52 edition.

The practical consequence was the good kind: both of today's rounds were priced before the US inflation figures at 13:30. A treasurer who drew down at either round took the rate without carrying the risk of that release.

Treasurer's read: the cheapest borrowing of the day was available before lunch, and it has not been available since. That is the second day running the morning half of the day has been the better half.

US INFLATION: EXACTLY AS FORECAST

All four US inflation measures landed exactly on forecast — an unusually clean result:

  • Headline, year on year: 3.4% (forecast 3.4%, previously 3.5%)
  • Core, year on year: 2.5% (forecast 2.5%, previously 2.6%)
  • Headline, month on month: 0.1% (forecast 0.1%, previously -0.4%)
  • Core, month on month: 0.2% (forecast 0.2%, previously 0%)

Both annual measures eased. UK government bond yields took a little more off the day in the ninety minutes that followed, and our estimate for the next PWLB round fell with them. That was the low-water mark.

THEN THE AFTERNOON TURNED

From about a quarter past two the move went into reverse, and by the close it had more than undone the morning. Yields on UK government bonds (gilts — the bonds PWLB rates are built on) finished higher on the day almost across the board, measured against last night's close:

  • 2-year: 4.306% (+0.8bp)
  • 5-year: 4.503% (-0.1bp)
  • 10-year: 4.969% (+0.7bp)
  • 20-year: 5.629% (+1.5bp)
  • 30-year: 5.708% (+1.1bp)
  • 50-year: 5.28% (+1.5bp)

The likeliest candidate remains the one this afternoon's edition named: a Gulf oil spill reported as the worst in years, with the Strait of Hormuz stand-off running alongside it. Yahoo Finance UK reported at 16:45 that UK shares fell on mixed US–Iran headlines. Higher oil feeds through to inflation expectations, and inflation expectations feed through to the price of long-dated government borrowing — which is where the biggest moves were.

The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — ended at 4.11%, +1.5bp on the day. Bank Rate itself is 3.75%, and the next move markets expect is a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: a day that opened as a cheap window closed as a slightly dearer one. Nothing in it changes the medium-term picture; it is a reminder that the discount on offer in the morning is not a floor to wait below.

TOMORROW: GDP LANDS BEFORE THE ROUND STRIKES

UK GDP is published at 07:00 tomorrow — the monthly figure, the preliminary quarterly figure and the preliminary annual figure, all together. Forecasts:

  • Monthly: forecast 0% (previously 0.1%)
  • Quarterly, preliminary: forecast 0.4% (previously 0.6%)
  • Annual, preliminary: forecast 1.1% (previously 0.9%)

The timing is the point. Today's two rounds were both struck before the day's big release. Tomorrow the release comes first: 07:00 publication, and the morning round strikes at about 09:00–09:15. Whatever the figure does to the market in those two hours will be in the rate the morning round sets.

The same Gulf disruption that drove this afternoon reaches tomorrow's figure from the other direction. Yahoo Finance UK carried a warning at 16:32 that the UK economy may grow by only 0.3% next year if Middle East disruption goes on — a forecast, not a figure, but it frames what a weak GDP number would be taken to mean.

Treasurer's read: if you have a drawdown pencilled in for tomorrow morning, this is the one morning this week where the 09:15 rate is not knowable from tonight's close. Weaker growth would ordinarily pull rate expectations down and the round with them; stronger growth the other way. If certainty matters more to you than a basis point or two, the lunchtime round gives you a second look with the figure already digested.

Nothing has fixed yet for tomorrow. On tonight's close the estimates stand at 5.259% for 2-year maturity, 5.523% for 5-year, 6.023% for 10-year and 6.564% for 20-year — each of them a guide to where a round would land if markets held from here, not a rate.

Against last night's close: 2-year 4.282% (−1.5bp), 5-year 4.491% (−1.4bp), 10-year 4.953% (−0.9bp), 20-year 5.611% (−0.3bp), 30-year 5.695% (−0.2bp), 50-year 5.263% (−0.2bp).

Today, as struck

Two rounds, both behind us. Notice 309/26 at 09:07 put the 10-year maturity rate at 6.02%; notice 310/26 at 12:04 took it to 6.00%, with 2-year 5.24%, 5-year 5.51%, 20-year 6.54%, 25-year 6.62% and 50-year 6.42%. Tomorrow is a UK morning

Worth remembering how thin the recent run has been: the economy grew 0.1% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and showed no growth in January. A soft print pulls the front end down; a firm one, against an oil story that is already pushing the other way, does not.

What actually printed

Headline inflation 3.4% year-on-year, from 3.5%. Core 2.5%, from 2.6%. Monthly headline 0.1%, after last month's −0.4%. Monthly core 0.2%, after 0%. Early reporting attributes the easing largely to food costs cooling.

Both annual measures fell and both monthly measures landed on the forecast. It is about as uneventful as a four-print release gets.

Where the curve sits now

Against last night's close: 2-year 4.272% (−2.5bp), 5-year 4.485% (−2.0bp), 10-year 4.940% (−2.2bp), 20-year 5.600% (−1.4bp), 30-year 5.678% (−1.9bp), 50-year 5.251% (−1.4bp).

The shape matters more than the size. Before the print the belly was leading and the front end was flat on the day; afterwards the 2-year has moved twice as far as the 20-year. That is a market unwinding a hedge against an upside surprise, not one changing its view on where rates settle.

Tomorrow morning

On the current curve the round striking tomorrow morning would come in near 5.994% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.505% at 5 years, 5.226% at 2 years and 6.535% at 20 years — a shade under where today's lunchtime round struck.

The unresolved risk is the one that has run all week and is not American. Iran maintains there are no ceasefire discussions, the Panama Canal is charging a record $1m a crossing with Hormuz closed, and UK petrol is at its highest since the conflict began — against which OPEC has now cut its demand growth forecast for a fourth month. Gilts have priced none of it either way.

⚠ A correction to this lunchtime's call. The round struck at 12:04, not in the 12:25 to 12:30 window it normally does. Our 12:15 edition said nothing had fixed yet and described the round as striking in the next few minutes; in fact it had already struck eleven minutes earlier and had not yet been published. Anyone who read that as time still available to act did not have it. The rates above are as struck.
i This round priced before the US inflation figures, as expected — with more margin than anyone planned. It struck at 12:04, an hour and a half ahead of the 13:30 release rather than the hour we set out this morning. Whatever prints at 13:30 now shapes tomorrow morning's round.

Notice 310/26 fixes the 10-year maturity rate at 6.00%, 2bp below this morning's round and 7bp below yesterday's lunchtime fixing. Across the maturity curve: 2-year 5.24%, 5-year 5.51%, 20-year 6.54%, 25-year 6.62%, 50-year 6.42% — 2 to 3bp lower than notice 309/26 at every point, with the belly and the long end giving up 3bp and the 10-year and 2-year 2bp.

On annuity terms the 10-year fixed at 5.57% and on EIP at 5.54%.

Where the day has moved

This morning's notice 309/26 struck the 10-year at 6.02%, itself 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round. Today's lunchtime fixing takes another 2bp off, leaving the 10-year 7bp below yesterday lunchtime and 9bp below yesterday morning. Two consecutive days of the oil scare unwinding have been worth close to a tenth of a point at ten years.

What the next round looks like

Against the new base the curve is now flat: on current gilt levels the next round would come in within a fraction of a basis point of today's lunchtime rates at every maturity. The market has stopped moving, which is what it does in the last half hour before a release it cannot call.

Gilts sit at 4.946% on the 10-year (−1.5bp on last night's close), 4.490% at 5 years and 4.284% at 2 years.

13:30

Four US inflation prints land together: headline expected at 3.4% year-on-year from 3.5%, core at 2.5% from 2.6%, headline monthly at 0.1% after last month's −0.4%, core monthly at 0.2% from 0%. The monthly headline is the swing figure — half a point of movement in a single month — and the geopolitical news through the morning has been oil-supportive rather than disinflationary.

Both of today's rounds are now behind us. The next fixing to carry the answer is tomorrow morning's.

i Part of the morning's improvement has already gone. An hour ago the same estimate stood about 3.2bp below the morning fix; it is now nearer 2.5bp. The rally into the print is being trimmed rather than extended, which is what usually happens as a release gets close and positions get squared.
⚠ The news flow is pulling the other way. Iran is reported as maintaining there are no discussions over a ceasefire extension because the pact no longer exists; the Panama Canal is charging ships a record $1m to cross with Hormuz closed; and the RAC says UK petrol has reached its highest since the war began. None of that has moved gilts yet. All of it is inflationary if it persists, and it is the risk to holding out for a better round later in the week.

Nothing has fixed yet. The round striking in the next few minutes would come in near 5.995% on the 10-year maturity rate — about 2.5bp below notice 309/26, which struck at 6.02% this morning. At 5 years it would come in near 5.513%, at 2 years near 5.235%, at 20 years near 6.542% and at 50 years near 6.433%.

This is the last round of the day that strikes before the US inflation figures at 13:30. Whatever prints then shapes tomorrow morning's round, not this one.

Against this morning

Notice 309/26 struck at 09:07 with the 10-year maturity rate at 6.02%, 2-year 5.26%, 5-year 5.54%, 20-year 6.57%, 25-year 6.65% and 50-year 6.45% — 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round.

On the current curve the round striking now would come in between roughly 1.7 and 2.8bp below that across the maturities, with the 20-year giving up most and the 50-year least.

The gilt market behind it

Against last night's close the 2-year gilt stands at 4.284% (−1.3bp), the 5-year 4.488% (−1.7bp), the 10-year 4.944% (−1.7bp), the 20-year 5.605% (−0.9bp), the 30-year 5.682% (−1.5bp) and the 50-year 5.253% (−1.2bp). One-year SONIA is 0.3bp lower on the day, having been 0.8bp lower an hour ago.

What lands at 13:30

Four US inflation prints together: headline expected at 3.4% year-on-year from 3.5%, core at 2.5% from 2.6%, the headline monthly figure at 0.1% after last month's −0.4%, and core monthly at 0.2% from 0%.

The monthly headline is the one to watch. A move from −0.4% to +0.1% is a swing of half a point in a single month, and the market's tolerance for an upside surprise looks thin given where the geopolitical news has gone this morning.

i Timing, not price, is today's decision. A 3bp improvement on a £30m draw is worth roughly £9,000 a year — real, but not on its own a reason to move. What makes the lunchtime round distinctive is that it is struck before the US inflation print rather than after it. Anything from tomorrow morning onwards carries the answer.
⚠ The front end has changed its mind. One-year SONIA was 0.5bp higher on the day at 10:15 and is now 0.8bp lower — a 1.3bp swing inside an hour. Short-dated expectations are doing more of the moving than the long end, which is why the 2-year implied is down 3.8bp against the 50-year's 2.2bp.

The curve has turned since the morning fix. Gilts have rallied about 2.5bp across the front and belly in the last hour, and on that basis the lunchtime round would come in near 5.988% on the 10-year — roughly 3bp below notice 309/26, which struck at 6.02% this morning. At 10:15 the same estimate stood about 1bp below the fix; the move has trebled since.

Nothing has been released to cause it. This is positioning ahead of the US inflation figures at 13:30, and it is showing up everywhere — gold near two-month highs, silver bid, European equities flat. The lunchtime round strikes around 12:25, an hour before that print, so it remains the last round of the day that prices without the answer in it.

Where the morning ended

Notice 309/26 struck at 09:07: 10-year maturity 6.02%, 2-year 5.26%, 5-year 5.54%, 20-year 6.57%, 25-year 6.65%, 50-year 6.45%. That was 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round and 7bp below yesterday morning's, with the oil scare of the last two days still unwound.

What has moved since

Against last night's close the 2-year gilt is at 4.272% (−2.5bp), the 5-year 4.480% (−2.5bp), the 10-year 4.938% (−2.4bp), the 20-year 5.601% (−1.3bp) and the 30-year 5.679% (−1.8bp). An hour ago the 20-year was the one point on the curve trading higher on the day; it is no longer.

On that curve the next round would come in near 5.988% at 10 years, 5.506% at 5 years, 5.222% at 2 years and 6.538% at 20 years — between 2 and 4bp below where this morning struck, with the shorter maturities giving up the most.

The rest of the day

US inflation lands at 13:30: headline expected at 3.4% year-on-year from 3.5%, core at 2.5% from 2.6%, and the headline monthly figure expected to turn positive at 0.1% after last month's −0.4%. Four high-impact prints in one release.

The lunchtime round strikes before it. The next round to carry the answer is tomorrow morning's.

FIXING REPORT — notice 309/26 fixes the 10-year maturity rate at 6.02%, 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round and 7bp below yesterday morning's, as the oil scare stays unwound

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.02%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.020% (0.0bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.537% (-0.3bp)1y SONIA swap4.11% (+1.0bp)

Notice 309/26 fixes the 10-year standard rate at 6.02%, down 5bp on yesterday's lunchtime round and 7bp below yesterday morning's 6.09%. The 5-year fixes at 5.54%. Every maturity is cheaper: 4bp at the short and long ends, 5bp through the middle.

More

Maturity loans: 5.26% at 2 years, 5.54% at 5, 6.02% at 10, 6.57% at 20, 6.65% at 25, 6.45% at 50. Annuity and EIP moved 3 to 5bp lower across the board.

For a borrower, £10m over ten years at this morning's rate costs about £5,000 a year less than at yesterday lunchtime and about £7,000 a year less than at yesterday morning — roughly £70,000 over the life of the loan.

What moved it: Tuesday's oil-driven 10bp scare unwinding and staying unwound. Gilts are 0.6 to 1.4bp higher on the day, which took the edge off the long end without undoing the move. The Middle East risk has not gone away — oil rose again this morning on the fresh Iran impasse — but the gilt market has stopped paying for the headline, and that is a decision it could reverse quickly.

The lunchtime round strikes about 12:25 and is currently tracking level with this morning's. US inflation at 13:30 lands after both of today's rounds, so it shapes tomorrow morning's fixing; UK GDP follows at 07:00 tomorrow.

What fixed

On maturity loans the standard rates are 5.26% at 2 years, 5.54% at 5, 6.02% at 10, 6.57% at 20, 6.65% at 25 and 6.45% at 50. Annuity and EIP loans moved the same way, 3 to 5bp lower across the board. The full table is below.

What moved it

Yesterday’s oil-driven scare unwinding, and staying unwound. The 10bp jump that hit Tuesday’s morning round faded by lunchtime and gilts closed below where they started; nothing overnight pulled them back. Gilts are 0.6 to 1.4bp higher on the day — a drift that took the edge off the long end without undoing the move. Treasurer’s read: the Middle East risk that drove Tuesday has not gone away, and oil rose again this morning on the fresh Iran impasse. What has changed is that the gilt market has stopped paying for the headline. That is a decision the market could reverse quickly.

The lunchtime round, and what comes after

The next round strikes about 12:25 and is currently tracking level with this morning’s — 6.020% at 10 years on the curve as it stands, against the 6.02% just fixed. An index-linked 2035 gilt auction lands at 10:00 in between. US inflation at 13:30 — 3.4% expected on the year against 3.5%, core 2.5% against 2.6% — comes after both of today’s rounds, so it bears on tomorrow morning’s fixing rather than anything striking today. UK GDP follows at 07:00 tomorrow.

The morning round is striking about now and nothing has fixed yet. On the 09:18 curve it would come in near 6.026% at 10 years — 4.4bp below yesterday's lunchtime fixing and 6.4bp below yesterday morning's 6.09% — and 5.544% at 5 years.

More

The discount is eroding through the morning. On last night's close the round tracked 5.3bp below yesterday's lunchtime fixing; at the open 4.6bp; now 4.4bp. A borrower at ten years and in still has most of what was on the table at 07:15; a borrower at twenty has lost half of it.

At 4.4bp on the 10-year the saving against yesterday lunchtime is worth roughly £4,400 a year on £10m over ten years; against yesterday morning, about £6,400.

Drift rather than repricing — a fraction of yesterday's 10bp scare, one-directional since the open, with oil climbing on the fresh Iran impasse. Notice expected about 09:30; we report it on publication rather than waiting for the next slot.

Where the round is striking

Every maturity is still below yesterday’s lunchtime fixing, but not by the same margin. The 5-year at 5.544% is 4.6bp below and remains the largest expected move; the 10-year at 6.026% is 4.4bp below; the 2-year and 1-year about 3.6bp below. The long end has given back most of its advantage — the 20-year at 6.588% is only 2.2bp below, against 3.8bp on last night’s close, and the 50-year at 6.461% 2.9bp below. A borrower at ten years and in is getting most of what was on the table at 07:15; a borrower at twenty has watched half of it go.

What is moving it

Nothing dramatic, and nothing scheduled. Gilts are 0.8 to 1.6bp higher across the curve, with the 20-year weakest — the 20-year benchmark at 5.631%, up 1.6bp. The 1-year SONIA swap is 1.2bp firmer at 4.11%. Oil has been climbing since the Iran talks hit a fresh impasse overnight, and the long end is where that shows up first. Treasurer’s read: this is drift, not repricing — the size of the move is a fraction of yesterday’s 10bp scare, and it has been one-directional since the open rather than jumping on any single headline.

After this round

The notice should publish about 09:30; we will report it as soon as it lands rather than waiting for the next slot. The lunchtime round strikes about 12:25, with an index-linked 2035 gilt auction at 10:00 in between. US inflation at 13:30 — 3.4% expected on the year against 3.5% — lands after both of today’s rounds and therefore bears on tomorrow morning’s fixing, not on anything striking today.

Overnight

Quiet, and quiet is the story. Last night’s wrap put this morning’s round 5.4bp below yesterday’s lunchtime fixing; it now sits at 5.3bp below, so the overnight session moved the estimate by about a tenth of a basis point. Gilts closed 2 to 3bp lower right across the curve — the 10-year benchmark at 4.962%, down 2.6bp — and the 1-year SONIA swap eased 1.9bp to 4.10%. The Middle East has not gone quiet: Iran and the United States clashed again over control of the Strait of Hormuz and equities were called lower on it. Treasurer’s read: the oil-risk premium that added 10bp to yesterday’s morning fixing is no longer transmitting into gilt yields — the market has stopped paying for the headline. That is worth watching rather than trusting; the same story reprices fast when a tanker is actually stopped.

Today's shape

Two rounds and one release, in that order. The morning fixing strikes about 09:15 and the lunchtime round about 12:25 — until the first of those, yesterday’s notice 308/26 rates stand. In between, an index-linked 2035 gilt auction at 10:00, low impact but the long end can twitch around one. On last night’s curve the 20-year would come in near 6.572% and the 50-year near 6.453%, each about 4bp below yesterday. Then US inflation at 13:30: 3.4% expected on the year against 3.5%, core 2.5% against 2.6%. It lands an hour after the lunchtime round has struck, so it shapes tomorrow morning’s fixing rather than anything priced today.

The week's real tests

Both arrive within eighteen hours. US inflation today is the one the oil story runs into, and the risk is two-sided: the Federal Reserve’s Susan Collins said overnight she would back a September rate rise if the data pointed that way, which is not the direction most had been leaning. Germany’s July inflation was confirmed accelerating, with core prices steadier. UK GDP tomorrow at 07:00 is forecast at +0.4% on the quarter against +0.6%, flat on the month against +0.1%, and +1.1% on the year against +0.9%. Treasurer’s read: a soft UK print pulls the front end down and would make tomorrow’s round cheaper again; a hot US print this afternoon does the opposite to the long end first. The Bank of England path is unchanged — a hold in September, the first rise priced for November, taking Bank Rate to 4.00%.

In local government

Andy Burnham said he wants to go “further” on business rates at the budget, and the City is trading talk of an early general election. Treasurer’s read: neither moves a gilt this week, but both sit on the revenue side of the same balance sheet as the borrowing decisions above — a business rates reform that shifts the local share changes what a council can afford to service, and an election changes the settlement timetable that most medium-term plans assume.

Tuesday 11 August 2026

17:15STORYend of day

A 10bp scare that unwound by lunchtime — the day ends with gilts below where it started, and tomorrow's round estimated 5.4bp under today's

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.07%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.016% (−5.4bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.535% (−5.5bp)1y SONIA swap4.099% (−1.8bp)

The day in one line. Borrowing costs rose sharply first thing on Middle East headlines, gave it all back by lunchtime, and drifted lower through the afternoon. Anyone who borrowed at the morning round paid about 10bp more than anyone who waited until the lunchtime one.

More

The two fixings. The morning round (notice 307/26) came in at 6.09% on the 10-year maturity rate, 10bp above Monday. The lunchtime round (308/26) landed at 6.07%. Both were struck while the Hormuz story was still moving, and both look expensive against where the market closed.

Where gilts finished. Yields are 2.2 to 2.7bp below Monday's close right across the curve — 10-year at 4.961%, 5-year at 4.506%, 30-year at 5.699%. That is the whole morning move reversed and a little more. The 1-year SONIA swap ended at 4.099%, 1.8bp lower.

What that means for tomorrow. On the closing levels, tomorrow morning's round would come in around 6.016% on the 10-year — 5.4bp below today's lunchtime fixing. The 5-year would be near 5.535%, also about 5.5bp lower. The 50-year would be near 6.454%. These are estimates from where the market closed, not a forecast of what tomorrow brings; anything overnight moves them.

If you are drawing down this week. Nothing in today's session changed the medium-term picture — market pricing still has the next Bank Rate move as a rise to 4.00% in November, not a cut. Today's fall is a retracement of a one-day scare, not a trend. The practical point is narrower: the morning and lunchtime rounds were 2bp apart today and 10bp apart from Monday's, so on days when a geopolitical story is live, which round you use is worth a moment's thought.

Thursday matters. UK GDP for the month lands at 07:00 on Thursday, with the market looking for −0.1% after +0.1%. A negative print would be the second weak month in a row and would sit awkwardly with pricing that still expects a hike. It is the first thing this week with the weight to move the long end on its own.

Council watch. The platform now carries a live calendar of every finance meeting on ModernGov with published papers. Fifteen fall in the next four weeks. Two of them — City of Lincoln and North Yorkshire, both on 18 August — have had their treasury papers read and written up.

15:25PULSEupdate

US housing data landed on forecast and changed nothing — gilts drift lower still, tomorrow's round now estimated 6.6bp below today's lunchtime fixing

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.07%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.004% (−6.6bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.521% (−6.9bp)1y SONIA swap4.092% (−2.6bp)

US Existing Home Sales printed at 4.06m against a 4.05m forecast — as close to in line as these things come, and gilts did not react to it.

More

The afternoon drift has continued regardless. Gilts are now 3.6 to 4.3bp below yesterday's close across the curve, and on current levels tomorrow morning's round would come in near 6.004% on the 10-year maturity rate — 6.6bp below today's lunchtime fixing and 8.6bp below this morning's. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.092%, 2.6bp under yesterday's close.

Nothing further is scheduled today. The overnight session and the Hormuz talks decide where tomorrow's round opens.

14:30STORYupdate

EARLY AFTERNOON — the day has fully turned: tomorrow morning's round now estimated near 6.014%, 7.6bp below this morning's fixing

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.07%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.014% (−5.6bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.526% (−6.4bp)1y SONIA swap4.095% (−2.3bp)

The day has fully turned. Gilts are below yesterday's close at every tenor — the 2-year at −3.5bp and the 10-year at −2.8bp, having been +7.2bp and +5.9bp when this morning's round struck. On current levels tomorrow morning's round would come in near 6.014% on the 10-year maturity rate: 5.6bp below today's lunchtime fixing and 7.6bp below this morning's.

More

Oil has given up its gains on optimism about the US–Iran talks over the Strait of Hormuz, though both sides set fresh conditions this afternoon. The premium that arrived overnight has more than gone.

Both of today's rounds are behind us. The morning struck at 09:08, the lunchtime round at 12:08. US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 and anything the Hormuz talks produce this evening reach the market after both — so they shape tomorrow's round, not today's.

The clearest read is the swap: the 1-year SONIA rate is 4.095%, now 2.3bp *below* yesterday's close against 3.4bp above it at the strike. A swing of nearly 6bp in what markets expect of the Bank of England, inside six hours, on no UK data at all. The Bank Rate path itself is unchanged — September hold, first 25bp step in November.

What today demonstrated: an 8bp round trip in the ten-year rate driven entirely by headlines about a waterway. Fixings are struck at a moment rather than averaged, so a council drawing at 09:08 paid about 8bp more than one drawing tomorrow on current levels. The Hormuz question is unresolved, so the same mechanism can run either way tomorrow.

i Nothing further fixes today. Both of today's rounds are done — 307/26 this morning at 6.09%, 308/26 at lunchtime at 6.07% on the 10-year maturity rate. Everything from here, including the 15:00 US release, bears on tomorrow's morning round, which currently estimates near 6.014%.
✓ The reversal has kept running. Gilts are now 2.7 to 3.6bp below yesterday's close across the curve, having been up to 7.2bp above it this morning. Oil has erased its gains as US–Iran talks on the Strait of Hormuz continue.

The day has fully turned. Gilts are below yesterday's close at every tenor — the 2-year at −3.5bp and the 10-year at −2.8bp, having been +7.2bp and +5.9bp when this morning's round struck. On current levels tomorrow morning's round would come in near 6.014% on the 10-year maturity rate: 5.6bp below today's lunchtime fixing and 7.6bp below this morning's.

The cause is the same one that drove the morning's rise, running the other way. Oil has given up its gains on optimism about the US–Iran talks over the Strait of Hormuz, though both sides set fresh conditions this afternoon. The risk premium that arrived overnight has now more than gone.

Both of today's rounds are behind us — this is about tomorrow

Worth being explicit, because it is the single most common timing error a borrower makes. The morning round struck at 09:08 and the lunchtime round at 12:08. Nothing else fixes today. US Existing Home Sales at 15:00, and anything the Hormuz talks produce this evening, reach the market well after both — so they shape tomorrow's morning round, not today's.

For a council with a drawdown scheduled this week, that is the practical frame: today's decision is made, and the live question is whether tomorrow morning is better than today was. On levels as they stand it would be, by about 7.6bp against this morning's fixing — roughly £7,600 a year on £10m over ten years.

These are estimates on live gilts and the overnight session has to happen first. Nothing is fixed until the notice publishes.

The rate-path repricing has fully unwound

The clearest read is in the swap rather than the gilt. The 1-year SONIA rate — what markets expect Bank Rate to average over the next year — is at 4.095%, now 2.3bp below yesterday's close. At the morning strike it was 3.4bp above. That is a swing of nearly 6bp in what the market expects of the Bank of England, inside six hours, on no UK data whatsoever.

The Bank Rate path itself has not moved: no change is still priced for the September meeting, with the first 25bp step to 4.00% in November. What moved was the compensation demanded to hold gilts against that path — up sharply this morning on the energy-inflation scare, and back out again this afternoon.

What today has actually demonstrated

An 8bp round trip in the ten-year PWLB rate, driven entirely by headlines about a waterway, with no economic release involved at any point. That is worth filing away for the autumn.

Two practical readings. First, headline-driven moves and data-driven moves behave differently: a premium priced for an event that has not happened can evaporate as fast as it arrived, where a repricing built on an inflation print generally does not. Second, the fixings are struck at a moment rather than averaged, so a borrower's cost depends on which side of a headline their round happened to fall. Today the morning round caught the top; a council drawing at 09:08 paid about 8bp more than one drawing tomorrow on current levels.

The Hormuz question is unresolved — both sides added conditions this afternoon — so the same mechanism can run in either direction tomorrow.

The day round-tripped, but the fixings did not

This is the part worth understanding, because it is where the cost sat.

Gilt yields have effectively returned to where they started. The 2-year is −0.3bp on yesterday's close and the 10-year +0.1bp — flat, after being +7.2bp and +5.9bp respectively when the morning round struck. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.111%, 0.6bp below yesterday's close, having been 3.4bp above it at nine o'clock. On the market's own reckoning, the oil-and-Hormuz risk premium that arrived overnight has gone.

But PWLB fixings are struck at a moment, not averaged across a day. The morning round struck at 09:08, near the top. The lunchtime round struck at 12:08 — before the last of the reversal came through, and forty-four minutes before the notice appeared. So both of today's fixings carry a premium the market had already begun to discard.

The practical consequence: a council that drew at either round today paid for an event that, by early afternoon, the market had stopped pricing.

This morning's round now looks like today's expensive one. Even so, the lunchtime round would still sit some 5bp above yesterday lunchtime's. Better than nine o'clock; not back to where the day started.

The lesson is about character, not size: a premium built on an event that has not happened can unwind as fast as it arrived. No data was involved at any point.

i This morning's round now looks like today's expensive one. If you drew at 09:08 you paid the top of the day so far. If your drawdown is still ahead of you, the lunchtime round is currently the better of the two.

The morning's move has gone. All of it, and a little more. The 2-year gilt was +7.2bp on yesterday's close when the morning round struck; it is now −0.6bp — below where it started the day. The 10-year has come from +5.9bp to +0.5bp.

Nothing has fixed yet. The lunchtime round is striking as this goes out and on gilts as they stand it would come in near 6.042% on the 10-year maturity rate, roughly 4.8bp below this morning's fixing of 6.09%. Every tenor is 4 to 6.5bp better, with the short end improving most.

What reversed

The oil-and-Hormuz premium that drove this morning's repricing has come out of the price. The read at 11:19 was that the market was pricing a Hormuz closure specifically rather than Middle East risk generally — and that is precisely what has unwound: reporting through the late morning has Middle East conflict fears easing, and the rate-expectations component has gone with it.

The clearest evidence is in the swap. The 1-year SONIA rate — what markets expect Bank Rate to average over the next year — is at 4.110%, now 0.8bp below yesterday's close. At the morning strike it was 3.4bp above. The entire inflation impulse that the morning fixing was built on has been priced back out inside three hours.

Note what did not reverse: the long end. The 20-year gilt is still +0.8bp and the 30-year +0.5bp, while the 2-year is negative. That is the shape of a rate-expectations move unwinding while term premium holds — consistent with the story being about the Bank Rate path rather than about gilt supply.

Even at these levels the lunchtime round would still sit some 5bp above yesterday's lunchtime fixing. The day is better than it was at nine o'clock; it is not yet back to where it started.

The treasurer's read

Labelled interpretation, not advice. The lesson of today is about the character of the move, not its size. A geopolitical risk premium arrived overnight, priced 10bp into the morning fixing, and came back out within three hours on nothing more than a change of tone in the reporting. No data was involved at any point.

For a borrower with discretion over timing, that argues for treating headline-driven moves differently from data-driven ones. A repricing built on an event that has not happened can unwind as fast as it arrived. A repricing built on an inflation print generally does not.

Nothing further is scheduled today that reaches a fixing. US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 lands after the lunchtime strike and bears on tomorrow's morning round.

The treasurer's read

Labelled interpretation, not advice. Three practical points.

First, if you drew this morning, you paid for a geopolitical repricing that had nothing to do with UK fundamentals. That is worth saying plainly, because it is the kind of move that reverses as readily as it arrives — if the Hormuz question resolves favourably, a good part of the last two sessions could come back.

Second, if you have a drawdown scheduled for this afternoon, the honest position is that the lunchtime round currently looks like a coin-flip against the morning one, with no data to move it either way. There is no edge in the timing today; there is only headline risk in both directions.

Third, and most usefully for anyone with a programme rather than a single draw: this is the second consecutive session where energy has driven the front of the gilt curve, and the market is not yet pricing an earlier Bank Rate rise — the September meeting is still priced for a hold, with the first 25bp step to 4.00% in November. What has moved is the compensation demanded for holding gilts, not the expected path itself. If oil stays where it is long enough to reach the inflation data, that distinction stops holding, and the repricing gets larger rather than smaller. That is the risk worth planning around, not today's ten basis points.

09:16ALERTupdate

AM FIXING CALL — nothing has fixed yet, but the round striking now would come in near 6.099% on the 10-year, 10.9bp above yesterday's lunchtime fixing, on oil-driven inflation fears

PWLB 10y — last fixed5.99%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.099% (+10.9bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.627% (+11.7bp)1y SONIA swap4.151% (+3.4bp)

Nothing has fixed yet. The morning round is striking as this goes out, and on gilts as they stand it would come in near 6.099% on the 10-year maturity rate — 10.9bp above yesterday's lunchtime fixing of 5.99%. Every tenor is 10–12bp dearer, the 5-year moving most at +11.7bp. On £10m over 10 years that is roughly £10,900 a year in extra interest. The actual lands about 09:30.

More

This is an oil story, not a UK data story. Brent is near $88 after a four-day climb and gold has reached a two-month high, as President Trump's new demands on Iran cloud the prospect of a deal reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The UK imports its energy, so a higher oil price feeds straight into the inflation path and therefore into what markets expect of Bank Rate. The front of the gilt curve is leading — 2-year +7.2bp against 10-year +5.9bp — which is the signature of a rate-expectations repricing rather than a supply one.

How it built. Yesterday's close +4.8bp, 07:20 +5.0bp, the gilt open +7.8bp, now +10.9bp. Asia added two-tenths of a basis point; the London open put on 2.8bp and the hour since another 3.1bp. The move is still running as the round strikes.

Nothing in the UK numbers explains it — the only overnight figure, the BRC retail sales monitor, came in at 1.0% against a 1.5% forecast, which pushes the other way. Both of today's rounds fall before the only scheduled release: US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 lands after the lunchtime strike and bears on tomorrow's morning fixing.

How the move built

The repricing did not arrive overnight. It came in three steps, and all of today's part of it has happened in London hours:

When10-year estimatevs last fixing
Yesterday, at the close6.038%+4.8bp
07:20, before the open6.040%+5.0bp
08:20, gilts open6.068%+7.8bp
09:16, now6.099%+10.9bp

Asia added almost nothing — two-tenths of a basis point between yesterday's close and 07:20. The London open put on 2.8bp and the hour since has added another 3.1bp. The move is still running as the round strikes.

What it costs, by tenor

Against yesterday's lunchtime fixing, on the maturity basis, per £10m drawn:

TenorLast fixedEstimate nowMovePer £10m/yr
5-year5.51%5.627%+11.7bp£11,700

Annuity and EIP move with it — the 10-year annuity rate would come in near 5.677% against 5.56% last fixed, and the 10-year EIP near 5.647% against 5.53%. These are estimates, and nothing is fixed until the notice is published.

Underneath: gilts and Bank Rate expectations

Gilt yields at 09:16, against yesterday's close — the short end leading, which is what a change in the expected Bank Rate path looks like:

  • 2-year 4.392%, +7.2bp
  • 5-year 4.593%, +6.1bp
  • 10-year 5.047%, +5.9bp
  • 20-year 5.694%, +5.9bp
  • 30-year 5.781%, +5.6bp

The 1-year SONIA swap — what markets expect the Bank of England's rate to average over the next year — is at 4.151%, 3.4bp above yesterday's close, and the 6-month forward is 2.0bp higher. Markets still price no change from the current 3.75% at the September meeting, with the first 25bp step to 4.00% in November and a second to 4.25% in February 2027. That path has not moved today — what has moved is the compensation being demanded to hold gilts at it.

The treasurer's read

Labelled interpretation, not advice. Two things a borrower can act on. First, if you were planning to draw this morning, the decision has effectively been made for you — the round is striking as you read this, and the level is about 11bp worse than the last one. Second, and more usefully: the lunchtime round strikes about 12:25, and there is no scheduled UK or US release between now and then. Anything further before that round comes from the oil price and the Hormuz headlines, not from data. If the Iran story quietens during the morning, some of this morning's 3.1bp could come back before 12:25; if it does not, the lunchtime round is likely to strike around this level or worse.

For anyone with a drawdown that can wait, the thing to weigh is that oil has now climbed four sessions running and the estimate has risen at every one of our passes since yesterday afternoon. That is a direction rather than a spike, and it will keep pushing the same way until the Hormuz question resolves one way or the other — which is a headline risk in both directions, not a one-way bet.

Elsewhere this morning

The Reserve Bank of Australia held its key rate, citing elevated inflation pressures — the same energy-driven story reaching a different central bank, and a reminder that this is not a UK-specific repricing. European equities opened flat to slightly higher. Gold's two-month high and the four-day gain in oil are the two prices carrying the Iran risk premium at the moment; both are worth watching through the morning as the better real-time guide to the lunchtime round than anything on the UK calendar, which is empty until tomorrow.

InterContinental Hotels reported slower revenue growth and attributed it to the Iran war — the first UK-listed earnings this week to name the conflict as a direct drag, and a small sign the conflict is reaching the real economy as well as the oil price.

DAY AHEAD — nothing fixed yet: on last night's close today's 09:15 round would come in about 5bp above yesterday's lunchtime fixing, 10-year estimated 6.040%

Gilts closed 6.5bp above Friday and nothing overnight has pulled them back. Nothing has fixed yet — yesterday's rates stand until 09:15. On last night's curve the morning round would come in near 6.040% at 10 years, 5.566% at 5 (the largest expected move), 6.587% at 20 and 6.460% at 50. The estimate re-anchors when gilts open at 08:00.

More

Overnight, two forces pulling opposite ways. Against higher rates: UK retail sales were soft, the BRC monitor at +1.0% year on year against 1.5% expected and 1.7% previously. For higher rates, and currently winning: a drone strike set fire to Libya's largest oil refinery, a second supply story on top of the Hormuz deadlock, with oil and gold near their highs and gold above $4,400. Australia's central bank held at 4.35% and said it had discussed a rise, not a cut.

Today is quiet, and both fixings come before the only scheduled release. The morning round strikes about 09:15 and the lunchtime round about 12:25; US existing home sales at 15:00 lands after both, so it bears on tomorrow rather than today. On last night's close the morning round would come in about 7bp above yesterday's 09:15 fixing — roughly £7,000 a year on £10m over ten years.

The week's real tests are still ahead: US inflation tomorrow 13:30 (3.4% expected, from 3.5%) and UK second-quarter GDP Thursday 07:00 (+0.4% on the quarter, from +0.6%). Bank of England path unchanged — September hold, first rise priced for November.

Overnight

Two things pulling in opposite directions, and the oil side is winning. Against higher rates: UK retail sales came in soft — the BRC monitor at +1.0% year on year against 1.5% expected and 1.7% previously, the weakest consumer read in some months. For higher rates: a drone strike set fire to Libya's largest oil refinery, adding a second supply story on top of the Hormuz deadlock; oil and gold are both near their highs, with gold above $4,400. Australia's central bank held at 4.35% but said it had discussed a rise, not a cut — a reminder that the global direction of travel is still upward.

Today's shape

A quiet diary. The morning fixing strikes about 09:15 and the lunchtime round about 12:25 — until then yesterday's rates stand. The only scheduled release of note is US existing home sales at 15:00 (4.04m expected, from 4.09m), which lands after both fixings and so shapes tomorrow rather than today. On last night's curve the 20-year would fix near 6.587% and the 50-year near 6.460%, each about 5bp up.

The week's real tests

Both still ahead. US inflation tomorrow at 13:30 — 3.4% expected against 3.5% — is the one the oil story runs into; markets are already positioning for it, which is part of why gold is bid. UK second-quarter GDP on Thursday at 07:00 is forecast at +0.4% on the quarter against +0.6%, with the monthly figure expected at −0.1%. A weak print there would pull against everything oil has done this week. The Bank of England path is unchanged: a hold in September, the first rise priced for November.

17:22STORYend of day

END OF DAY — this morning's 09:15 fixing was the day's cheapest window; the afternoon undid it and more. Tomorrow's round estimated at 6.038% on the 10-year

PWLB 10y — last fixed5.99%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.038% (+4.8bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.563% (+5.3bp)1y SONIA swap4.12% (+3.9bp)

Three moves. At 09:15, notice 305/26 took every maturity 1bp lower — the last of the discount from Friday's weak US jobs report, and the cheapest moment of the day at 5.97% on the 10-year. At 12:15, notice 306/26 came back 2bp (50-year 1bp), more than reversing it and leaving rates a basis point above Friday's close. Through the afternoon, with no third fixing, the selling continued: oil rose almost 2% as the Hormuz closure dragged on, US shares opened lower and Treasury yields rose.

More

Gilts closed 6.3bp above Friday on the 10-year and 6.6bp on the 5-year, the day's weakest point. On that curve tomorrow's 09:15 round prices at 6.038% for 10 years, 5.563% for 5 and 6.587% for 20 — some 4.7 to 5.3bp above today's lunchtime fixing, and back above 6%.

For a borrower, this morning's fixing and tomorrow's estimate are about 6.8bp apart: roughly £6,800 a year on £10m over ten years. Nothing is fixed until 09:15 and an overnight reversal in oil would take much of it back.

This week: US inflation Wednesday 13:30 (3.4% expected, from 3.5%) and UK second-quarter GDP Thursday 07:00 (+0.4% expected, from +0.6%; the monthly figure forecast at −0.1%). Either can move the fixings by more than today did. The Bank of England path is unchanged — a September hold, the first rise priced for November.

The day in three moves

09:15 — notice 305/26. Every maturity 1bp lower, the last of the discount from Friday's weak US jobs report. 12:15 — notice 306/26. All tenors 2bp higher (50-year 1bp), more than reversing the morning and leaving rates a basis point above Friday's close. Afternoon. No third fixing, but the selling continued: oil rose almost 2% as the Hormuz closure dragged on, US shares opened lower and Treasury yields rose. The 5-year was the day's weakest point.

Where that leaves tomorrow

On the closing curve, the 09:15 round prices at 6.038% for 10 years, 5.563% for 5 and 6.587% for 20 — each roughly 4.7 to 5.3bp above today's lunchtime fixing. The estimate barely moved after 15:20, so the move ran in the European afternoon rather than building through the US session. It re-anchors when gilts open at 08:00.

What to watch this week

Two set-pieces, both capable of moving the fixings by more than today did. US inflation, Wednesday 13:30 — 3.4% expected against 3.5% previously. UK second-quarter GDP, Thursday 07:00 — the preliminary quarterly reading is forecast at +0.4% against +0.6%, with the monthly figure expected at −0.1%. A soft GDP print would pull against the oil story rather than with it. What the market expects from the Bank of England is unchanged after all of this: a hold in September, the first rise priced for November.

The sell-off has accelerated through the afternoon. Oil is up almost 2% with the Hormuz stalemate unresolved, US shares opened lower and Treasury yields rose — and UK gilts have followed, now 5 to 6 basis points above Friday's close right across the curve. Tomorrow's 09:15 fixing is currently estimated at 6.034% for the 10-year, back above 6% and 4.4bp above today's lunchtime round.

What is driving it

One story, three transmissions. Oil rose almost 2% as the Gulf hardened its position on Hormuz, which lifts the inflation path; US Treasury yields rose with it; and the UK curve, which has tracked the oil story all day, took both cues. The 5-year gilt is the day's weakest point at +6.2bp, with the 10-year at +6.0bp and the 2-year +5.4bp — the belly of the curve leading, which is where a rate path gets repriced rather than a risk premium. One-year SONIA is 4.2bp higher on the day.

What it means for tomorrow

On these levels the morning round would print near 6.034% at 10 years, 5.559% at 5 and 6.578% at 20 — each about 4 to 5bp above today's lunchtime fixing. Two caveats worth holding onto. This is an estimate made seventeen hours before the strike, and an overnight reversal in oil would unwind much of it; the estimate re-anchors when the gilt market opens at 08:00. And nothing has actually fixed — today's rates stand until 09:15.

The week ahead

Neither of the week's set-pieces has landed yet. US inflation lands Wednesday at 13:30 — 3.4% expected, down from 3.5% — and UK second-quarter GDP on Thursday at 07:00, forecast at +0.4% against +0.6% previously. Either can move the fixings by more than everything that has happened today. What the market expects from the Bank of England is still a September hold with the first rise priced for November.

What moved it

Gilts sold off steadily through the morning as the Hormuz talks stayed stuck and oil held its gains. By lunchtime the 10-year gilt yield was 4.94%, up 1.5bp on Friday's close, and the 2-year was up 2.0bp — the front end took the larger hit, which is the market trimming its enthusiasm for near-term easing rather than repricing the long end. The PWLB fixing simply followed: it is set off the gilt curve at the moment it is struck, and the curve at 12:15 was higher than the curve at 09:15.

How our call did

The 12:19 estimate said this round would land 0.8 to 1.5bp above the morning fixing. It landed 2bp above — the direction was right and the size was about a basis point light. Across the five benchmark maturities the estimates were between 0.2 and 1.1bp below the printed rates, all in the same direction. Worth logging honestly: on a day when the market is moving one way all morning, our estimates lag the move slightly rather than overshooting it.

What happens next

That is both of today's fixings done — the next reset is tomorrow at 09:15, and it is currently priced flat to half a basis point above this afternoon's levels. There is no scheduled UK or US data left today, so anything that moves tomorrow morning's round will come from the oil story overnight. The week's real set-pieces are still ahead: US inflation on Wednesday at 13:30 (3.4% expected, down from 3.5%) and UK second-quarter GDP on Thursday at 07:00 (+0.4% expected, down from +0.6%). Either is capable of moving the fixings by more than today's 2bp. What the market expects from the Bank of England is unchanged: a hold in September, the first rise priced for November.
